title: Missouri Security Deposit Rules
bodyText: Missouri limits a security deposit to two months' rent and requires you to keep it in a federally insured bank, credit union or depository institution (any interest is yours). Within 30 days after the tenancy ends you must return the full deposit or give the tenant a written itemized list of damages with the balance; mailing to the tenant's last known address is enough. You may withhold only for unpaid rent, restoring the unit to its move-in condition beyond ordinary wear and tear, and actual damages from the tenant's failure to give proper notice to end the tenancy (after trying to reduce them). Before the move-out inspection, give the tenant reasonable written notice of its date and time; the tenant may attend. If you wrongfully withhold any part, the tenant recovers twice the amount wrongfully withheld. A pet deposit is not a security deposit under this law.

title: Security Deposit Cap
bodyText: You may not demand or receive a security deposit of more than two months' rent. The limit covers any deposit of money or property, however you label it, that secures the tenant's performance of the lease, so be careful about extra 'deposits' that push the total over two months' rent. A deposit labelled as a pet deposit does not count. Cities and counties may not impose a lower cap.

title: No Interest Owed on Deposits
bodyText: Missouri does not require you to pay the tenant interest on a security deposit. Any interest the deposit earns belongs to you.

title: Where to Hold the Deposit
bodyText: Hold every security deposit for the tenant in a bank, credit union or depository institution insured by an agency of the federal government. Missouri does not require a separate account for each tenant, a particular in-state bank, or notice to the tenant of where the deposit is held. Housing authorities and other government landlords are exempt from this holding rule.

title: Move-Out Inspection Notice
bodyText: Before you inspect the unit after the lease ends to decide what to withhold from the deposit, give the tenant reasonable written notice of the date and time, delivered to the tenant's last known address or in person. Hold the inspection at a reasonable time; the tenant may be present. Missouri has no move-in inspection or checklist requirement, but a signed move-in condition record helps prove the unit's condition at the start of the tenancy, which is the baseline for any deduction.

title: Pet Deposits
bodyText: A deposit labelled as a pet deposit is not a 'security deposit' under Missouri's deposit law, so it does not count toward the two-month cap and is not covered by the 30-day return and double-damages rules. Your lease should say how a pet deposit is used and returned. A servicemember who ends a lease under Missouri's military termination law gets the full security deposit and pet deposit back if the lease was otherwise followed. No Missouri statute limits pet rent or pet fees for ordinary pets; you may not charge pet fees for an assistance animal.

title: No Holding Deposit Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on holding deposits or other money taken before a lease is signed. Because Missouri's deposit law covers any deposit, however labelled, that secures performance of the rental agreement, a holding deposit that is kept and applied once the lease starts may be treated as part of the security deposit, so count it toward the two-month cap and handle it under the deposit rules.

title: No Deposit Installment Rule
bodyText: Missouri does not require you to let a tenant pay the security deposit in installments, and does not prohibit it.

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit
bodyText: A tenant may not use the security deposit to pay rent, including the last month's rent. Missouri has no specific rule on collecting the last month's rent in advance, but because the deposit cap reaches any deposit 'however denominated', prepaid last month's rent that functions as security may be counted toward the two-month cap.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: Missouri has no statute requiring a seller to transfer security deposits to a buyer or releasing the seller once it does. The 30-day return duty applies to 'the landlord' at the end of the tenancy, so settle deposit transfers in the sale contract and tell tenants who now holds their deposit. Before a new owner can sue tenants for rent, it must give them adequate written notice of the transfer, with a copy of the recorded deed (or, in first-class counties, a notarized affidavit signed by the old and new owners).

title: No Late Fee Cap
bodyText: Missouri has no statute capping late fees or requiring a grace period for residential rent. Set a fee that is a reasonable estimate of your cost of late payment; a court may refuse to enforce a fee it sees as a penalty. A late fee is not 'rent' for a rent-and-possession action, so an unpaid late fee alone will not support an order for possession in that action.

title: Fees Are Not Rent in a Possession Case
bodyText: In a Missouri rent-and-possession case you may join a claim for other unpaid sums the lease requires (such as fees), however the lease labels them, but those sums are not rent for purposes of that action, and a judgment for them does not by itself entitle you to possession. Labelling a fee as 'additional rent' in the lease does not change this.

title: No Application Fee Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute limiting rental application or screening fees or requiring refunds.

title: No Local Rent Control
bodyText: No Missouri county or city may enact, maintain or enforce an ordinance regulating the amount of rent for privately owned residential rental property. Local governments may still regulate their own property, make voluntary rent agreements for subsidized properties, and restrict rent on properties assisted with community development block grant funds.

title: Rent Increases
bodyText: Missouri has no statute setting a notice period for raising rent on a house or apartment, and local rent control is preempted. During a fixed term, rent changes only as the lease allows. For a month-to-month tenancy, the practical route is to give written notice ending the tenancy on a rent-paying date at least one month after the tenant receives it, and offer a new tenancy at the new rent. Mobile home land lease communities have their own rule.

title: No Rent Receipt Rule
bodyText: Missouri does not require a landlord to give receipts for rent, including cash rent. Giving receipts is good practice.

title: Sales Tax and Residential Rent
bodyText: Missouri's state sales tax on rooms applies to rooms furnished at hotels, motels, inns, tourist cabins and other places that regularly serve rooms to the public; ordinary residential rent is not in that list. Short-term rentals and local lodging taxes are outside this library.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText: When a written lease sets no interest rate, Missouri law allows interest at 9% a year on money due under it from the date it becomes due and payable. A higher contract rate raises usury questions this library has not reviewed, so the library offers no interest clause.

title: Accepting Late or Partial Rent
bodyText: No Missouri statute says that accepting late or partial rent waives a landlord's rights. Courts can still find a waiver from a pattern of conduct, such as repeatedly accepting late payments, so if you accept rent after giving a notice or demand, say in writing that you are reserving your rights.

title: Repairs and Habitability
bodyText: Missouri's landlord-tenant statutes do not impose a general duty to keep a rental in repair. Your duties come from the lease, local housing and building codes, and court decisions. Missouri does give tenants a limited repair-and-deduct remedy for local code violations, a receivership remedy that local governments and neighborhood groups can use against code-violating buildings, and a defense to rent when a residence is destroyed by a disaster the tenant did not cause.

title: Tenant Repair and Deduct
bodyText: A Missouri tenant may repair and deduct only if all of these apply: the tenant has lawfully lived there six consecutive months, paid all rent and charges, and had no uncured written lease or rule violation notice in that time; the condition violates a local housing or building code and harms habitability, sanitation or security; it costs less than $300 or half the periodic rent, whichever is greater, and no more than one month's rent; and you fail to fix it within 14 days of the tenant's written notice (or sooner in an emergency). If you dispute the need in writing within that period, the tenant must first get written certification from the local government that the condition violates the code. The tenant must use workmanlike repairs and give you an itemized statement with receipts. The remedy is unavailable for a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent, and is limited to one month's rent in any 12 months. No lease may waive it.

title: Housing Code Receivership
bodyText: If a building violates building or housing codes in a way that threatens health or safety, a county, city, local housing corporation or neighborhood association may, after 60 days' written notice to interested parties, ask a court to appoint a receiver who collects the rents and fixes the property. Rent a tenant pays to the receiver under the court's order is a defense to an eviction for nonpayment. A lease term waiving a tenant's protections under these sections is void. Occupants have their own duties under this law (paying rent, keeping the unit sanitary, not damaging it, and not taking in extra occupants without the owner's consent).

title: Unpaid Heat Utilities in Master-Metered Buildings
bodyText: In a building of two or more units where the owner pays for gas or electric heat service, if the owner falls behind and the utility gives notice of termination, the utility must tell tenants at least five days before shutoff, and any tenant or the utility may ask the associate circuit court to appoint a receiver to collect rents and pay for heat. The utility may not cut off heat while a receivership exists, or while a petition is pending (if a tenant filed it, once the utility has had at least 24 hours' prior written notice of the filing). An owner who collects rent while a receiver is appointed is in contempt of court.

title: Water and Sewer Bills
bodyText: Municipal and district water and sewer service is treated as furnished to both the occupant and the owner, so the provider may sue either or both for unpaid bills. Once the occupant is 30 days behind, the provider must try in good faith to tell the owner; the owner is not liable for more than 90 days of service, and any termination notice must go to both. Where several residences share a water or sewer line, the property owner is liable. Services billed directly to the owner under an owner's account are the owner's responsibility.

title: No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs
bodyText: You may not remove or exclude a tenant or the tenant's belongings, or remove or change the locks, without judicial process and a court order, except under Missouri's abandonment procedure. You may not willfully interrupt, or cause the interruption of, essential services such as electricity, gas, water or sewer to the tenant or the premises, for any reason other than health or safety. A landlord who does either is guilty of forcible entry and detainer, and the tenant may sue to get back in, with double the damages found.

title: No Entry Notice Statute
bodyText: Missouri has no statute setting when or with how much notice a landlord may enter a rental. Entry rights come from the lease; the library's lease gives 24 hours' notice except in emergencies.

title: No Retaliation Statute
bodyText: Missouri has no general statute barring a landlord from retaliating against a tenant for complaining about conditions or using legal rights. Specific protections still apply: you may not evict because a resident has an elevated blood lead level or because of lead enforcement, or deny or evict a tenant because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. Federal fair housing law bars retaliation for exercising fair housing rights.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires a residential landlord to install or maintain smoke or carbon monoxide alarms. Local building, fire and housing codes often do, so check the code where the property is located.

title: Notice to End a Tenancy
bodyText: How much notice Missouri requires depends on the kind of tenancy. A fixed-term lease ends on its end date with no notice to quit. A month-to-month tenancy ends by written notice from either party ending it on a rent-paying date at least one month after the other party receives it. A tenancy at will, by sufferance or for less than a year (such as week-to-week) may be ended by the landlord on one month's written notice. A year-to-year tenancy needs written notice at least 60 days before the end of the year. A lease that is not in writing and signed is treated as month-to-month. These notices are not needed before a rent-and-possession case for unpaid rent. A mobile-home lot tenancy has a longer 60-day rule. Missouri also lets the parties dispense with the notice to quit by special agreement (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.070). The library does not offer a clause that does this: it would remove the one-month notice from a month-to-month tenancy, how far a court lets such an agreement reach has not been reviewed, and a term like this is read strictly against the landlord who drafted it. It is lawful, so a landlord who still wants it can add a custom clause, after taking advice.

title: Demand for Rent Before Filing
bodyText: Missouri has no pay-or-quit notice period for unpaid rent. Before filing a rent-and-possession case, you must demand the rent that is due from the tenant or the person occupying the property; the demand is valid any time after the rent is due, and in a suit for possession when one month's rent or more is in arrears and you have a right by law to re-enter for the nonpayment, serving the complaint and summons counts as the demand. If your written lease declares the lease forfeited for nonpayment 'for a specified time', you cannot start the case until that time has passed, so avoid building a grace period into a forfeiture clause unless you mean it. If your property has a federally backed mortgage or is in a covered federal housing program, see Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties.

title: Missouri Eviction Process
bodyText: Missouri has two main eviction tracks. A rent-and-possession case (for unpaid rent) is filed with an associate circuit judge after a demand for rent; the court date must be within 21 business days of the summons unless you agree to later, the tenant may stop the case by paying all rent and costs on the judgment date, and the officer must deliver possession within 5 days of receiving the execution. An unlawful detainer case covers a tenant who holds over after the lease ends and refuses to leave after a written demand for possession; execution for possession may issue no sooner than 10 days after judgment, and the judgment awards double damages and double monthly rent until possession is restored. In a rent-and-possession case the tenant has 10 days from the judgment to move to set it aside or apply for a trial de novo, and in either track an appeal stays execution only with a sufficient bond (in rent cases, one covering rent). If service is only by posting and mailing and the tenant defaults, no money judgment is entered. Unlawful detainer is not available against a person who has stayed in peaceable possession for three whole years after the lease ended, or who has been in uninterrupted or quiet possession for three whole years before the complaint is filed; another kind of action is needed. Self-help eviction is prohibited, and local governments may not impose eviction moratoriums.

title: Lease Violations and Illegal Use
bodyText: Missouri gives no cure period for lease violations. If a tenant violates a condition of a written lease, assigns or sublets without your written consent (for terms of two years or less, at will or by sufferance), or commits waste, you may give 10 days' notice to vacate (in writing, to be safe) and then recover possession through the courts. If a tenant allows illegal gaming, a bawdyhouse or the illegal possession, sale or distribution of controlled substances on the premises, the lease becomes void and you have the same remedies as against a tenant holding over. You are not liable for relying on a written notice from law enforcement that the premises are being used for illegal drug activity.

title: Expedited Eviction for Drug Activity and Emergencies
bodyText: A landlord or prosecutor may bring an expedited eviction in the associate circuit court, heard within 15 days of service, where drug-related criminal activity occurred on or near the property or the tenant's household or guests engaged in it, or where an emergency makes ordinary eviction too slow to prevent physical injury or major property damage (only after first trying to abate it through police or mental health services). No notice to vacate is needed first, except that if someone other than the tenant committed the activity, you must give the tenant 5 days' written notice and a chance to seek a protective order or report it to police. An innocent tenant who did not know of the activity can defend, and the court may then remove only the person responsible. On eviction the tenant has 24 hours to vacate. Rent continues to accrue during the case. If your property has a federally backed mortgage or is in a covered federal housing program, see Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties.

title: Property Left After an Eviction
bodyText: When a judgment for possession is carried out, you are not liable for loss of or damage to the tenant's belongings you remove or dispose of under the court-ordered execution, except for willful, wanton or malicious acts. But if property left behind is conspicuously and permanently labelled as belonging to a third party, you must notify that person by certified mail, return receipt requested, and give them five business days after receiving the notice to recover it. If the officer has not delivered possession within seven days after receiving the writ, you may, within 60 days of the judgment and with a local law enforcement officer present, remove the locks, take possession and remove belongings, after showing the officer the judgment and execution and filing the officer's written acknowledgment with the court within five days.

title: Removing Squatters
bodyText: Since August 28, 2024, a property owner may file a verified petition to remove people unlawfully occupying a residential property who were never tenants. The court issues an ex parte removal order immediately on good cause, with a hearing within 48 hours, and the sheriff enforces it. This fast track is available only if, among other things, the property had not been leased to anyone for three consecutive months, the occupants are not current or former tenants or immediate family, and there is no pending litigation with them. A person wrongly removed may recover $1,000 in statutory damages plus actual damages. For current or former tenants, use the ordinary eviction process.

title: Holdover Damages
bodyText: Missouri sets several double measures for tenants who stay too long. A tenant for life or years who willfully holds over after the term ends, and after you make a demand and give written notice requiring possession, owes double the yearly value of the property for the time you are kept out. A tenant who gives written notice of intent to leave on a date and does not leave owes double the rent for as long as the tenant stays. In an unlawful detainer judgment, the court awards double the damages found and double the monthly rent found until possession is restored. After a written lease ends, oral evidence that it was renewed or extended is not admissible in a possession suit. Each of these measures needs a willful holdover, your written demand, the tenant's own notice to quit or a court judgment; for other holdover days you recover your actual damages, or the daily holdover charge in your lease if you choose to include one.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Missouri does not require a reason to end a tenancy at the end of a fixed term or on proper notice for a periodic tenancy. Specific limits still apply: you may not end or refuse a tenancy for a discriminatory reason, because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, or because a resident has an elevated blood lead level or because of lead enforcement, and a condominium conversion requires 120 days' notice with added rights for some elderly and disabled tenants. The expedited drug-eviction law expressly preserves a landlord's right to refuse to renew.

title: Domestic Violence, Sexual Assault and Stalking Protections
bodyText: You may not deny tenancy to, evict, or find a lease violation against an applicant or tenant because the person is, has been, or is in imminent danger of becoming a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, if the person otherwise qualifies. The protection does not apply if the person let the named abuser into the premises, or if you reasonably believe the named abuser threatens other occupants or the property. A tenant who vacates has a defense to rent for the period after leaving if a court finds the tenant was a victim or in imminent danger and the tenant notified you and gave any documentation you asked for (a signed statement from a victim-service provider or health professional, or a police, court or agency record). You may charge a reasonable termination fee when a tenant ends a lease early under this law. False information may be grounds to deny or evict. Missouri has no domestic-violence lock-change statute.

title: Military Lease Termination
bodyText: A member of the U.S. Armed Forces on active duty, or a Missouri Army or Air National Guard member on full-time duty or serving as a civil service technician, may end a residential lease after receiving permanent change of station orders, temporary duty orders of more than 90 days at least 25 miles away, discharge or release from that duty, or orders to live in government quarters. The member gives written notice of termination effective on a stated date at least 15 days after service, and gives you a copy of the orders or a signed letter from the commanding officer before that date. The final payment is due by the termination date, and the member is entitled to the full return of the security deposit and any pet deposit if the lease and the deposit law were otherwise followed. The federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act gives additional rights.

title: Occupancy Limits
bodyText: Missouri presumes an occupancy limit of two persons per bedroom to be reasonable. Children born to the tenants during the lease do not count against that limit. Fair housing law protects families with children, so any stricter limit should rest on a lawful local or state occupancy standard.

title: Tenant Must Report Lawsuits for the Property
bodyText: A tenant served with a summons in an action to recover the property must promptly notify the landlord (or the landlord's agent). A tenant who fails to do so forfeits to the landlord the value of three years' rent.

title: Assignment and Unauthorized Occupants
bodyText: A tenant for a term of two years or less, at will or by sufferance, may not assign or transfer the lease without the landlord's written consent. In a rent or possession case, if the tenant let another person come into sole possession without the landlord's permission, the court may award damages of up to twice the rent due, in addition to the rent. Assignments of leases must be in writing.

title: Tenant Waste
bodyText: A tenant may not commit waste on the leased property. A tenant for life or years who commits waste without written permission may be sued, loses the thing wasted and must pay three times the assessed damage. Committing waste is also a ground for 10 days' notice to vacate.

title: When the Tenant Causes Damage
bodyText: If a tenant causes damage, Missouri law gives you these points. The rule that a tenant owes no rent after a disaster destroys the residence does not apply if the tenant caused the disaster. A tenant who commits waste owes treble damages, and waste is a ground for 10 days' notice to vacate. But no action may be brought against a tenant in whose home a fire accidentally begins, and a repair promise in a lease does not require a tenant to rebuild after a fire the tenant did not cause through procurement, connivance or neglect unless the tenant specially agreed to rebuild. Whether a careless fire counts as 'accidental' under that rule is unsettled.

title: Fire, Storm and Other Disasters
bodyText: If a residence is destroyed by an act of God, such as a fire, tornado or other natural or man-made disaster, and the tenant did not cause it, the tenant owes no rent for the rest of the lease term. Missouri has no statute giving either party a right to end the lease after a fire or other casualty, or governing partial damage, so the lease should cover those cases.

title: Attorney Fees
bodyText: No Missouri statute awards attorney fees in ordinary landlord-tenant cases or bars a lease attorney-fee clause. Whether and how courts enforce a lease fee clause is a matter of court decisions this library has not reviewed; the library's lease uses a mutual prevailing-party fee term.

title: Missouri Fair Housing Law
bodyText: The Missouri Human Rights Act bars refusing to rent, setting different terms, misrepresenting availability, or advertising a preference because of race, color, religion, national origin, ancestry, sex, disability or familial status. You must allow reasonable disability modifications at the tenant's expense (and may, where reasonable, require restoration of the interior) and make reasonable accommodations in rules and policies. Exempt, except from the advertising ban: a private owner renting a single-family house without a broker or advertising who owns no more than three such houses, and rooms or units in an owner-occupied building for four or fewer families. Missouri does not protect source of income or age in housing; federal law adds its own rules and exemptions.

title: Disability Modifications
bodyText: A tenant with a disability may make reasonable modifications to the unit at the tenant's own expense when needed for full enjoyment of the premises. For a rental, you may, where reasonable, condition permission on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted. Missouri does not require that restoration condition to appear in the lease.

title: Source of Income
bodyText: Missouri law does not protect a renter's source of income, and since August 28, 2025 no county or city may enact, maintain or enforce an ordinance that bars a landlord from refusing to rent because the renter's income includes federal or other housing assistance. A city or county may still bar discrimination against recipients of veterans' benefits. If your multifamily project received additional subsidies from the Missouri Housing Development Commission, your agreement must bar you from refusing housing vouchers or Section 8 certificates in partial payment of rent and from discriminating against households that use them or receive public assistance. Note that a landlord receiving public funds from a housing authority may not ban firearms in the lease.

title: Tenant Screening Criteria
bodyText: No county or city may restrict your use of income-qualifying methods, credit scores, credit reports, eviction or property damage history, or criminal history under your own customarily applied criteria, or bar you from asking for that information. Fair housing law still applies, and federal consumer reporting rules govern screening reports.

title: Assistance Animal Misrepresentation
bodyText: Knowingly misrepresenting an animal as an assistance animal to get a housing accommodation under the federal Fair Housing Act is a class C misdemeanor (class B for a repeat), and the person is civilly liable for actual damages. That includes falsely documenting an animal, fitting it with a vest or sign, or misleading a health care provider to get documentation. Missouri law says documentation for an assistance animal must come from a qualified professional as the federal Fair Housing Act permits.

title: Lead Hazards
bodyText: Besides the federal lead disclosure, Missouri requires an owner who receives written notification of a lead hazard to abate it or establish interim controls in a way the state health department allows, within the applicable time; an owner of a rental may instead take it off the rental market. You may not evict a tenant because someone with an elevated blood lead level or suspected lead poisoning lives there, or because of action required of you under the lead law; other lawful reasons for eviction are not affected.

title: Manager and Owner Disclosure
bodyText: At or before the start of every tenancy, give the tenant in writing the name and address of the person authorized to manage the property and of an owner or agent authorized to accept service of process and receive notices and demands. Keep it current; the duty passes to later landlords, owners and managers. Anyone who fails to make the disclosure becomes the landlord's agent for service and notices and for performing the landlord's obligations, including collecting rent. If the owner's address is a post office box, papers may be served by first-class mail.

title: Agents for Nonresident and Corporate Landlords
bodyText: If you are not a Missouri resident or are a corporation, Missouri requires you to designate, in writing filed with the Secretary of State, an agent in Missouri (a resident or a corporation authorized to do business here) on whom legal papers can be served; if you do not, service may be made on the Secretary of State. In St. Louis City, an owner who lives outside the city must also register with the city assessor an agent to accept service for building, occupancy and other city code violations. Other general filings also reach out-of-state owners. An out-of-state limited liability company must register with the Secretary of State, naming a Missouri registered agent, before transacting business in Missouri, and an out-of-state corporation must obtain a certificate of authority; until they do, neither may maintain any suit, an eviction included, in a Missouri court, and each faces a fine of at least $1,000, though their leases stay valid and they may defend a suit (Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 347.153, 347.163, 351.572, 351.574). Neither statute's list of activities that are not transacting business mentions owning or renting out real estate, so whether renting here counts is a case-law question (not searched); get advice or register before you need to file. Anyone, an individual or an entity, who rents under a name other than their true name must register it as a fictitious name with the Secretary of State within five days of starting business under it, and doing business under an unregistered fictitious name is a misdemeanor (Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 417.200, 417.210, 417.230). And whoever you are and wherever you live, owning, using or possessing real estate in Missouri lets a Missouri court hear a claim arising from it, with the papers served on you personally outside the state (Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 506.500, 506.510).

title: Condominium Conversion
bodyText: A declarant converting a building to condominiums must give each residential tenant at least 120 days' notice before requiring them to leave, plus the original sale certificate at least 60 days before they must vacate, may not require a tenant to leave on shorter notice except for nonpayment of rent, waste or conduct that disturbs other tenants, and may not change the terms of the tenancy during that period. Tenants get a 60-day right to buy their unit. In buildings of six or more units, some low- or moderate-income elderly and disabled tenants may keep their units for extended periods.

title: Buying a Rented Property
bodyText: A buyer of a rented property may sue for rent and possession for rent that falls due after the transfer, under the prior owner's lease, once it gives tenants adequate written notice of the transfer, its method and its date, attached to a copy of the recorded deed (or, in first-class counties, a notarized affidavit signed by the old and new owners). A tenant who paid the old owner before getting notice is protected. The new owner must also give the manager and owner disclosure. Since August 28, 2024, transfers of rental properties with outstanding collectible judgments must be filed in the circuit court within 30 days after the transfer.

title: Tenants After Foreclosure
bodyText: After a trustee's foreclosure sale, the new owner must give a residential tenant written notice that the sale occurred, who the new owner is, and that the tenant has at least 10 business days from the notice before any action for possession, by certified or registered mail (or regular mail addressed to 'Occupant' if the name is unknown, in an envelope marked 'Notice to Occupant Following Foreclosure') and posted on the door, in substantially the statutory text. Remaining after the notice does not make the occupant the new owner's tenant. Federal law may give tenants more time.

title: Delivering Notices
bodyText: Missouri sets delivery rules for some notices; where a statute requires a notice but names no method (for example a notice ending a month-to-month tenancy), delivering a copy to the person, or leaving a copy at the person's home with a family member over 15, is valid service. Notices ending a tenancy must be in writing. An unlawful detainer demand for possession may be delivered to the person in possession, left with someone over 15 who lives on or is in charge of the premises, or posted if no one is there. The abandonment notice must be both posted and mailed by first-class and certified mail. Deposit statements may be mailed to the tenant's last known address. Missouri's electronic transactions act does not exclude leases or notices, but the statutes that require posting or mail still control.

title: When a Lease Must Be in Writing
bodyText: A lease for longer than one year is unenforceable unless it, or a memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party to be charged. A lease that is not in writing and signed creates only a tenancy at will, and an unwritten rental of a house or other building is treated as month-to-month.

title: Merchandising Practices Act
bodyText: Missouri's Merchandising Practices Act prohibits deception, fraud, false promises, misrepresentation, unfair practices and concealing material facts in connection with the sale or advertisement of merchandise, and it defines merchandise to include real estate and sale to include a lease. A tenant who leases for personal or household use may sue for actual damages if the tenant shows an ascertainable loss, that the tenant acted as a reasonable consumer would, that the practice would lead a reasonable person into the lease, and damages that can be calculated with reasonable certainty; the court may also award punitive damages, and attorney fees to whichever side prevails. Be accurate in listings, applications and the lease.

title: Lease Terms Missouri Law Voids
bodyText: Missouri has no general list of banned lease terms, but specific provisions void particular terms: a waiver of the tenant's repair-and-deduct right; a waiver of an occupant's protections under the housing-code receivership law; a ban on firearms by a housing authority or a landlord receiving public funds from one; in leases signed after December 8, 2022, a ban on lawfully possessing marijuana or consuming it other than by smoking; and, in a sale-leaseback of a home, any term of an agreement executed, modified or extended after August 28, 2026 that modifies or waives a duty or remedy under the sale-leaseback law. Other limits on lease terms, such as penalties and exculpatory clauses, come from court decisions.

title: Firearms
bodyText: A housing authority, or a landlord receiving public funds from a housing authority, may not prohibit a tenant, household member or guest from possessing firearms in the residence or common areas or carrying them to and from the residence as the law allows; such a lease term is void. Such a landlord is generally not liable for damages caused by a tenant's possession or use of a firearm. No Missouri statute addresses firearm rules in other private leases.

title: Towing From Rental Property
bodyText: To have a vehicle towed from your property without a police officer's authorization, you (or a full-time property or security manager) must be present, and either post a sign in plain view at every entrance at least 17 by 22 inches with letters at least 1 inch high that prohibits public parking, states that unauthorized vehicles will be removed at the owner's expense, discloses the maximum towing and storage fee, and gives the phone number of the local traffic law enforcement agency or a 24-hour staffed emergency information line, or notify police and wait 10 hours (owner-occupied property of four units or fewer) or 96 hours (other private property). You must complete the state's abandoned property report. Knowingly authorizing a tow that breaks these rules is a class C misdemeanor.

title: Marijuana in Rentals
bodyText: Under the Missouri Constitution, a lease signed after December 8, 2022 may not prohibit a tenant from lawfully possessing marijuana or consuming it by means other than smoking. You may ban smoking marijuana, and you may prohibit or limit cultivation, distribution, processing, sale and display of marijuana on your property. Whether vaping marijuana counts as 'smoking' is unsettled; the library's lease does not ban it.

title: Nuisance Actions Against Rental Owners
bodyText: A building used for possessing, keeping, distributing or manufacturing controlled substances is a public nuisance; if the owner knew or had reason to know, a court may close it for up to a year. In the cities described by the statute's population tests (St. Louis City, Kansas City, Springfield and St. Charles, per the section heading), property owners within 1,200 feet and neighborhood organizations may sue an owner over a nuisance property after 60 days' mailed notice, which must also go to the tenant (or 'occupant').

title: County Habitability Rules (Boone County)
bodyText: One county in the population bracket set by statute (Boone County, per the section heading) may adopt habitability rules for rented homes covering protection from the elements, water including hot water, sewer, electricity, heat and basic security. Enforcement is by written complaint from a current lawful tenant, notice to the owner, and a county hearing; the county may not charge fees, inspect except in response to a written complaint, or require licensing, registration or certification of a rented home on a regular schedule or before it is offered for rent.

title: Deaths, Crimes and Illness at the Property
bodyText: Missouri law says that a property's being the site of a homicide, other felony or suicide, or that an occupant had HIV, AIDS or another disease highly unlikely to spread through occupancy, is not a material fact that must be disclosed in a 'sale, exchange or other transfer of real estate', and no claim lies against a real estate agent or broker for not disclosing it. Whether this covers leases is not settled; answer a tenant's direct question truthfully.

title: No Landlord Lien on Household Goods
bodyText: Missouri gives landlords liens only on crops grown on the leased land. For unpaid rent, a court may issue an attachment against a tenant's personal property in listed situations (such as when the tenant is removing property or rent is unpaid after demand), only after you post a bond for double the amount claimed, and property exempt from execution is also exempt from attachment for rent. Seizing a tenant's belongings yourself is forcible entry and detainer.

title: Where Missouri Landlord-Tenant Law Lives
bodyText: Missouri has no single landlord-tenant code. The main rules are in Chapter 441 (tenancies, notices, repair-and-deduct, abandonment, receivership, expedited drug evictions and domestic violence protections), Chapter 535 (rent-and-possession actions, manager disclosure and security deposits) and Chapter 534 (forcible entry, unlawful detainer and squatter removal), with other rules elsewhere. The chapters' definitions reach manufactured and mobile homes. Cities such as Kansas City and St. Louis have their own tenant ordinances, which this library does not cover.

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Missouri requires no radon testing or disclosure for rentals.

title: No Mold Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose or remediate mold in a rental.

title: No Bed Bug Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on bed bug disclosure, inspection or treatment in rentals.

title: No Flood Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Missouri does not require a landlord to disclose flood risk or flood history to a tenant.

title: No Tenant Death Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute ending a residential lease when a tenant dies or setting how a landlord handles a deceased tenant's belongings. The lease continues as a contract with the tenant's estate under general law. Use the estate's personal representative or a court process before disposing of property.

title: No EV Charging Rule
bodyText: Missouri gives tenants no statutory right to install electric vehicle charging, and sets no landlord-tenant rule on it. If you provide or bill for charging, see EV Charging: Rules for Owners for the utility and weights-and-measures rules that apply.

title: No Immigration Status Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on asking about or acting on a renter's immigration status. National origin and ancestry are protected under Missouri fair housing law.

title: No Right-to-Call-Police Statute
bodyText: Missouri has no statute protecting a tenant's right to call police or emergency services or barring lease penalties for doing so. Missouri does bar evicting or finding a lease violation against a tenant because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking.

title: No Lock or Security Device Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute requiring deadbolts, door viewers or rekeying between tenants. A landlord may not change or remove locks to exclude a tenant without a court order. Where a county adopts habitability rules under Missouri's county authority, they must require basic security including locking doors and windows.

title: No Eviction Record Sealing
bodyText: Missouri has no statute sealing or expunging eviction case records.

title: Re-Renting After a Tenant Leaves Early
bodyText: Missouri has no general statute requiring a landlord to re-rent or reduce damages when a tenant leaves early, or saying whether the lease survives for rent. The only statutory mitigation rule is in the deposit law: you may withhold from the deposit for a tenant's failure to give proper notice to end the tenancy only if you make reasonable efforts to mitigate. Whether a broader duty to mitigate applies is a matter of court decisions, so the library's lease commits to reasonable efforts where the law requires them.

title: No Utility Submetering Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on landlords billing tenants for utilities through submeters or allocation formulas, or on disclosures for that billing. Utility regulators' rules and local ordinances were not reviewed.

title: No Lease Copy Rule
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires a landlord to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease. Giving each tenant a signed copy is still good practice.

title: Waiving Habitability
bodyText: Missouri has no statute that lists a landlord's habitability duties, and none that says whether a lease can waive them. Any broader duty to keep a rental fit to live in comes from court decisions, which this library has not reviewed, so the library does not offer a habitability waiver; the cautious course is to assume a court will not enforce a lease term giving up the tenant's right to a livable home. Two statutory rights apply whatever the lease says: no lease may waive the tenant's limited right to repair a housing-code violation and deduct the cost from rent, and any lease term that waives an occupant's protections under the housing-code receivership law is void. Local housing and building codes, and in Boone County any habitability rules the county has adopted, apply regardless of the lease.

title: Changing Repair Duties by Agreement
bodyText: Missouri has no statute listing the repairs or services a landlord must provide, so there is no statutory duty list for a lease to modify, and no statute requiring a separate document or a rent reduction when a tenant takes on a task. The lease may assign everyday upkeep, such as yard care or replacing light bulbs, to the tenant. Three statutory limits apply. A general promise by the tenant to repair does not require the tenant to rebuild or repair after a fire not brought about by the procurement, connivance or neglect of the tenant or the tenant's agents or servants, unless the tenant specially agreed to rebuild or repair after fire damage, and no one may sue a tenant over a fire that begins accidentally in the tenant's home. No lease may take away the tenant's limited right to repair a housing-code violation and deduct the cost. And where Boone County's habitability rules apply, a utility that is off because the tenant did not pay for it is not a violation. Duties that local housing codes place on owners, and any court-made duty to keep the home fit to live in (case law this library has not reviewed), cannot reliably be shifted by the lease.

title: How Serious a Defect Must Be
bodyText: Missouri has no general rule on how serious a defect must be before a tenant has a remedy. Each statutory remedy sets its own threshold. The tenant's repair-and-deduct right applies only to a condition that harms the habitability, sanitation or security of the home and also violates a local housing or building code. A housing-code receivership can be sought only for a code violation that is believed to threaten public health, safety or welfare. Under Boone County's habitability rules, the county may order a fix only for a dangerous condition harmful to the tenant's health, safety or welfare. The rent release after a disaster applies only when the residence is destroyed. Whether a lesser defect gives a tenant any other remedy is a matter of court decisions this library has not reviewed, so treat any code violation that affects health or safety as one to fix promptly.

title: No Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: No Missouri statute creates a presumption about housing conditions in a dispute between landlord and tenant, such as a presumption that a code violation was the landlord's fault or that a tenant's eviction after a complaint was improper. Each side proves its own case. The tenant's repair-and-deduct right instead requires proof of the facts it lists, including, if you dispute the repair in writing, a written certification from the local government that the condition violates the code. Where a court in a housing-code receivership orders rent paid to a receiver, paying it that way is a defense to an eviction for nonpayment of that rent.

title: No Required Habitability Statement
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires a lease to state that the home is, or will be kept, fit to live in, or to describe the tenant's habitability rights. You may describe your maintenance commitments in the lease, and the library's maintenance clause does, but no particular wording is required by state law. Check local ordinances, which this library has not reviewed.

title: Rights a Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Missouri has no landlord-tenant act with a general rule that tenant rights cannot be waived. Instead, particular laws protect particular rights from the lease: no lease may waive the tenant's limited repair-and-deduct right for housing-code violations; a lease term waiving an occupant's protections under the housing-code receivership law is void; a housing authority, or a landlord receiving public funds from one, may not ban lawful firearm possession, and a lease term doing so is void; a lease signed after December 8, 2022 may not ban a tenant from lawfully possessing marijuana or consuming it other than by smoking; and in a sale-leaseback of a home, the seller-tenant's protections cannot be modified or waived by agreement. Other statutes, such as the ban on lockouts and utility shutoffs and the domestic violence protections, say nothing about waiver; treat them as rules the lease cannot change. Some rules are expressly waivable: a lease for a fixed term needs no notice to quit, and notice can be dispensed with by special agreement, and a low- or moderate-income elderly tenant's or a disabled tenant's rights in a condominium conversion can be waived only in a written agreement, and only if the notice of conversion fully disclosed those rights.

title: Notice for Showings
bodyText: Missouri has no statute setting how much notice you must give before entering a rental, for showings or otherwise, so there is no statutory notice period for a tenant to waive and no rule that a waiver be in a separate document. The notice you give for showings is whatever the lease says. The library's entry clause gives 24 hours' notice, and its optional showing clause lets you set a shorter notice and fixed hours for showings near the end of the tenancy. Entry without the lease's notice, or entry that drives a tenant out, can still lead to claims under the lease or court decisions, so follow the notice you agreed to.

title: Jury Trial Waivers
bodyText: Missouri's constitution keeps the right to a jury trial inviolate where it existed historically. Most eviction and rent cases are heard by an associate circuit judge, where a jury trial is treated as waived unless a party files a written demand at least five days before the return date or trial date, whichever is later (the judge may still allow one for good cause); in an unlawful detainer or forcible entry case either side may have a jury on a timely request. Some proceedings have no jury at all: housing-code receivership cases, and hearings before the landlord-tenant commissioners in the City of St. Louis and Jackson County, where a party may move for a hearing in associate circuit court. The statute lists the ways a party waives a jury (not appearing, written consent filed with the court, oral consent in court, or going to trial before the judge without objecting); it does not mention a waiver signed in advance in a lease. Whether a Missouri court would enforce a lease jury waiver, and whether a jury is available at all in a rent-and-possession case, are questions of case law this library has not reviewed, so the library does not offer a jury-waiver clause. If you want one, get legal advice first.

title: Arbitration Clauses
bodyText: Missouri's Uniform Arbitration Act makes a written agreement to arbitrate future disputes valid and enforceable, but it expressly excludes contracts of insurance and contracts of adhesion, and a contract it covers must carry, next to or above the signature lines, a notice in ten-point capital letters substantially reading THIS CONTRACT CONTAINS A BINDING ARBITRATION PROVISION WHICH MAY BE ENFORCED BY THE PARTIES. A party's right to a lawyer in the arbitration cannot be waived in advance. Whether a standard residential lease is a contract of adhesion, and whether the Federal Arbitration Act applies to a particular lease instead, are questions of case law this library has not reviewed. Missouri's Merchandising Practices Act also reaches residential leases: an unfair practice in connection with a lease is unlawful, and a tenant who leases for personal or household use may sue for actual damages if the tenant shows an ascertainable loss, that the tenant acted as a reasonable consumer would, that the practice would lead a reasonable person into the lease, and damages that can be calculated with reasonable certainty; the court may also award punitive damages, and attorney fees to whichever side prevails. Whether putting an unenforceable term in a lease is an unfair practice depends on how courts apply the Attorney General's unfair-practice rules, and those decisions have not been reviewed for this library. For both reasons this library does not offer an arbitration clause for Missouri. If you want one anyway, have a Missouri lawyer draft it, keep rent-and-possession and unlawful detainer cases in the associate circuit court and small claims in small claims court, and include the statutory notice.

title: Penalty for Using Prohibited Lease Terms
bodyText: No Missouri statute penalizes a landlord simply for putting a prohibited term in a lease or for trying to enforce one. The statutes that bar particular terms (a waiver of the tenant's repair-and-deduct right, a waiver of housing-code receivership protections, a firearm ban by a housing authority or a landlord it funds, and a marijuana-possession ban in leases signed after December 8, 2022) make the term void or forbid it, and stop there; the deposit law's double-damages penalty applies to wrongfully withholding a deposit, not to lease wording. The real exposure is Missouri's Merchandising Practices Act, which covers residential leases. The Attorney General's rules under it make it an unfair practice to use an unconscionable contract term, and, where the practice risks or causes substantial injury to consumers, to engage in a practice that offends a public policy set by statute or that violates a state law meant to protect the public. A lease term a statute forbids can fit those words. A tenant who leases for personal or household use may sue for actual damages if the tenant shows an ascertainable loss, that the tenant acted as a reasonable consumer would, that the practice would lead a reasonable person into the lease, and damages that can be calculated with reasonable certainty; the court may also award punitive damages, and attorney fees to whichever side prevails; the Attorney General can also enforce the Act. Whether a particular term qualifies is decided by the courts case by case, so leave every prohibited term out of your lease and never try to enforce one.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: Missouri has no statute letting a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable residential lease or lease term. The unconscionability sections of the Uniform Commercial Code cover sales and leases of goods, not leases of homes. The Uniform Condominium Act has its own unconscionability section for contracts in condominiums created after September 28, 1983, but it is framed around sales of real estate, and whether it reaches a lease of a condominium unit is unsettled. Courts can still refuse to enforce a grossly one-sided contract term under their own decisions, which this library has not reviewed, and Missouri's Merchandising Practices Act bars unfair practices in connection with a lease. The cautious course is to keep lease terms balanced and avoid terms that take away a tenant's basic remedies.

title: Waiving the Notice to Quit
bodyText: Missouri lets the parties dispense with the notice to quit by special agreement, and a lease for a fixed term ends on its end date without one. The library does not offer a clause that waives or shortens the notice: it would remove the one-month notice from a month-to-month tenancy, how far a court lets such an agreement reach has not been reviewed, and a term like this is read strictly against the landlord who drafted it. A landlord who still wants one can add a custom clause, after taking advice. Some notices stay in place whatever the lease says: where a tenant who lives in and has an ownership interest in a mobile home rents the lot under a tenancy of less than a year, the landlord's written notice must end the tenancy no sooner than 60 days from the next rent due date, despite any earlier termination term in the lease, and federal law requires a 30-day notice to vacate in covered federally backed or assisted properties (see the federal notice row). A notice to quit is not needed before a rent-and-possession case for unpaid rent.

title: Confession of Judgment
bodyText: Missouri law allows a judgment by confession without a lawsuit, for money due or to become due, but only through a written statement signed by the debtor and sworn to by affidavit that states the amount, the facts it arose from and that the sum is justly due, which is then filed with the court; a confession through a power of attorney is allowed only for a debt on a note, bond or bill of exchange. Missouri bans confession-of-judgment terms in rental-purchase agreements for goods, consumer credit contracts and retail time contracts, but no statute addresses one in a residential lease. Whether a confession clause signed with the lease would meet the statute's requirements, or be enforced, is a question for the courts that this library has not reviewed, and the lease route to possession is a rent-and-possession or unlawful detainer case in court. The library does not offer a confession-of-judgment clause; get legal advice before using one.

title: Homestead and Exemption Waivers
bodyText: Missouri protects a debtor's homestead and certain personal property from attachment and execution. The homestead exemption covers a dwelling and land the person uses as a homestead, up to $15,000 in value, rising to $40,000 on January 1, 2027; it protects an owner's interest, and whether a tenant's leasehold can be a homestead is a question for the courts. Personal property exemptions include household goods and furnishings up to $3,000 (rising to $15,000 on January 1, 2027), a wedding ring, health aids, tools of the trade, a motor vehicle and public benefits, and a head of a family may claim more. These exemptions also limit a landlord's court attachment for rent, except for crops grown on the rented land. No Missouri statute says whether a lease may waive them; Missouri voids such waivers in consumer credit contracts, and whether a court would enforce one in a lease is case law this library has not reviewed. The library does not offer an exemption or homestead waiver; seizing a tenant's belongings yourself is never allowed.

title: Waiving Casualty and Re-Renting Rules
bodyText: Missouri has no casualty-termination statute, so whether either side may end the lease after a fire or other casualty, and what happens to rent after partial damage, is left to the lease (the library's casualty clause covers both). Two statutes set rules the lease works around. A tenant who did not cause a disaster that destroys the residence owes no rent for the rest of the term; the statute does not say whether a lease can change that, so do not rely on a lease term that does. And a general promise by the tenant to repair does not require rebuilding after a fire not brought about by the procurement, connivance or neglect of the tenant or the tenant's agents or servants, unless the tenant specially agreed to rebuild after fire damage. Missouri has no general statute requiring you to re-rent when a tenant leaves early, but you may keep part of the deposit for a tenant's failure to give proper notice only if you make reasonable efforts to mitigate, and a lease cannot remove that condition from the deposit rule. Whether a broader duty to mitigate exists, and whether a lease may waive it, are questions of case law this library has not reviewed; the library's lease commits to reasonable efforts where the law requires them.

title: Tenant Remedies When the Landlord Breaches
bodyText: Missouri has no statute giving tenants a general set of remedies, such as ending the lease, withholding rent or recovering damages, when a landlord breaches the lease or fails to keep the home in repair. Those questions are governed by the lease and by court decisions this library has not reviewed. Specific statutes give these remedies: a qualifying tenant may repair a housing-code violation that harms habitability, sanitation or security and deduct the cost from rent, within set limits; a landlord who locks a tenant out or removes the tenant's belongings or doors or locks without a court order (other than after an abandonment handled under the statutory procedure), or willfully cuts off essential utilities (other than for health or safety reasons), is liable for forcible entry and detainer, and the tenant can get back in and recover double damages and double the monthly rents and profits found; a landlord who wrongfully withholds a deposit owes twice the amount withheld; in a housing-code receivership a court may order rent paid to a receiver, and paying it is a defense to eviction for that rent; a tenant whose home is destroyed by a disaster the tenant did not cause owes no further rent; and a tenant who suffers a loss from an unfair or deceptive practice in a lease may sue under the Merchandising Practices Act. In Boone County, if the county has adopted habitability rules, a lawful tenant who signed a lease and is current on rent may also file a written complaint under them.

title: Smoke Drift and Smoke-Free Areas
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on secondhand smoke drifting between units, and none on whether a tenant may waive claims about it; those questions are left to court decisions this library has not reviewed, and the library does not offer a smoke-drift waiver. Missouri's Indoor Clean Air Act bars tobacco smoking in public places except in designated smoking areas, and defines a public place to include any enclosed indoor area used by the general public or serving as a place of work, including corridors and elevators; private residences are excluded. The Act does not say whether the enclosed hallways, lobbies or laundry rooms of an apartment building are public places, but where your staff work there or the public uses them the Act may apply, and a person in control of a public place must post no-smoking signs and make reasonable efforts to prevent smoking. The cautious course is to ban smoking in enclosed common areas, as the library's smoking clause does. Some cities have stricter smoke-free ordinances.

title: Promises to Repair
bodyText: No Missouri statute says that a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve a rental must be in writing, carry a completion date or be made before the lease is signed. But Missouri's Merchandising Practices Act, which covers residential leases, makes a false promise or misrepresentation in connection with a lease unlawful, and a tenant who suffers a loss from one may sue for damages. A promise you do not keep can therefore cost more than the repair. Put every promised item in the lease with a completion date, and keep later promises in writing; the library's optional promised-repairs clause does this.

title: Fixing a Tenant's Breach Yourself
bodyText: No Missouri statute gives a landlord the right to fix a tenant's breach, such as damage or a sanitation problem, and charge the tenant the cost, and none forbids it. The right comes only from the lease; the library's optional clause lets you give written notice, do the work if the tenant does not, and bill the reasonable cost. That cost is a sum due under the lease but not rent: in a rent-and-possession case you may join a claim for it, but it cannot by itself get you possession. You may enter only as the lease allows, and you may never change the locks, remove the tenant's belongings or shut off utilities to force payment.

title: Clauses Excusing Landlord Liability
bodyText: No Missouri statute says whether a residential lease may excuse the landlord from liability for injury or property damage, or require the tenant to hold the landlord harmless. That question is left to court decisions, which this library has not reviewed, so the library's Missouri lease does not use broad clauses saying the landlord is not liable: its storage, parking and renter's insurance clauses are the versions without a liability disclaimer. Assume a clause excusing you from your own negligence will not protect you. A few statutes limit a landlord's liability whatever the lease says. You are not liable for property you remove or dispose of under Missouri's abandonment procedure. You are not liable for loss of a tenant's belongings removed when a judgment for possession is carried out, except for willful, wanton or malicious conduct; if you remove them yourself with a law enforcement officer present because the sheriff did not act in time, you are also liable for negligence, and for failing to get and file the officer's written acknowledgment. You are not liable for damages from relying on a law enforcement agency's written notice that the premises are being used for illegal drug activity; a housing authority, or a landlord receiving public funds from one, is generally not liable for harm caused by a tenant's possession or use of a firearm; and a landlord who rents to a person whose criminal record has been expunged is immune from claims arising from misconduct related to the expunged record, unless the landlord failed to use reasonable care.

title: Eviction Fees and Penalties
bodyText: No Missouri statute bans a lease clause charging the tenant a fee or penalty if you file for eviction, and none authorizes one. In a rent-and-possession case the judgment awards possession, the rent due and court costs, and the tenant can stop the case by paying all rent in arrears and all costs on the judgment date. You may join a claim for other sums the lease requires, such as fees, but they are not rent, and a judgment for them alone does not give you possession. Attorney fees are recoverable only as the lease and the law allow. A fixed eviction charge that is out of proportion to your actual cost may be refused by a court as a penalty; that is case law, which this library has not reviewed, so the library does not offer an eviction-fee clause and recovers actual costs and fees instead.

title: Agreed Damages in the Lease
bodyText: No Missouri statute says whether a residential lease may fix in advance the damages a tenant owes for a breach, such as a flat charge for leaving early. Courts decide whether such a term is a valid estimate of damages or an unenforceable penalty, under decisions this library has not reviewed; the cautious course is to tie any agreed amount to a reasonable estimate of your actual loss. Missouri statutes set some damages measures themselves: a tenant who willfully holds over after the term ends and after your written demand for possession owes double the yearly value of the premises for the time held; a tenant who gives written notice of leaving and does not leave on that date owes double rent while staying on; a judgment for unlawful detainer awards double the damages and double the monthly rents and profits found; and you may keep part of the deposit for actual damages from a tenant's failure to give proper notice only if you make reasonable efforts to re-rent.

title: Shifting Maintenance to the Tenant
bodyText: Missouri has no statute listing a landlord's maintenance duties, so no statute says what a lease must give in return, or what form it must take, when it makes the tenant responsible for upkeep. A lease may assign tasks such as yard care, snow removal, replacing filters and bulbs, or keeping the unit clean, as the library's tenant maintenance, snow removal and landscaping clauses do; name each task so there is no dispute. Missouri law sets these limits. A tenant whose term is two years or less, or who holds at will or by sufferance, may not commit waste on the premises. A tenant's general promise to repair does not make the tenant rebuild or repair after a fire not brought about by the procurement, connivance or neglect of the tenant or the tenant's agents or servants, unless the tenant specially agreed to rebuild or repair after fire damage, and no one may sue a tenant over a fire that begins accidentally in the tenant's home. Such a special agreement is lawful on its face, but how it fits with that fire rule is unsettled, so the library does not offer one; get advice before adding it. And shifting repairs to the tenant does not take away the tenant's right to repair-and-deduct for code violations the tenant did not cause, which no lease may waive. Duties that local housing codes place on owners stay with you.

title: Agreements for the Tenant to Do Repairs
bodyText: No Missouri statute governs an agreement for the tenant to do specified repairs, maintenance or minor remodeling, so there is no required separate document, rent reduction or limit to single-family homes; the agreement may be part of the lease. The library's optional clause lists the specific tasks, lets you state what you give in return, and keeps work needed to meet building and housing codes with you. Two statutes still apply: a general repair promise does not make the tenant rebuild or repair after a fire not brought about by the procurement, connivance or neglect of the tenant or the tenant's agents or servants, unless the tenant specially agreed to that, and the tenant keeps the limited right to repair-and-deduct for housing-code violations the tenant did not cause, which no lease may waive.

title: No Statutory Confidentiality Rule for Domestic-Violence Information in Missouri
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires a landlord to keep confidential the statement or documents a tenant or applicant gives you to claim Missouri's protections for victims of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, or limits how you may use or share them. Missouri's address confidentiality program (Safe at Home, run by the Secretary of State) gives a participant a designated address, but it binds government agencies and courts, not private landlords: agencies and courts accept the designated address for new public records, and a court may compel disclosure of a participant's actual address only after notice and findings that it is needed and there is no other practicable way. Cautious course: keep any statement, police report, court record or professional's statement in a separate, secure file; use it only to handle the tenancy; never share it, or the victim's whereabouts, with the person named as the abuser, other household members, screening services or reference callers unless the tenant agrees in writing or a court or law requires it; and if the tenant is a Safe at Home participant, send mail to the designated address when the tenant asks. If the home is federally assisted housing, federal rules on handling this information may also apply; check them.

title: Deposits When a Domestic-Violence Victim Leaves in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri sets no special security-deposit timetable when a tenant leaves because of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking. Missouri's protection for these victims doesn't end the lease by itself: it gives a tenant who vacates a defense to rent for the period after leaving, if a court finds the tenant was a victim or in imminent danger and the tenant notified you and gave any documentation you asked for. The ordinary deposit rule applies: within 30 days after the tenancy ends, return the full deposit or mail an itemized list of damages with the balance to the tenant's last known address, after giving written notice of your move-out inspection. Missouri law doesn't say when the 30 days start if the victim leaves but a co-tenant stays and the tenancy goes on, and no case on that was read. Cautious course: once the victim has moved out and given you the statement, agree in writing with all tenants how the deposit will be handled, or account to the victim for the victim's share within 30 days of moving out and hold the rest for the continuing tenancy. Don't take rent for the period after the victim moved out from the deposit of a tenant who gave you the statement and any documentation you asked for, because a court may find that rent isn't owed and wrongful withholding costs twice the amount withheld. You may withhold only for unpaid rent, restoring the unit (ordinary wear and tear excepted) and actual losses from inadequate notice to end the tenancy, after reasonable efforts to re-rent. A reasonable termination fee for this early exit isn't on that list, so the cautious course is to bill it separately rather than take it from the deposit.

title: No Eviction Because of Domestic Violence in Missouri
bodyText: In Missouri you may not evict a tenant, deny an applicant, or treat a tenant as violating the lease because the person is, has been, or is in imminent danger of becoming a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, if the person otherwise qualifies to rent or live there. That includes using a lease clause on disturbances, police calls or criminal activity against the victim for the abuse itself. The protection has two exceptions: it doesn't apply if the tenant let the person named in the victim's documentation into the premises, or if you reasonably believe that person threatens the safety of other occupants or the property. A tenant qualifies by giving you a statement of the abuse; if you ask, the tenant must also give documentation (see the qualifying-documents row). False information can be grounds to deny, evict or find a lease violation. The rule applies only to residential property. Missouri has no statute letting you end the lease of only the abuser and keep the victim, so removing one co-tenant needs that tenant's agreement, a court order, or an ordinary eviction on a ground that tenant gave you. A court's protection order can bar the abuser from entering the victim's home even when the abuser is on the lease; if a tenant shows you one, don't let the restrained person in or give that person a key. In federally assisted housing, federal rules also apply; check them.

title: No Domestic-Violence Lock-Change Statute in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no statute giving a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking a right to have the locks changed, requiring you to change them, or saying who pays. You may agree to a victim's request, and the cautious course is to change or re-key promptly when asked. Be careful when the person the victim fears is also a tenant. In Missouri a landlord who removes or excludes a tenant without judicial process and court order, or causes the removal of the doors or locks, is guilty of forcible entry and detainer (the only exception is the abandoned-premises procedure). So don't lock out a co-tenant on the victim's word alone. A court's order of protection can bar the abuser from entering the victim's home even when the abuser is on the lease; if the victim gives you a copy of such an order, the cautious course is to change the locks for the victim as the order allows and not to give the restrained person a key or let that person in; no statute says in so many words that a landlord may or must do this. Keep a copy of the order with the change. If no order excludes a co-tenant, tell the victim that an order of protection can be sought from the circuit court. Missouri law doesn't say who pays for a victim's lock change; follow your lease's key and lock terms, and consider waiving the charge.

title: Domestic Violence Law Citations Current in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri's domestic-violence law for landlords hasn't moved. The tenant protection still borrows its definitions of domestic violence, sexual assault and stalking from the Adult Abuse Act's definitions section, and that section still holds all three, so the cross-reference is current. Orders of protection are still issued under the Adult Abuse Act (and, for children, the Child Protection Orders Act) in the same chapter. An ex parte order, issued before the abuser is heard, or a full order after a hearing can bar the abuser from entering the victim's home whether the home is leased jointly or by the victim alone; a full order can also require the abuser to pay rent on the victim's home where the abuser owes support, and give the victim temporary possession of keys. An order is effective throughout the state. The address confidentiality program (Safe at Home) is still run by the Secretary of State under its own sections. When a tenant shows you an order, read what it says about the home and follow it.

title: Proof of Domestic Violence for Missouri Tenant Protections
bodyText: Missouri has one list of qualifying documents, and it serves every part of its protection for victims of domestic violence, sexual assault and stalking (no denial, eviction or lease violation because of the abuse, and the defense to rent after the victim moves out). An applicant or tenant qualifies by giving you a statement of the abuse. You may ask for documentation; if you do, the person must give you one of these: (1) a document signed by an employee of a victim service provider, or by a health care or mental health professional the victim went to for help, stating under penalty of perjury that the signer believes the incident happened and that it meets the legal definition, and also signed by the victim; or (2) a record of a federal, state or local law enforcement agency (including a police report), a court, or an administrative agency about the incident. An order of protection is a court record, so it qualifies. The law sets no time limit on how recent the document must be and no deadline for providing it, and it doesn't require a particular form. For the rent defense, the tenant must have notified you and given any documentation you asked for. Ask for documentation in writing, accept any listed form, and don't demand more than one. False information can be grounds to deny, evict or find a lease violation. In federally assisted housing, federal documentation rules also apply; check them.

title: Police Cooperation and Reporting Duties in Missouri
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires or regulates a crime-free lease addendum, requires you or your tenants to cooperate with police investigations, requires you to give police information about tenants or access to their units, or bars a lease penalty for calling the police or emergency services. One firm limit applies: you may not evict, deny or find a lease violation against a tenant because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, so draft any criminal-activity or disturbance term so it can't reach the victim.
