Some reporting duties bind any person, landlords included: (1) if a person dies by violence (homicide, suicide or accident), suddenly while apparently in good health, unattended by a physician in the prior 36 hours, or in any unusual or suspicious manner, anyone who knows of the death must immediately notify the county coroner or medical examiner (in practice, call 911 and leave the unit as it is); (2) anyone who discovers the body of, or first learns of the death of, an infant between one week and one year old who died suddenly while apparently healthy must immediately notify the coroner or medical examiner; (3) anyone with reasonable cause to suspect that an adult aged 60 or older, or a disabled adult aged 18 to 59, who can't protect his or her own interests or meet essential needs, faces a likelihood of serious physical harm or bullying and needs protective services must immediately report it to the Department of Health and Senior Services; (4) anyone with reasonable cause to suspect abuse or neglect of a person in the care of a Department of Mental Health program must report it to that department. Child-abuse reporting is mandatory only for listed professionals and caregivers, but anyone may report. Cautious course: don't let police into a tenant's home without the tenant's consent or a warrant unless there is an emergency, and keep a record of any request.

title: Who May Appear in Court for an Entity Landlord in Missouri
bodyText: Who may appear for a company landlord. In small claims court (claims up to $5,000), parties may present their own cases without a lawyer, and a corporation or unincorporated association may appear through an officer or authorized employee; Missouri law says that isn't the unauthorized practice of law. For rent-and-possession and unlawful detainer cases, Missouri's statutes let the landlord's agent make the rent demand and file the statement or complaint, and let a party appear by agent or attorney. But Missouri also defines the practice of law to include appearing for another in a representative capacity and drawing pleadings for a court case, and only licensed lawyers may practice law; doing so without a license is a misdemeanor and can cost treble the fees paid. The Supreme Court's civil rules require every court filing to be signed by an attorney of record or by the self-represented party itself, and an unsigned filing is struck. Whether a company acting through a non-lawyer manager or employee counts as self-represented in an eviction, given the agent wording in the eviction statutes, is decided by Missouri Supreme Court case law not read for this library. Cautious course: an individual owner may file for himself or herself; an LLC, corporation or partnership should file and appear in an eviction or a suit over $5,000 through a Missouri lawyer, and a non-lawyer manager should not sign or argue court papers for the owner. An out-of-state LLC, corporation or limited partnership that does business in Missouri must register (or, for a corporation, get a certificate of authority) first; until it does, it can't bring a suit in a Missouri court, though its leases stay valid and it can defend a suit. Renting under a name other than the owner's true name requires a fictitious-name registration with the Secretary of State within five days; failing to register is a misdemeanor, but the statute doesn't bar suing. A nonresident who owns or rents out Missouri real estate is subject to Missouri courts for claims arising from it and can be served outside the state.

title: Foreign Ownership and Leasing in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no foreign-adversary property law and no restriction on renting a home to a person who isn't a U.S. citizen. Nonresident aliens and foreign corporations may acquire, hold and lease out Missouri real estate on the same terms as citizens, except agricultural land. The agricultural-land limit matters for a lease only in a narrow case: agricultural land means a tract of more than five acres (adjacent parcels under the same ownership count as one) capable of supporting farming, and a person who takes a lease of agricultural land for ten years or longer, or with renewal options that could total ten years, is treated as acquiring it. A nonresident alien, or a business controlled by nonresident aliens, may not acquire agricultural land while total foreign holdings exceed one percent of Missouri's farm acreage, unless an exception applies (land for nonfarm use, holdings grandfathered by family descent, or a person who is a bona fide U.S. resident), and a foreign person who acquires or transfers such an interest, including a leasehold of ten years or more, must report it to the Director of Agriculture within 30 days, on pain of a civil penalty of up to 25% of the interest's value. An ordinary residential lease shorter than ten years, or of a home on five acres or less, falls outside these rules. If you lease more than five acres of farmable land to a nonresident alien or foreign-controlled business for ten years or more (counting renewal options), take advice first. Missouri puts no duty on you to ask about a tenant's citizenship, and fair-housing law limits how you may treat national origin.

title: Habitability: What Missouri Law Has and Lacks
bodyText: How Missouri compares on habitability rules found in other states. Present in Missouri statutes: (1) a limited tenant repair-and-deduct remedy for conditions that violate a local housing or building code and affect habitability, sanitation or security, which no lease may waive; (2) court-appointed receivers who collect rents and fix buildings with dangerous code violations, on application by a county, city, local housing corporation or neighborhood association, with rent paid to the receiver a defense to eviction for nonpayment; (3) a receivership and shutoff protection when the owner of a master-metered building falls behind on heat utilities; (4) no rent owed for the rest of the term when a residence is destroyed by fire, tornado or another disaster the tenant didn't cause; (5) a ban on willfully interrupting a tenant's essential services such as electricity, gas, water or sewer, for any purpose other than health or safety reasons; (6) county habitability rules in one county (Boone) covering protection from the elements, water including hot water, sewer, electricity, heat and locking doors and windows. Absent from Missouri statutes: a statutory warranty of habitability or general duty to keep a rental fit and in repair (whether courts imply one is case law not read for this library, so keep rentals safe and code-compliant), rent withholding or rent escrow for bad conditions, a statutory right to end the lease for uninhabitable conditions, statewide smoke or carbon monoxide alarm rules, lock or security-device rules, a general ban on retaliation for complaints about conditions, and mold, bed-bug or radon rules. Local building, housing and fire codes fill many of these gaps; check the code where the property is. See the individual rows for each.

title: When Missouri Law Lets a Tenant End a Lease Early
bodyText: Missouri law lets a tenant get out of a lease early in only a few situations. (1) Military service: an active-duty member of the U.S. Armed Forces, or a Missouri National Guard member on full-time duty or serving as a civil service technician, may end a residential lease after permanent change of station orders, temporary duty orders of more than 90 days at least 25 miles away, discharge or release from that duty, or orders to live in government quarters, by written notice effective at least 15 days later plus a copy of the orders or a commanding officer's letter before that date. Federal law (the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act) separately lets a servicemember end a lease after entering service or receiving qualifying orders; for a monthly lease, termination takes effect 30 days after the next rent due date following delivery of notice, and you may not charge an early termination fee. (2) Domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking: Missouri gives no notice-based termination right, but a tenant who vacates has a defense to rent for the period after leaving if a court finds the tenant was a victim or in imminent danger and the tenant notified you and gave any documentation you asked for; you may charge a reasonable termination fee. (3) Destruction by disaster: if the residence is destroyed by fire, tornado or another disaster the tenant didn't cause, the tenant owes no rent for the rest of the term. Missouri has no statute letting a tenant end a lease early because of age, illness, disability or moving into care, because the landlord misrepresented something, or because the unit became uninhabitable short of destruction, and none that forfeits rent for leaving a required sentence out of the lease. Any other early exit is a matter for the lease; your early-termination clause must leave these statutory exits intact.

title: No Early Termination for Age or Illness in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no statute letting a tenant end a lease early because of age, illness, disability, or a move into a nursing home, assisted living or other care, and no statute ending a tenancy when a tenant becomes incapacitated. The lease controls: a fixed-term lease continues, and a month-to-month tenancy ends on ordinary written notice to end on a rent-paying date at least one month after the notice is received (for a tenant who lives in and has an ownership interest in a mobile home and rents the lot, your notice must allow at least 60 days from the next rent due date). Apart from fair housing law, the only statutes giving elderly or disabled tenants a special right to stay in their homes are in condominium conversions, where qualifying low- or moderate-income elderly tenants and disabled tenants of a converted building can claim a right to keep occupying their unit; they are not an early-exit right. Fair housing law still applies: a request to end a lease early because of a disability can be a request for a reasonable accommodation, so consider it on its facts. Cautious course: if a tenant or the tenant's family asks to end the lease because the tenant must move into care, consider agreeing to a written early termination, and in any case try to re-rent before claiming rent for the rest of the term.

title: When Missouri Bars Collecting Rent
bodyText: No Missouri statute forbids you to demand or collect rent because a unit has been cited for code violations, placarded or declared unfit, as some states do. Rent stops or moves elsewhere only in these cases: (1) when a court in a housing-code receivership case finds the building is a nuisance and orders tenants to pay rent to a receiver, the tenants pay the receiver, and rent paid under the order is a defense to your eviction for nonpayment; (2) when a court appoints a receiver of rents because the owner of a master-metered building fell behind on heat utilities, an owner who collects or tries to collect rent from tenants while the order is in force is in contempt of court; (3) when the residence is destroyed by fire, tornado or another disaster the tenant didn't cause, the tenant owes no rent for the rest of the term. A tenant's limited repair-and-deduct right can also reduce one month's rent. Otherwise Missouri requires only that you demand the rent due before filing a rent-and-possession case, with no waiting period. Federal law adds one: if the property has a federally backed mortgage or is in a covered federal housing program, you may not require the tenant to vacate until 30 days after a notice to vacate, so give that notice before filing for possession (see the federal CARES Act row). Cautious course: fix code violations promptly, and don't rent or collect rent for a unit a local authority has ordered vacated.

title: No Hardship Delay of Evictions in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri statutes give a court no general power to delay an eviction because of the tenant's hardship (illness, weather, holidays or the like), and no county or city may impose or enforce a moratorium on evictions unless state law specifically allows it. Execution for possession can be stopped only in these ways: (1) in a rent-and-possession case, if the tenant pays or brings into court all rent in arrears and costs on the day of the money judgment, the case stops, and if the tenant pays the money judgment and costs before the judgment becomes final, execution for possession stops (if the judgment is for possession only, there is no stay except by appeal bond, court rule or agreement); (2) the tenant applies for a trial de novo or appeals and posts a bond within ten days covering damages, costs and rent due, and then pays later rent into court within ten days after it falls due; (3) in an expedited drug-related eviction, the court may stay execution if the person shows by clear and convincing evidence that immediate eviction would pose a serious danger that outweighs the community's and landlord's safety, and must stay it, with probationary tenancy, if the person meets a list of conditions (such as entering drug treatment or not having aided the activity, no weapon, no prior stay). Possession is normally delivered within days: in a rent-and-possession case the officer delivers possession within five days of receiving the execution; in an unlawful detainer case execution for possession issues no sooner than ten days after judgment; and in either case the court may order delivery within 15 days after the judgment becomes final. Court rules (not read here) may also govern stays; follow any order the court enters.

title: Serving Eviction Papers in Missouri
bodyText: Who serves and who may receive eviction papers in Missouri. Serving: the summons is served as in other civil cases, at least four days before the court date, by the sheriff or a deputy, or by a special process server the court or circuit clerk appoints under local court rules. In a rent-and-possession case you may also ask the clerk for an order that the officer post a copy of the summons and complaint conspicuously on the dwelling and mail a copy by ordinary mail, each at least ten days before the court date; and if the officer can't find the tenant, you or your agent aged 18 or older may do the posting and mailing yourselves. With posting-and-mailing service you can get possession but no money judgment against a tenant who doesn't appear. Receiving: an individual tenant is served personally, or by leaving the papers at the tenant's home with a family member over 15, or by delivering them to an agent the tenant has appointed to receive service. A company tenant is served through an officer, partner, managing or general agent, or registered agent. A lease could try to have each tenant appoint a co-tenant as agent to receive service; Missouri's service statute recognizes an agent authorized by appointment, but whether a clause in a form lease is enough is untested in the statutes read, so this library doesn't offer that clause. A landlord who wants it should take advice first. Your side: you must tell tenants in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of the manager and of the owner or person authorized to receive service of process and notices (see the manager and agent disclosure clause). A tenant in Missouri's address confidentiality program (Safe at Home) has designated the Secretary of State as agent for service of process; if you know a tenant is a participant, ask the court clerk how to serve and how to keep the participant's address out of the public record.

title: Bonds in Missouri Eviction Cases
bodyText: Missouri has no bond that a tenant must post to stay in the home while an eviction case is pending before judgment, no bond that a landlord can post to get possession early, and no statutory end-of-term possession bond. The bond rules apply only after judgment: in a rent-and-possession case, a tenant's application for a trial de novo or appeal doesn't stop execution unless, within ten days after judgment, the tenant posts bond with security enough to pay all damages, costs and rent then due, on conditions to stay waste and to pay later rent into court within ten days after each payment falls due; in an unlawful detainer case, the appeal doesn't stop restitution of the premises unless the tenant posts bond within the time for appeal for the amount of the judgment, on the same waste and rent conditions (subject to the judge's discretion), reduced by any rent subsidy the tenant receives. If the tenant posts a sufficient bond, execution for possession waits for the trial de novo or appeal; if later rent isn't paid into court as the bond requires, ask the court to act. A separate bond applies if you seek to attach a tenant's goods for rent (see the landlord attachment row).

title: No Rent-Into-Court Requirement for Tenant Defenses in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri doesn't require a tenant to pay rent into court before raising a defense or counterclaim in an eviction case, and doesn't make any counterclaim mandatory. Rent goes into court in Missouri only in these cases: (1) a tenant in a rent-and-possession case who brings into court (or tenders to you) all rent in arrears and costs on the day of the money judgment stops the case; (2) a tenant who seeks a trial de novo or appeals and wants execution for possession stayed must post a bond and pay later rent into court within ten days after each payment falls due; (3) in a housing-code receivership the court can direct rents to a receiver, and rents deposited in court can pay for repairs. In an unlawful detainer case in the associate circuit division, affirmative defenses and counterclaims must be filed in writing by the return date of the summons unless the court allows more time; a rent-and-possession case follows the Missouri rules of civil procedure, which weren't read for this library. Expect a tenant to raise conditions (for example a repair-and-deduct deduction or receivership payments) as defenses; Missouri law doesn't let you insist on rent being deposited first.

title: Minors as Tenants and Eviction Defendants in Missouri
bodyText: In Missouri a person can make a binding contract, including a lease, at 18. There is one statutory exception below 18: a 16- or 17-year-old may contract for housing if the minor is homeless or a victim of domestic violence (unless under the supervision of the Children's Division or the juvenile court), is self-supporting without a parent's or guardian's physical or financial support, and the parent or guardian has expressly or impliedly consented to the minor living independently (implied consent includes barring the minor from home, refusing all support, or abuse or neglect, or a signed letter from a homeless-services agency director, a school homeless liaison, social worker or counselor, or the minor's attorney confirming the minor is an unaccompanied youth). The statute says consent given under it can't later be disaffirmed because of the minor's age, and a legally constituted entity or licensed provider that contracts with such a minor is immune from civil or criminal liability for deciding to do so unless its decision or conduct was grossly negligent, willful or wanton; the statute doesn't say whether an individual landlord counts as such an entity. Outside that rule, a lease signed by someone under 18 is governed by common law (not read for this library), under which a minor can usually disaffirm. Cautious course: sign leases with adults; if a 16- or 17-year-old applies on their own, keep a written record of the facts that make the statutory rule apply (for example the agency or school liaison letter); otherwise have an adult sign as tenant or guarantor. In court: anyone 18 or older may sue or defend in their own name. Missouri statutes don't bar naming a minor in an eviction case, but a suit against a defendant under 18 can't go forward after service until a guardian ad litem is appointed, so name the adult tenants and adult occupants and ask the clerk how to handle minor household members. Never refuse to rent because a household includes children; familial status is protected.

title: Deadlines for Landlord and Tenant Lawsuits in Missouri
bodyText: How long you have to sue in Missouri. Missouri's general limitation periods apply to landlord-tenant claims; there is no special period for rent. An action upon a writing for the payment of money has ten years; other contract claims (express or implied) and claims on a liability created by statute other than a penalty have five years; a claim on a statute for a penalty or forfeiture given to the party aggrieved has three years. Whether a written lease's rent promise is a writing for the payment of money (ten years) or an ordinary contract claim (five years) is case law not read for this library, so treat five years from each missed payment or damage as your deadline. A contract claim is measured from when the damage is sustained and capable of ascertainment, and, where there are several items of damage, from the last item. A promise or acknowledgment revives a barred contract claim only if it is in a writing signed by the person to be charged, though the law keeps the effect of an actual payment of principal or interest. If the person you would sue is a Missouri resident who is out of the state when the claim accrues, the period runs from that person's return. An unlawful detainer or forcible entry case can't be brought against someone who has been in quiet possession for three whole years before the filing, or three whole years after the lease ended. A judgment, including one for unpaid rent, is presumed paid after ten years unless revived or paid on, and a judgment for unpaid rent may be revived by publication. For a tenant's deposit claim (twice the amount wrongfully withheld), whether the three-year penalty period or the five-year statutory period applies is case law not read; act promptly either way.

title: Landlord Remedies When a Missouri Tenancy Ends
bodyText: Your remedies when a Missouri tenancy ends or the tenant defaults, and how to pursue them. (1) Possession only through court: never lock out, remove belongings or cut essential services. (2) Unpaid rent: a rent-and-possession case gives a judgment for possession and for the rent then due plus costs; you may instead sue for possession alone, and you may join other unpaid sums the lease requires (not property damage), but those sums aren't rent and don't by themselves support possession. With posting-and-mailing service, a defaulting tenant can be ordered out but no money judgment is entered. Once a possession judgment in that case is executed, the tenant is barred from re-entry and you hold the premises discharged from the lease. (3) A tenant who willfully holds over after the term ends and does not leave after your written demand for possession: an unlawful detainer case awards possession plus double the damages found (including waste) and double the monthly rent found until possession is restored. (4) Allowing illegal gaming, a brothel, or the illegal possession, sale or distribution of controlled substances on the premises, or, for a tenant whose term is two years or less (or who holds at will or by sufferance), violating a condition of a written lease, assigning without your written consent or committing waste: after ten days' notice to vacate you may re-enter by the procedure the law specifies (a court case). (5) Money only: sue for rent and damages in the associate circuit court, or in small claims up to $5,000, where a company may appear through an officer or employee. (6) After the tenant leaves early: you may keep from the deposit actual losses caused by the tenant's failure to give adequate notice, but only after reasonable efforts to re-rent. Missouri has no statute on accelerating all future rent when the tenant defaults or on measuring rent for the rest of the term after you retake possession; those are case-law questions not read for this library, so claim rent and charges accrued to date plus actual, mitigated losses rather than the whole remaining term.

title: When a Tenant Files for Bankruptcy in Missouri
bodyText: When a tenant files for bankruptcy, a federal automatic stay immediately stops you from starting or continuing an eviction, enforcing a judgment, or collecting rent owed from before the filing. Two federal exceptions apply to a home the tenant rents. First, if you obtained a judgment for possession before the filing, you may usually continue the eviction; the stay stays in place for 30 days only if the tenant certifies with the petition that state law lets the default be cured after judgment and deposits the next 30 days' rent with the bankruptcy court, and it continues only if the tenant then certifies a full cure. Missouri lets a tenant in a rent-and-possession case stop the eviction by paying the whole money judgment and costs before the judgment becomes final, so expect this route in that window. Second, an eviction based on the tenant endangering the property or using illegal drugs there may go ahead 15 days after you file and serve a sworn certification with the bankruptcy court, unless the tenant objects and the court rules for the tenant. In a Chapter 7 case the lease is treated as rejected if the trustee does not assume it within 60 days, unless the court extends the time. No Missouri statute adds a landlord procedure of its own. What Missouri does decide is which property a Missouri debtor keeps: Missouri has opted out of the federal exemption list, so a debtor in bankruptcy claims Missouri's exemptions (and non-bankruptcy federal ones) instead. Those include household furnishings and goods (up to $3,000 in total value until December 31, 2026, and $15,000 from January 1, 2027), a homestead the debtor owns ($15,000, rising to $40,000 on January 1, 2027), and the right to receive Social Security, unemployment, public assistance, veterans' and disability benefits. The same exemptions limit what you can take to collect an ordinary rent judgment outside bankruptcy. Cautious course: as soon as you learn a tenant has filed, stop eviction and collection steps (including deducting pre-filing rent from the deposit) unless one of the exceptions plainly applies, keep accepting current rent, and ask the bankruptcy court for relief from the stay when in doubt.

title: No Late-Benefit Defense in Missouri Evictions
bodyText: Missouri has no statute giving a tenant a defense, a continuance or reinstatement because a Social Security check, other public benefit or housing-subsidy payment arrived late. A tenant who falls behind for that reason can be sued for rent and possession like any other. Two rules still help such a tenant: in a rent-and-possession case, paying or bringing into court all rent in arrears and costs on the day of the money judgment stops the case, and paying the money judgment and costs before it becomes final stops execution for possession; and if a tenant whose rent is reduced by a local, state or federal subsidy appeals an unlawful detainer judgment, the appeal bond is reduced by the amount of the subsidy. In subsidized housing, the program's own federal rules and contracts may require notices or limit eviction for the housing authority's late share; check them. Cautious course: if you know a benefit or subsidy payment is late, accept it when it comes, and consider waiting a short time before filing for possession over a delay the tenant didn't cause.

title: Checked Across All of Missouri Law
bodyText: These points were checked across all of Missouri's statutes, not only the landlord-tenant chapters. (1) Squatters: Missouri has a fast removal procedure for people occupying a residential property who were never tenants: a verified petition, an immediate ex parte removal order on good cause, a hearing within 48 hours and enforcement by the sheriff, available only if, among other conditions, the property hadn't been leased to anyone for three consecutive months (see the squatter row). (2) Receipts for cash rent: no statute requires a landlord to give a rent receipt; the general receipt duties found bind particular businesses and officials (for example consumer lenders must give a receipt for each payment made in currency), not landlords. A written receipt for every cash payment is still the cautious course. (3) Registration before eviction: no Missouri statute makes rental registration, licensing or a certificate of occupancy a condition of an eviction or rent suit, and the one county authorized to adopt rental habitability rules may not require rental licensing, registration or certification on a regular schedule or before a home is offered for rent. Some cities have their own rental registration or licensing ordinances; check locally. (4) Company landlords: an out-of-state LLC, corporation or limited partnership doing business in Missouri without registering may not bring a suit in a Missouri court until it registers, though its leases stay valid; renting under an unregistered fictitious name is a misdemeanor but doesn't bar a suit (see the entity-representation row). (5) Nonresident owners are subject to Missouri courts for claims about their Missouri property and can be served outside the state. (6) Some reporting duties bind anyone, landlords included: reporting certain deaths to the coroner or medical examiner, and suspected abuse or neglect of vulnerable adults (see the police-cooperation row). (7) When title to a rental property with outstanding collectible judgments is transferred, the transfer must be filed in the circuit court within 30 days.

title: Other Rules Missouri Does Not Have
bodyText: Missouri has no comprehensive residential landlord-tenant act, so many rules common in other states don't exist here. Each absence below is explained, with what Missouri does have nearby, in its own row of this library. Money: no cap on late fees or required grace period; no limit on application fees; no holding-deposit rule; no rule on paying the deposit in installments; no interest owed on deposits; no rule on transferring deposits when the property is sold; no rent-receipt duty; no notice period for rent increases. Entry and conditions: no statute on landlord entry or notice to enter; no lock or security-device rule; no statewide smoke or carbon monoxide alarm rule; no mold, bed-bug, radon or flood disclosure rule; no utility submetering rule. Ending the tenancy: no just-cause requirement; no general anti-retaliation statute; no statute saying acceptance of late rent waives your rights; no general duty to mitigate by re-renting (only the deposit law's mitigation condition); no early termination for age or illness; no lease-ending rule on a tenant's death. Court: no rent-into-court requirement before a tenant raises defenses; no defense for late benefit or subsidy payments; no statutory hardship stay of an eviction; no bond a tenant must post to stay in possession before judgment; no sealing of eviction records. Domestic violence: no lock-change right and no confidentiality duty for the tenant's information, though Missouri bars evictions because a tenant is a victim. Other: no copy-of-lease duty; no immigration-status rule; no general landlord lien on household goods (attachment for rent requires a court order and a bond). Where a statute is silent, Missouri case law and the lease decide, so draft carefully and take advice on anything unusual.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri's unclaimed property law (the Uniform Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act, run by the State Treasurer) doesn't mention security deposits, but its catch-all reaches a deposit refund you owe and can't deliver, such as a refund check the former tenant never cashes. A refund that stays unclaimed for five years after it became payable is presumed abandoned (three years if the landlord is a housing authority or other government body). You then become a holder with these duties: if the refund is fifty dollars or more and you know or can find the tenant, contact the tenant first; within twelve months before turning the money over, send a first-class letter to the last known address marked for address correction; report the property to the State Treasurer before November 1 each year as of the preceding June 30, and pay the money over with the report; and keep records for five years after reporting. Once you pay it over, you are released from the tenant's later claims. Intentionally failing to report or to perform these duties can bring a penalty of five percent of the value for each month (at least $100, up to 25 percent in all), and intentionally refusing to pay over can bring daily penalties of at least $100 (up to $10,000) and a misdemeanor; the Treasurer can also impose up to 20 percent for failing to use reasonable diligence to find the tenant. Missouri has no rule letting you keep an unclaimed refund, and its deposit law lets you withhold only for unpaid rent, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear and losses from inadequate notice to end the tenancy, so don't put a clause in the lease forfeiting an unclaimed refund to you. Mailing the refund to the last known address within 30 days meets the deposit deadline, but the money is still owed until the tenant cashes it or it goes to the State Treasurer. The Treasurer's reporting forms and rules govern the details.

title: No Move-Out Notice Condition on Deposit Refunds in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no rule that lets you make the security deposit refund depend on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out, returning keys by a deadline or giving a forwarding address. Within 30 days after the tenancy ends you must return the full deposit or give the tenant a written itemized list of damages with the balance; mailing them to the tenant's last known address is enough. If the tenant fails to give the notice to end the tenancy that the law or the lease requires, you may withhold only your actual damages from that failure, after reasonable efforts to re-rent, not the whole deposit. Keeping more than the law allows exposes you to twice the amount wrongfully withheld. You may ask the tenant for a forwarding address in writing, but a missing address doesn't extend your deadline.

title: Waiving Deposit Rights in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri's security deposit law has no sentence saying a tenant cannot waive it, and no Missouri statute voids a lease term that gives up deposit rights. That doesn't make a waiver safe. The law's rules are written as mandatory: the deposit may not exceed two months' rent, it must be held in a federally insured institution, it must be returned or accounted for within 30 days after the tenancy ends, and you may withhold only for unpaid rent, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear and actual losses from inadequate notice to end the tenancy. It also applies to any money or property that secures the tenant's performance, whatever the lease calls it, so renaming a deposit doesn't take it outside the law (a pet deposit is the one exception). Whether a court would enforce a lease term that gives up any of these rules is decided by case law, and wrongful withholding costs twice the amount withheld. Cautious course: don't put any term in the lease that reduces the tenant's deposit rights, such as a longer return period, a nonrefundable portion of the deposit or extra grounds for keeping it.

title: No Deposit Standards Disclosure in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri doesn't require you to post or give tenants the standards you use to set security deposit amounts, even if you charge different tenants different deposits. The limits that apply: no deposit may exceed two months' rent, and the Missouri Human Rights Act and federal fair housing law bar setting a higher deposit, or other different terms, because of race, color, religion, national origin, ancestry, sex, disability or familial status. Cities and counties can't limit deposit amounts by ordinance. Cautious course: write down the criteria you use (for example, credit or rental history) and apply them the same way to every applicant, so you can show how each deposit was set.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no special procedure for an early or expedited return of the security deposit, and no rule allowing a fee for one. You may return the deposit, or give the itemized list of damages with the balance, at any time up to 30 days after the tenancy ends; doing it sooner is allowed. You may not take an administrative or processing fee out of the deposit: the only amounts you may withhold are unpaid rent, the cost of restoring the unit beyond ordinary wear and tear, actual losses from inadequate notice to end the tenancy, and an agreed carpet-cleaning charge if the lease includes the required notice. Wrongful withholding costs twice the amount withheld. Cautious course: don't charge a fee for processing the deposit early.

title: Deposit-Alternative Fees in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on fees or surety or insurance products offered in place of a security deposit: none requires you to offer a regular deposit instead, lets the tenant switch, or limits how a damage claim is reported. What Missouri's deposit law does say is that a security deposit is any money or property, whatever it is called, that the tenant gives you to secure performance of the lease, including against damage. So a monthly fee you keep outright to pay for a deposit-replacement product is not on its face a deposit, but a payment you hold, or apply to unpaid rent or damage, is a security deposit and must follow the deposit rules: no more than two months' rent in total, held in a federally insured institution, and returned or accounted for within 30 days after the tenancy ends. Cautious course: make the program optional, offer a regular deposit as the alternative, say in writing that the fee is not a deposit and is not refundable, and don't also hold a deposit that would bring the total above two months' rent. If you sell or arrange the insurance or surety product yourself, check with the provider whether Missouri insurance licensing applies.

title: Nonrefundable Fees and Deposits in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri doesn't require any special notice before you charge a nonrefundable fee, but it limits what can be nonrefundable. Any money or property the tenant gives you to secure performance of the lease, including against damage, is a security deposit whatever the lease calls it, so calling it nonrefundable, a fee or a cleaning deposit doesn't take it outside the deposit rules: it counts toward the two-month cap and must be returned or accounted for within 30 days after the tenancy ends, less only the amounts the law allows. A charge that pays for a service or item and isn't held as security, such as a pet fee, can be nonrefundable if the lease says so. A deposit labelled as a pet deposit isn't a security deposit, so the lease should say whether and when it is refunded. Cautious course: list each nonrefundable fee, its amount and what it pays for in the lease, and don't make any cleaning or damage charge nonrefundable; Missouri allows an agreed carpet-cleaning charge only on the terms its deposit law sets.

title: No Separate Notice for Nonrefundable Fees in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri doesn't require a separate written notice, form or signature for a nonrefundable deposit or fee. A payment that secures the tenant's performance can't be made nonrefundable at all, because it is a security deposit whatever it is called. A true nonrefundable fee for a service or item only needs to be agreed, and the lease is the right place to state it. The one deposit charge Missouri ties to lease wording is carpet cleaning: an agreed carpet-cleaning amount may be withheld only if the lease itself tells the tenant they may be liable for actual carpet-cleaning costs beyond ordinary wear and tear.

title: No Required Fee List in Missouri
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires your lease to list every fee the tenant may owe, or sets a notice period for adding a new fee. A fee you can collect is one the tenant agreed to, so a fee the lease doesn't provide for is hard to collect, and charging one, or misstating what is owed, can expose you to a claim under Missouri's Merchandising Practices Act, which covers residential leases; a tenant who leases for personal or household use may sue for actual damages if the tenant shows an ascertainable loss, that the tenant acted as a reasonable consumer would, that the practice would lead a reasonable person into the lease, and damages that can be calculated with reasonable certainty; the court may also award punitive damages, and attorney fees to whichever side prevails. Other Missouri rules on fees: a returned check you don't refer to the prosecuting attorney may carry a service charge of no more than $25 plus your bank's actual charge for the return; fees aren't rent in a rent-and-possession case, so an unpaid fee alone won't get you possession; and you can't take fees from the security deposit except as the deposit law allows. Cautious course: list every fee, its amount or how it is figured, and when it is due in the lease, and don't add a new fee during a fixed term without the tenant's written agreement. On a month-to-month tenancy, give written notice of a new fee that takes effect on a rent due date at least one month after the tenant receives it, the notice Missouri requires to end a month-to-month tenancy.

title: No Fee Transparency Law in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no rental-fee transparency law: no rule that rent be advertised or stated as one all-in figure, that fees appear on the first page of the lease, or that a statutory fee notice be used. Missouri's general consumer-protection law, the Merchandising Practices Act, does cover residential leases. It makes it unlawful to use deception or misrepresentation, or to conceal or omit a material fact, in connection with leasing, before, during or after the lease is signed, and the Attorney General's rules treat unfair practices the same way even without proof of deception. A tenant who leases for personal or household use may sue for actual damages if the tenant shows an ascertainable loss, that the tenant acted as a reasonable consumer would, that the practice would lead a reasonable person into the lease, and damages that can be calculated with reasonable certainty; the court may also award punitive damages, and attorney fees to whichever side prevails. Cautious course: state every mandatory fee in the lease with its amount, include mandatory fees when you quote or advertise the monthly cost, and don't collect any charge the lease doesn't provide for.

title: Fees for Services Not Provided in Missouri
bodyText: No Missouri statute specifically bars charging a tenant a fee for a service you don't provide, such as a trash, amenity, pest-control or valet fee for a service that never happens. But a charge for something the tenant doesn't receive is risky under Missouri's Merchandising Practices Act, which covers residential leases and makes deception, misrepresentation and unfair practices unlawful before, during and after the lease is signed. The Attorney General's rules treat breaking clear terms of a consumer contract, and failing to act in good faith in performing it, as unfair practices. A tenant who leases for personal or household use may sue for actual damages if the tenant shows an ascertainable loss, that the tenant acted as a reasonable consumer would, that the practice would lead a reasonable person into the lease, and damages that can be calculated with reasonable certainty; the court may also award punitive damages, and attorney fees to whichever side prevails. Cautious course: charge a service fee only for a service you actually provide, describe the service in the lease, and stop charging or credit the tenant for any period the service isn't available.

title: No Notice-Service Fee Rule in Missouri
bodyText: No Missouri statute authorizes or bars a lease charge for preparing or serving a notice, such as a demand for rent or a notice to end the tenancy. Missouri doesn't require a served notice before you file a rent-and-possession case: you must demand the rent before filing, and a demand is good any time after the rent is due; only in the separate suit for possession when a month's rent or more is in arrears and you have a right by law to re-enter does serving the complaint and summons count as the demand. A lease charge for a notice wouldn't be rent, so it couldn't support possession, and it can't be taken from the security deposit. A fixed notice fee that is more than your actual cost may be refused by a court as a penalty, which is decided by case law this library hasn't reviewed, so the library doesn't offer a notice-fee clause. If you want one anyway, limit it to your actual out-of-pocket cost (such as certified mail or a process server), itemize it, and take advice first. Court costs in an eviction case are awarded by the court.

title: Collection Costs in Missouri
bodyText: No Missouri statute regulates a lease charge for the cost of collecting unpaid rent or other money the tenant owes, and Missouri has no rule letting you add collection costs the lease doesn't provide for. If you want the tenant to pay what a collection agency charges you, the lease has to say so; limit the charge to what the agency actually charges, with a cap, and give the tenant written notice of the amount. A collection charge isn't rent, so it can't support possession, and it can't be taken from the security deposit. Under the Merchandising Practices Act rules, suing or threatening to sue on a household debt that is time-barred, discharged in bankruptcy, declared void or settled is an unfair practice. The collection agency must also follow federal debt-collection law. Attorney fees are a separate matter, covered by the lease's attorney-fee term.

title: Late Fees and the Usury Laws in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no statute capping late fees on residential rent or requiring a grace period, and no separate cap for mobile-home lots. Missouri's usury laws limit interest, not late fees by name: a written agreement may set interest of up to ten percent a year on money due under a contract (or a higher quarterly market rate), and without an agreed rate the legal rate on overdue sums under a written contract is nine percent a year. Overcharging interest lets the payer recover twice the interest paid, and charging more than two percent a month for the use of money is a crime. Whether a court would treat a flat late fee as interest is decided by case law this library hasn't reviewed. A court may also refuse a fee it sees as a penalty. The only Missouri late-fee figure is for self-storage units, not homes. Cautious course: set one modest flat late fee that reflects your real cost of late payment, and if the lease also charges interest on overdue amounts, keep it within the usury limits. An unpaid late fee isn't rent, so it alone won't support possession.

title: Missouri Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Missouri's statutory money limits and measures for a residential tenancy: the security deposit may not exceed two months' rent, and wrongfully withholding any of it costs twice the amount withheld. A returned check may carry a service charge of no more than $25 plus your bank's actual charge. Interest on overdue sums may be agreed in writing at up to ten percent a year (or the higher quarterly market rate); with no agreed rate the legal rate is nine percent a year, and charging more than two percent a month is a crime. Holdover: a tenant who willfully stays after the term and after your written demand for possession owes double the yearly value for the time held; a tenant who gives written notice of leaving and doesn't leave owes double rent; and an unlawful detainer judgment awards double damages and double the monthly rents and profits. If a tenant lets someone else take sole possession without your permission, a court in a rent or possession case may add damages of up to twice the rent due. A tenant's repair-and-deduct is limited to code-violation repairs costing under $300 or half a month's rent, whichever is greater, never more than one month's rent, and no more than one month's rent a year. A tenant ending the lease as a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking may be charged only a reasonable termination fee. Missouri sets no cap on late fees, application or screening fees, pet fees or rent, and cities and counties can't cap rent or deposits.

title: No Alarm Tampering Fee Rule in Missouri
bodyText: No Missouri statute authorizes or limits a fee for removing, disabling or tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, and no state statute requires you to provide alarms in a rental (local building, fire and housing codes often do). You may make the tenant responsible for the reasonable cost of repairing or replacing an alarm the tenant or the tenant's guests remove, disable or damage, and you may take that cost from the security deposit as damage beyond ordinary wear and tear. A fixed tampering fee is riskier: a court may refuse a fixed charge it sees as a penalty, under case law this library hasn't reviewed, so the library offers only the actual-cost term. If you want a fixed fee anyway, keep it close to your real cost and take advice.

title: Government Fees and Tenants in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no statewide rental license, registration or inspection fee, and no statute that allows or bars passing a government fee on to a tenant. Some cities and counties run rental registration or inspection programs with their own fees and rules, and an ordinance may say who pays; check the local rules where the property is. Without a lease term you have no right to recover a government fee from the tenant. If you want the tenant to reimburse fees the tenant causes, such as a false-alarm response fee, a special trash pickup or a reinspection caused by a condition the tenant created, the lease must say so; limit it to the amount actually charged, with no markup, and don't pass on fees for licenses or inspections the law requires you to hold. A reimbursed fee isn't rent, so it alone won't support possession, and it can't be taken from the security deposit.

title: Carpet Cleaning and the Deposit in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri's deposit law has its own carpet-cleaning rule. Without anything in the lease, you may withhold carpet cleaning from the deposit only as part of restoring the unit to its move-in condition, beyond ordinary wear and tear. With the right lease term, you may agree with the tenant on the amount or fee for carpet cleaning and withhold what you actually spend, but only if the lease also tells the tenant they may be liable for actual carpet-cleaning costs that exceed ordinary wear and tear, which may also be withheld. Within 30 days after the tenancy ends, you must give the tenant a receipt for the actual carpet-cleaning costs. Missouri has no rule requiring that the carpets were professionally cleaned before the tenancy, and no carpet-age test. Use the library's Missouri carpet-cleaning clause, which carries the required notice, rather than a clause that charges carpet cleaning to the deposit as damages for breaking the lease.

title: Late Fees in Subsidized Tenancies in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no rule on late fees when part of the rent is paid by a housing subsidy or voucher program, and no state late-fee cap for any tenancy. For a voucher or other federally assisted tenancy, the federal program rules, your housing assistance payments contract and any required lease addendum control what you may charge and when; read them before charging a late fee. Cautious course: charge a late fee, if at all, only on the tenant's own share of the rent and only when the tenant's share is late, never because the program's payment arrived late, and keep the fee modest. An unpaid late fee isn't rent, so it alone won't support possession.

title: Rent Rights and Landlord Duties in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no statute, like the uniform act some states adopted, saying that the right to receive rent can't be separated from the landlord's duties to maintain the property, whether by lease, assignment of rents, deed or mortgage. Missouri hasn't adopted that act. The tenant's code-repair remedy (repair and deduct) can't be waived in a lease, and it runs against whoever is the landlord. Whether someone who collects the rent, such as a lender under an assignment of rents or a manager, also takes on the landlord's duties is decided by case law this library hasn't reviewed. Cautious course: if you assign or pledge the rents, or hand rent collection to someone else, make sure the agreement says who will meet the landlord's duties to the tenants, and tell the tenants in writing where to pay and whom to call for repairs.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri doesn't allow a lockout for unpaid rent, even with advance notice, key access or a lease clause agreeing to it. Removing or excluding a tenant or the tenant's belongings, or removing or changing the locks, without judicial process and a court order (other than under Missouri's abandoned-premises procedure) is forcible entry and detainer, and so is willfully cutting off or interrupting a tenant's electricity, gas, water, sewer or other essential services for any reason other than health or safety. The tenant can sue to get back in and recover double the damages found and double the monthly rents and profits until restored. The only exception is Missouri's abandonment procedure: you must reasonably believe the tenant has left for good, the rent must be unpaid for thirty days, you must post and mail the statutory notice, and the tenant must fail to pay or reply in writing within ten days. Otherwise, file a rent-and-possession case. After a judgment, if the officer doesn't deliver possession within seven days of receiving the writ, you may change the locks only with a law enforcement officer present and on the other conditions the law sets.

title: Utility Deposits in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no separate rule for a utility deposit you collect from a tenant. Money you hold to cover utility charges the lease makes the tenant pay is a security deposit under Missouri law, whatever you call it: it counts toward the two-month-rent cap, must be held in a federally insured institution, and must be returned or accounted for within 30 days after the tenancy ends. Missouri's deposit law lets you withhold for unpaid rent, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear and losses from inadequate notice, and doesn't name utility charges; whether unpaid utility bills you pass on to the tenant count as rent for this purpose is unsettled. Cautious course: bill unpaid utility charges to the tenant separately, or get the tenant's written agreement at move-out before deducting them, and itemize any deduction. A deposit the tenant pays a utility company is governed by the utility's rules, not by you; if never claimed, it eventually goes to the State Treasurer as unclaimed property.

title: No State Health-District Rental Rules
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires you to give tenants a health department's rental regulations, to refer tenants to a health department, or to follow a separate set of state health-district rules for rentals. Local health rules can still reach your property: county commissions and county health center boards may adopt health orders, ordinances, rules and regulations (they may not conflict with the state health department's rules, and violating a published county health ordinance is a misdemeanor), and cities have their own code powers. One county in a population bracket set by statute (Boone County) may adopt habitability rules for rented homes that are enforced only on a paying tenant's written complaint. Under the state lead law, if the state health department or a licensed local health department finds a lead hazard, it notifies the owner and an adult occupant in writing, and you must abate it or put in interim controls in the time given, or take the home off the rental market. No state law blocks local health codes for rentals: Missouri's ban on local rent control and on local source-of-income, screening, deposit-limit and right-of-first-refusal ordinances does not reach them (Boone County's habitability rules carry their own statutory limits). Check the county health department's rules and the city code where the property is.

title: No Statewide Lead-Safe Certification
bodyText: Missouri has no statewide lead-safe or lead-free certificate for rental housing: no state law requires you to have a home inspected or certified lead-safe before renting it, or to attach a lead certificate to the lease. What Missouri does require: if the state health department or a licensed local health department finds a lead hazard at a home (inspections and risk assessments of a home follow notice that a resident of the home has an elevated blood lead level), it gives you and an adult occupant written notice with options and a deadline, and you must abate the hazard or put in interim controls as allowed, or take the home off the rental market; you may not otherwise evict a tenant because of a resident's elevated blood lead level or because of action the lead law requires of you (eviction for any other lawful reason is not affected). State law expressly lets cities, villages and other local governments adopt their own lead poisoning control systems with the same or higher standards, so a local lead-safe certificate or inspection requirement is not preempted; check the city or county code where the property is. The federal lead-based paint disclosure still applies to homes built before 1978.

title: No Required Tenant Rights Guide
bodyText: Missouri does not publish a statutory landlord-tenant rights and responsibilities guide that you must give tenants, and no state law requires you to hand tenants any summary of their rights before signing or at renewal, or to get a signed acknowledgment of one. The only state-published material the statutes call for is lead information: the state health department must post on its website educational information explaining the rights and responsibilities of property owners and tenants under the lead law, but you are not required to deliver it. Separate required notices still apply where their own facts arise (for example, a condominium conversion notice must set out the tenants' rights under that law, and the federal lead-based paint disclosure applies to homes built before 1978). No state law bars a city or county from requiring a local tenant-rights notice, so check the local code where the property is.

title: No Good-Cause Eviction Notice
bodyText: Missouri has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law, so there is no Missouri notice telling a tenant whether the home is covered by one, no statutory form, and no reason you must state when you end a periodic tenancy or decline to renew. A fixed-term lease ends on its end date with no notice to quit. A month-to-month tenancy ends by written notice ending it on a rent-paying date at least one month after the other party receives it, and a tenancy at will or for less than a year ends on one month's written notice (if the tenant lives in and has an ownership interest in a mobile home and rents the lot, your notice must end a tenancy of less than a year no sooner than 60 days from the next rent due date); the notice need not give a reason. No state statute bars a city or county from adopting its own just-cause rule (the statute limiting local housing ordinances covers rent amounts, source of income, screening criteria, deposit limits and rights of first refusal, and a separate statute bars local eviction moratoria), so check the local code where the property is. If the tenancy is in federally assisted housing or under a housing choice voucher, federal program rules may add their own requirements for ending it; check those rules.

title: Changing Lease Terms
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on notice for changing the terms of a tenancy. Nothing lets you serve a notice that by itself rewrites a lease, and nothing sets a separate notice period for raising a fee or changing any other term. During a fixed term, terms change only by written agreement with the tenant. For a month-to-month tenancy, the route is to end the tenancy and offer a new one: give written notice ending it on a rent-paying date at least one month after the tenant receives it, and offer the new terms; a tenancy at will or for less than a year ends on one month's written notice. If the tenant lives in and has an ownership interest in a mobile home and rents the lot it sits on, your notice ending a tenancy of less than a year must end it no sooner than 60 days from the next rent due date. Put the new terms in a signed writing: once a written lease has ended, a court will not accept oral evidence that it was renewed or replaced, and a notice ending a periodic tenancy can be changed only by a later dated writing. The library offers an optional clause that builds this route into a month-to-month lease. A manufactured or mobile home land lease community may not raise rent (other than for property taxes) in the 60 days before giving its 120-day notice of a change in use, or at any time after giving it. Local rent control is preempted, so a city cannot cap the increase itself.

title: No State Limit on Renting in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: No Missouri statute limits renting homes in single-family zones, requires an owner to live on the lot before renting there, or limits short-term letting of homes in those zones. Zoning is local: cities, towns and villages may regulate population density and the use of buildings and land for residence, and counties may zone their unincorporated areas under the county zoning statutes, so a local zoning or occupancy ordinance may affect whether and how a home can be rented. State law does set some fixed points: for zoning purposes a single-family dwelling includes a home where eight or fewer unrelated people with disabilities live (with up to two houseparents) and a licensed foster home for fewer than seven children, and zoning by a first-class charter county may not take away an existing lawful use from an owner or tenant except by reasonable rules for gradually eliminating nonconforming uses. No state law preempts a local rule tying rentals to owner occupancy (the statute limiting local housing ordinances covers rent amounts, source of income, screening criteria, deposit limits and rights of first refusal), and whether a city may treat rented homes differently from owner-occupied ones is a question for the courts. Check the zoning and rental code of the city or county where the property is.

title: No Accessory Dwelling Unit Statute
bodyText: Missouri has no accessory dwelling unit statute. State law neither requires cities and counties to allow accessory dwelling units nor restricts them, and it sets no owner-occupancy rule, minimum rental term or other condition for renting one. Whether you may build or rent an accessory unit (a backyard cottage, garage apartment or basement unit) is decided by the city or county zoning code, under the general power of cities, towns and villages, and of counties under the county zoning statutes, to regulate population density and the use of buildings and land for residence. No state law preempts a local owner-occupancy or rental rule for these units. If you rent one, the ordinary landlord-tenant rules apply to it like any other home, and the library offers an optional clause that records which areas and utilities the unit shares with the main house.

title: Landlord Registration
bodyText: Missouri has no statewide landlord or rental-property registration or licensing. A few narrower state rules apply instead. If you are not a Missouri resident or are a corporation, you must file with the Secretary of State a written designation of a Missouri agent for service of legal papers. If you own real estate in the City of St. Louis and live outside the city, you must register with the city assessor an agent to accept service for city building, occupancy and other code violations, and re-register any change within 30 days; failing to do so is a misdemeanor (the revisor notes a 2002 court decision striking down a provision of the 2000 bill that amended this law, so confirm its current terms with the city). A state statute lets municipalities and St. Louis County charge, by ordinance, a semiannual registration fee of up to $200 on a home that has stood vacant for at least six months with housing-code violations (its wording can be read to reach every municipality or only those over one million inhabitants). Boone County's optional habitability rules may not require rentals to be licensed, registered or certified on a regular schedule or before they are offered for rent. Apart from that, no state law bars a city or county from requiring rental registration, licensing or inspection (the statute limiting local housing ordinances covers rent amounts, source of income, screening criteria, deposit limits and rights of first refusal), so check the city and county code where the property is.

title: Recording a Lease
bodyText: Missouri does not require you to register or record a residential lease, and recording one changes none of the landlord-tenant rules between you and the tenant. Missouri's general recording law does reach leases: a written instrument that affects real estate (which the recording law defines to include chattels real, the traditional legal term for leasehold interests) may be recorded with the recorder of deeds of the county where the property is, once it has been acknowledged in the form the recording law requires. An unrecorded lease is fully valid between you and the tenant and against anyone who actually knows of it, but it is not valid against others, such as a later buyer or lender without notice, until it is deposited for record; recording gives everyone notice of its contents. Whether a tenant's possession alone gives a later buyer or lender notice of an unrecorded lease is a question for the courts. For an ordinary one-year or month-to-month lease, recording is rarely done; for a long lease, or one with an option to buy or renew, the cautious course is to record it (or have the tenant's rights confirmed in any later sale or loan).

title: Renting in a Condominium or HOA Community
bodyText: If you rent out a condominium unit or a home in a homeowners' association, the association's documents and Missouri's association statutes affect the tenancy. Condominiums: the declaration may restrict the use, occupancy and leasing of units, and the association may adopt rules and, after notice and an opportunity to be heard, levy reasonable fines for violations; fines and assessments are charged against the unit owner and become a lien on the unit, so you, not the association's tenant, are answerable to the association. If you fall more than 60 days behind on assessments, the association may send your tenant a written demand (with a copy to you) to pay later rent to it until you are current, the association releases the tenant or the tenant leaves; a tenant who pays the association after that demand cannot be sued by you for that rent, and a tenant who does not pay the association can be evicted by it. The declaration can also give tenants the vote on specified matters. Amending a condominium declaration generally takes owners holding at least 67% of the votes, and changing the uses to which units are restricted takes unanimous consent; whether a new leasing restriction counts as a change of use, and whether it binds owners who already rent, is a question for the courts. Covenants: no deed restriction or covenant running with the land may ban fixed, ground-mounted political signs, rooftop solar panels on a roof the owner owns, controls and maintains, sale signs, or up to six chickens on a lot of two-tenths of an acre or more, though a homeowners' association (the statute's term excludes condominium associations) may adopt reasonable rules; and no association document may contain a discriminatory covenant. Missouri sets no cap on association lease-approval fees, no limit on the tenant information an association may request, and no association-held tenant deposit rule. If your lease makes the tenant pay fines the tenant causes, collect them separately: Missouri's deposit law lets you keep deposit money only for unpaid rent, damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, and losses from inadequate notice to end the tenancy, so do not deduct an association fine from the deposit, and do not rely on labelling it rent in the lease: Missouri's rent-and-possession chapter, which also holds the deposit law, says other lease sums are not rent for its purposes however the lease labels them.

title: Association Documents and the Lease
bodyText: Missouri does not require a lease of a condominium unit or of a home in a homeowners' association to disclose the association's obligations, rules or documents to the tenant, or to include any statement about them. The condominium act's resale certificate (the declaration, bylaws, rules, assessments and other association information) is owed to a purchaser, and an ordinary tenant is not one: a lease counts as a purchase only if it runs, with renewal options, for 20 years or more. If you sign a lease that long for a unit in a condominium created after September 28, 1983, give the tenant a resale certificate before signing, which you can get from the association within ten days of asking. For ordinary leases, giving the tenant the association's rules and the restrictions that limit use of the home is still the practical course, because the tenant has to follow them and the association's notices about violations go to you; the library offers an optional clause recording that you did so.

title: Flags, Signs and Displays
bodyText: Missouri gives tenants no statutory right against a landlord to display flags, signs or other items, so you may set reasonable display rules in the lease. Three state rules touch displays. Deed restrictions and covenants running with the land, homeowners' association covenants among them, may not ban political signs (fixed, ground-mounted signs for or against a candidate or ballot measure); the association may set reasonable rules on time, size, place, number and manner, may remove a sign in the common ground or one that is unsafe or unlawful, and must give the homeowner three days after written notice before removing a sign from the homeowner's property or fining for it. No city, town or village ordinance may regulate the display of a properly displayed United States flag, but that limits governments, not landlords. And no local ordinance may stop an owner or agent from posting a sign of reasonable size advertising the property for sale or lease. Whether the political-sign rule reaches a lease restriction (it speaks of deed restrictions, covenants and similar agreements running with the land) has not been settled; the cautious course, for a home in a homeowners' association, is not to ban a tenant's political yard sign outright but to limit it by reasonable rules. Apply any display rule in the same way to every tenant whatever the message, because singling out religious or other protected displays can be housing discrimination, and allow a display or fixture a tenant needs as a reasonable accommodation for a disability. The library offers an optional display-rules clause.

title: EV Charging: Rules for Owners
bodyText: Missouri gives tenants no statutory right to install electric vehicle charging and sets no landlord rules for allowing it, so any permission, conditions, cost-sharing and electricity charges are for the lease. Three state rules matter if you do provide or allow charging. First, someone not otherwise in the business of producing or selling electricity who owns, leases, operates or manages EV charging stations is not an electrical corporation, so letting tenants charge, or charging them for it, does not by itself make you a regulated electric utility. Second, Missouri's weights and measures law applies to electrical charging stations, and a utility-type meter is exempt from it only if it is not used for charging electric vehicles at a retail location; whether a charger that bills tenants by the kilowatt-hour is a commercial device under that law has not been settled, so if you meter and bill charging by use, check with the state Department of Agriculture's weights and measures division (a flat charge stated in the lease avoids the question). Third, no city or county may require EV charging stations, or wiring for future ones, on a parking lot owned by or leased to a church or tax-exempt nonprofit; local building codes may otherwise require EV-ready parking in new construction, so check them. Any money you hold to secure a tenant's charging obligations is part of the security deposit and counts toward the two-month limit. The library offers an optional installation clause.

title: EV Chargers When the Tenancy Ends
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on who owns, removes or pays for an electric vehicle charger when a tenancy ends. Whether equipment a tenant attached becomes part of the property is decided by court-made fixture law, so settle it in the lease: the library's optional installation clause lets you choose whether the tenant removes the charger and repairs the damage, or leaves it in place as your property. The library does not also offer a separate end-of-tenancy charger clause for Missouri, because its wording (the charger stays the tenant's property) would conflict with the second choice. At move-out you may withhold from the deposit what is reasonably needed to restore the home to its condition at the start of the tenancy, ordinary wear and tear excepted, which covers repairing damage from a charger's installation or removal; list it on the itemized statement within 30 days.

title: Solar Panels and Plug-In Solar Devices
bodyText: Missouri gives tenants no right to install solar panels or plug-in (balcony) solar devices, so whether a tenant may do so is for you and the lease. Two state rules apply around it. No deed restriction or covenant running with the land may limit or prohibit rooftop solar panels or collectors on a roof the owner owns, controls and maintains, though a homeowners' association (the statute's term excludes condominium associations) may adopt reasonable placement rules that do not prevent installation, impair or restrict the device, or adversely affect its cost or efficiency; that protects you as owner, not the tenant against you. Under the net metering law, a customer who owns or operates a renewable generator on premises it owns, leases or controls can net meter with the utility, but no one may connect or operate a generator in parallel with the utility's lines without the utility's written approval, and the utility may disconnect service immediately and without notice if someone does. A plug-in solar device that feeds power into the home's wiring can fall within that rule, so require your written consent and the utility's approval before any device is connected. If a tenant with a disability needs a modification, the fair housing rules on reasonable modifications still apply. The library offers an optional solar-device clause.

title: Cable, Internet, Phone and Antennas
bodyText: Missouri gives tenants no right to the cable, internet or phone provider of their choice and gives providers no right of access to a rental building, so wiring, provider access and installation are for you and the lease. Federal law protects many antennas: a lease rule that unreasonably delays or prevents the installation, maintenance or use of a satellite dish or other reception antenna one meter or less across (or a broadcast television antenna), or unreasonably increases its cost, on property within the tenant's exclusive use or control, such as a balcony or patio, is prohibited, except for a clearly defined safety rule or a historic-preservation rule that is no more burdensome than necessary; any fee must be reasonable. You may still bar installations on roofs, exterior walls and common areas that the tenant does not exclusively control. Missouri's own rule is about phone service in multi-unit property: if you let another voice provider install on the condition that the local phone company is excluded during construction, take incentives for excluding it, or collect mandatory charges for another provider's voice service through rent, fees or dues, the local phone company is released from its duty to serve the occupants, and you must then tell every occupant (and any later owner) that it has no facilities there and been released, and who provides phone service and by what technology; a buyer must also be told in writing of any exclusive-provider arrangement. Once those conditions end and no company is providing voice service there, a petition of more than half the residents (or your written request) can bring the local phone company back. The library offers an optional clause on installations.

title: No Political Canvassing Access Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute giving candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators or other canvassers a right to enter an apartment building, gated community or other private rental property, and none barring you from restricting their access to common areas. Missouri's political-sign rule is about display, not access: deed restrictions and covenants running with the land, homeowners' association covenants among them, may not ban fixed, ground-mounted political signs. Tenants may still invite visitors, including campaign workers, to their own homes under the lease's guest terms. Missouri's constitutional rights of speech and peaceable assembly limit government, and whether they reach a private owner's property is a question for the courts. Check the city code, since local rules on solicitation may apply.

title: No Religious Display Statute
bodyText: Missouri has no statute giving tenants a right to display religious or cultural items, such as a mezuzah, wreath or symbol on the entry door, and none limiting how you regulate them. Missouri's fair housing law still applies: you may not discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental because of religion, national origin or another protected class, so a rule that bans or singles out religious or cultural items, or is enforced only against some faiths, risks a discrimination claim. Keep any display rule neutral (the same limits on size, placement and damage for every item and every tenant), and consider allowing small items on or beside the entry door. A religious organization (or a nonprofit it operates, supervises or controls) renting housing it owns or operates for other than a commercial purpose may limit or prefer occupants of the same religion, unless membership in that religion is restricted because of race, color or national origin. The library's optional display-rules clause applies the same limits to every item whatever its message.

title: No Tenant Organizing Statute
