bodyText: Missouri has no statute giving tenants a right to form or join a tenants' association, to meet in common areas or to distribute organizing materials, and no statute barring a landlord from retaliating against organizing; Missouri also has no general retaliation statute. The constitutional right to organize and bargain collectively is for employees, not tenants, and the rights of speech and assembly limit government. Some state rules involve resident groups: a not-for-profit neighborhood association may petition for a housing-code receivership of a neglected building, and the Kansas City housing authority's board has one seat elected by its tenants, while a resident organization chooses two of the five members of the committee that nominates the appointed members. Federal fair housing law bars interfering with or retaliating against people for exercising fair housing rights, and federally assisted housing may carry federal rules on tenant organizing; check them if they apply. The cautious course is not to penalize tenants for meeting or organizing.

title: Utility Allowances and Overage Charges in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no general law that limits a utility allowance in a lease or what you may charge a tenant for a utility you pay, so an allowance with a tenant-paid overage is a contract term. The exception is a rental project financed with a Missouri Housing Development Commission housing trust fund loan or grant: its rent cap includes utilities, and if the tenant pays utilities directly the maximum rent drops by the Commission's utility allowance; federally assisted and tax-credit housing follow their own program allowances. Missouri does not treat an overage charge as rent in a rent-and-possession case; you can join a claim for it in that case, but a judgment for it does not by itself get you possession. Cautious course: charge the tenant only the provider's actual charge above the allowance, with a copy of the bill, and don't resell electricity, gas or water to tenants through your own meters at a markup, since that could raise the question whether you are acting as a regulated utility (ask the Public Service Commission first).

title: Splitting Shared Utility Costs in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no law that voids or limits a lease term making the tenant pay a share of utilities that are not separately metered to the unit, so how you split shared utility costs is a contract term. If you use one, say in the lease which utilities are shared, how each tenant's share is figured (for example by unit, by occupants or by square footage) and when it is due, and charge only your actual cost. For city, town or district water and sewer service, where several homes share one water or sewer line, the property owner is liable to the provider for the whole bill whatever the lease says, so collecting the tenant's share is your job. An unpaid share is not rent in a rent-and-possession case.

title: No Utility Disclosure Attachment in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri requires no utility disclosure attached to or delivered with a residential lease: no statement of how shared or submetered utilities are billed, no past bills or average costs, and no utility addendum. Your right to charge a tenant for a utility comes from the lease itself, so write the terms into it: which utilities the tenant puts in the tenant's own name, which you provide, and how any utility you bill to the tenant is figured and paid. The disclosures Missouri does require are covered elsewhere in this library (the owner and manager address, methamphetamine production you know of, radioactive or hazardous contamination a report has told you of, and federal lead-based paint).

title: Utility Shutoff Notices to Landlords in Missouri
bodyText: For city, town, village or district water and sewer service to a home with its own lines, Missouri law already brings you into the loop: once the tenant is 30 days behind, the provider must make a good-faith effort to tell you, and any termination notice must go to both the tenant and you. You don't need to sign anything for this. For electricity, gas, water and sewer from a utility regulated by the Public Service Commission, neither Missouri's statutes nor the Commission's shutoff rules give you or the tenant a way to sign you up for copies of the tenant's shutoff notices; a utility's own tariff or program may offer one, so ask. The Commission's rules do require the utility, at least 10 days before a shutoff for nonpayment, to post notices in the public areas of a single-metered apartment building, and to give written notice to an occupant who isn't the utility's customer once it knows. If the utility needs to reach a meter inside your building to shut off one tenant, it may ask you in writing to arrange access; if you don't make and keep reasonable arrangements, it can get in at your expense, including legal fees, court costs and locksmith charges. Electric cooperatives and city-owned electric systems follow their own rules. In the meantime, don't count on hearing from the utility: the lease can require the tenant to keep the utilities on and to give you a copy of any shutoff notice right away.

title: No Submetered Utility Shutoff Rules in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no special rules for shutting off electricity or another utility that you supply to a tenant through your own submeter, such as required notices or a meter-reading request. The general rule applies instead: if you willfully interrupt, or cause the interruption of, essential services such as electricity, gas, water or sewer to the tenant or the premises, you commit forcible entry and detainer, and the tenant can sue to be restored and recover double damages. The only exception is action taken for health or safety reasons. So don't cut off submetered service for nonpayment; collect an unpaid utility charge as a debt under the lease or through the courts.

title: Utility Shutoff Rules in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri law limits when utilities may shut off a home for nonpayment, which matters for utilities in your name and for tenants who fall behind on their own accounts. Cold weather rule: from November 1 to March 31, gas or electric service used for heat (or to run the only heating equipment) may not be cut off for nonpayment on a day when the local forecast for the next 72 hours calls for temperatures below 32 degrees, or when the utility can't reconnect the next day and freezing weather is forecast. This covers all residential users, including apartment tenants. Hot weather rule: from June 1 to September 30, gas or electric service used for cooling may not be cut off for nonpayment when the forecast calls for more than 95 degrees or a heat index above 105, with the same reconnection limit. The Public Service Commission's own rules add further protections and notice terms for the utilities it regulates; its discontinuance rule (posted notices in single-metered apartment buildings, notice to occupants who aren't the customer, owner meter access) is covered in the library's shutoff-notice entry, and its own cold weather rule wasn't reviewed here. If you pay for heat in a building of two or more units and fall behind, the utility must post notice for tenants at least five days before shutoff, and tenants can ask the court for a receiver to collect rents and pay for heat. For a residence with its own private water and sewer lines, city, town and district water and sewer termination notices go to both the occupant and the owner (service the owner applied for and is billed for directly is the owner's account), and water may be cut off for sewer charges more than three months behind after notice. Missouri has no statute barring shutoffs during a declared storm or other emergency. Whatever the utility may do, you may not interrupt a tenant's utilities yourself except for health or safety reasons.

title: No Utility Cutoff for Untransferred Accounts in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no rule letting you cut off a utility still in your name because the tenant didn't move the account into the tenant's own name, within three days or any other period. Don't put a clause like that in a Missouri lease and don't act on one: willfully interrupting, or causing the interruption of, electric, gas, water or sewer service to a tenant or the premises is forcible entry and detainer unless you act for health or safety reasons, and the tenant can recover double damages. Instead, have the lease say which utilities the tenant must put in the tenant's own name and by what date, and that the tenant will reimburse you the provider's actual charges for any period the account stays in your name. For city or district water and sewer service you applied for in your own name, the bill is your responsibility to the provider, so collect the tenant's reimbursement under the lease.

title: Reselling Electricity to Tenants in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no disclosure rule for landlords who bill tenants for electricity through submeters. The bigger question is whether you may resell electricity at all. Missouri's utility law treats anyone who owns or manages equipment used to distribute or sell electricity as an electrical corporation subject to the Public Service Commission, and its exception for distributing electricity to tenants on private property covers only electricity that is not for sale to others. So reselling electricity to tenants by the kilowatt-hour could be read to make you a regulated utility. Separately, the Commission's metering rule requires a separate electric meter for each home in an apartment building whose construction began after June 1, 1981, and for each mobile home in a mobile home park begun after that date, with exceptions for transient housing such as dormitories and rooming houses and for electricity used in central heating, hot water, ventilating and air-conditioning systems. The rule says nothing about submetering by a landlord. Cautious course: have each unit served and billed directly by the utility, or include electricity in the rent or a flat utility charge you set in the lease, and ask the Commission before submetering and reselling electricity, gas or water to tenants.

title: No Energy Data Release Rule in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on releasing a tenant's energy or water usage data to you, for building benchmarking or any other purpose, and no statewide benchmarking requirement; a lease clause doesn't by itself make a utility hand over a tenant's account data. If you want the data, get the tenant's written authorization in the lease and a promise to sign the utility's own release form, limit it to usage data and stated purposes, keep the data private, and let the tenant withdraw consent without it being a lease breach. Each utility sets its own release rules, and a city ordinance may impose benchmarking where the building is located.

title: No Meter Conservation Charge Rule in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no statute that attaches an energy-efficiency repayment charge to a utility meter so that later customers at the same address keep paying it, and no rule requiring you to tell a new tenant about one or to reduce rent for it. Missouri also has no statute on submetered water that sets the rate you may charge tenants or requires a meter statement. If a utility's own program (set in its tariff) puts a charge on the bill for improvements at your property, tell the tenant before signing and say in the lease who pays it.

title: Unpaid Water and Sewer Bills as Liens in Missouri
bodyText: In Missouri, city, town, village and district water and sewer service is treated as furnished to both the occupant and the owner, so the provider can sue you for your tenant's unpaid bill, though for no more than 90 days of service once the tenant is more than 90 days behind. Unpaid sewer charges of a city, a sewer district or a public sewer district can also become a lien on your land once the provider files a notice of delinquency with the recorder of deeds, and a public sewer district's lien ranks just behind state and county taxes. Those lien laws don't exempt an owner when the tenant was the customer, and no law lets a lease clause or an affidavit keep a tenant's unpaid bill off your property. A water supply district's lien, by contrast, arises only when the property owner is the person who owes for the water. Cautious course: require the tenant to keep water and sewer accounts current and show proof on request, act quickly on any delinquency notice the provider sends you, and consider keeping water and sewer in your name and recovering the cost through the rent.

title: No Statewide Heat Standard in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri's statutes don't require a landlord statewide to supply heat or keep a rental at a minimum temperature, and they don't limit a lease term making the tenant pay for heat; who provides and pays for heat is set by the lease. Local housing and property maintenance codes often do set heat standards, and if a heating problem violates the local code, a qualifying tenant may use Missouri's limited repair-and-deduct remedy. One county (Boone County) may adopt habitability rules requiring heat to rented homes, though a utility the tenant fails to pay for doesn't count against you. If you pay for the gas or electric service that runs the heat in a building of two or more units and fall far enough behind that the utility gives written notice that service is subject to termination, tenants (or the utility) can ask the court for a receiver of the rents to keep the heat on; and you may not interrupt heat or the utilities that run it except for health or safety reasons. One statewide safety rule does reach heating equipment: a steam or hot water heating boiler or a hot water supply boiler must have a state inspection certificate (renewed every two years for low-pressure boilers) unless it is exempt; the exemptions cover, in a private home or an apartment house of fewer than six families, steam heating boilers of up to 15 psig, hot water heating boilers of up to 30 psig and hot water supply boilers of up to 160 psig or 250 degrees Fahrenheit, and, in any building, steam heating boilers of up to 10 psig rated at no more than 1,200 square feet of radiation and hot water heating boilers of up to 20 psig rated at no more than 2,000 square feet of radiation; a boiler outside these limits needs a certificate even in a small building. Operating one without a valid certificate is a misdemeanor. This doesn't apply in a city or charter county that regulates boilers by its own ordinance, and ordinary household water heaters are exempt. Courts may also recognize habitability duties that this library hasn't reviewed, so the cautious course is to keep heating equipment you supply in working order.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no statute requiring you to set a water heater to a maximum temperature, before a new tenant moves in or at any other time, or to supply hot water at a set temperature. Ordinary household water heaters are also exempt from the state's boiler inspection law; other hot water supply boilers are exempt only in private homes and apartment houses of fewer than six units, and only up to 160 psig or 250 degrees Fahrenheit. Local plumbing and housing codes may set hot water standards, and one county (Boone County) may require access to hot water in rentals. Setting the temperature low enough to prevent scalding is the cautious course.

title: No Steam Radiator Cover Rule in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no statute requiring you to install steam radiator covers, on request or otherwise, and no required lease rider about them. Local housing codes may address exposed heating surfaces, and covering hot radiators in a home with young children is a sensible precaution. If the building's heat comes from a steam or hot water boiler, the state boiler inspection rules may apply, depending on the boiler's pressure and rating and the size of the building (see the heating row).

title: No Stove or Refrigerator Rule in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no statute requiring a landlord to supply a stove, oven or refrigerator in a rental. Whether appliances come with the home, and who maintains them, is up to the lease, so list the appliances you provide and say who repairs them. Local housing codes may require cooking or refrigeration facilities, or require appliances you do provide to work safely; check the code where the property is located.

title: Excluding Appliances in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no statute presuming that appliances at the property are supplied by you, and none barring a lease from excluding them. The lease decides: list the appliances you supply, and if you leave items at the property that you won't maintain (such as a prior occupant's washer), name them in the lease as not included. Don't use an exclusion for anything whose failure could seriously affect health or safety, such as a gas appliance, water heater or furnace, or for anything the local housing code requires you to provide. A lease can't take away a qualifying tenant's right to repair a local code violation and deduct the cost, and whether a lease can excuse you from liability for injuries is left to court decisions.

title: No Portable Cooling Device Rule in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no law giving tenants a right to install a portable or window air conditioner, and none requiring a lease that restricts window units to say so. You may allow, limit or forbid them in the lease, for example by requiring your approval, safe installation that doesn't damage window frames, and removal at move-out. Missouri also doesn't require a landlord to provide air conditioning, though local codes may. Utilities may not cut off a tenant's electric or gas service used for cooling for nonpayment on forecast days above 95 degrees or a heat index above 105 between June 1 and September 30. A request for a cooling unit as a disability accommodation is decided under fair housing law, not the lease alone.

title: No Window Guard Rule in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no statute requiring window guards or window stops in rentals where children live, no required lease notice about them, and no state rule on burglar or security bars over windows. Local building and property maintenance codes may require bedroom windows to open for emergency escape and may limit bars that can't be released from inside, so check the local code before installing bars. Installing window stops or guards on upper-floor windows in homes with young children is a sensible precaution.

title: Pool Safety in Missouri Rentals
bodyText: Missouri has no statute requiring a residential landlord to fence a pool, install a pool alarm or cover, or give tenants a pool safety notice; local building and pool codes usually set those rules, so check the code where the property is located. A few state rules do reach rental pools. At a pool serving apartments, condominiums or another group of five or more living units, it is a misdemeanor to knowingly refuse to let someone use a life jacket when a physician's signed statement says the person needs one. Missouri's law limiting landowner liability for recreational use does not protect you for injuries in a swimming pool or a residential area. If you run a place that rents five or more rooms to the public for hire, such as an apartment hotel, it needs a state lodging license and its pools and spas must meet the health department's code or the local code. A private pool that charges admission must carry at least $1 million of liability insurance and register with the state, but an amenity pool included in the rent is not that kind of pool.

title: Fire and Building Codes in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no statewide fire code or building code for ordinary rental housing. Fire and building standards come from the city or county where the property is located: cities adopt their own codes, and a first- or second-class county may adopt a nationally recognized building code (with voter approval if it had none before 2001). A qualifying tenant can use Missouri's limited repair-and-deduct remedy for a violation of the local housing or building code. One old statewide rule does apply: the owner or lessee of every hotel, boarding or lodging house and tenement house (and other listed buildings) three or more stories tall must provide fire escapes, built and kept in repair to the approval of the city building commissioner or fire chief (or the county sheriff outside a city). Newer buildings may meet this with interior fireproof stair shafts. Failing to comply is a misdemeanor, each day a separate offense. Treat any apartment building of three or more stories as covered. If you rent five or more rooms to the public for hire, as in an apartment hotel, you also need a state lodging license and must meet the health department's fire safety code or the local code.

title: Fire Sprinklers in Missouri Rentals
bodyText: Missouri has no statewide law requiring a residential landlord to install sprinklers or retrofit an existing rental building with them. Whether an apartment building must have sprinklers depends on the building and fire code the city or county adopted, usually for new construction or major renovation. For new one- and two-family homes and townhouses, the builder must offer the buyer the option of sprinklers at the buyer's cost, and local codes may not take away the buyer's right to decline; that rule concerns buyers, not rentals. Licensed residential care and assisted living facilities have their own sprinkler requirements. If your building has sprinklers, keep them inspected and maintained as the local code requires, and don't let tenants hang items from sprinkler heads.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Rule in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no law requiring you to tell tenants whether the building has a fire sprinkler system, before signing or in the lease, and no state grant, loan or tax credit for voluntarily adding sprinklers to a private rental. Telling tenants whether the unit is sprinklered, and asking them not to tamper with or hang things from sprinkler heads, is still good practice.

title: Asbestos in Missouri Rentals
bodyText: Missouri has no law requiring a residential landlord to inspect for asbestos, tell tenants about asbestos-containing materials, or include an asbestos notice in the lease. Missouri does regulate asbestos work. For projects covered by the state program (which follows the federal asbestos air-pollution rule), anyone who inspects for or removes asbestos must be state-certified, contractors must register, and removing or disturbing at least 160 square feet, 260 linear feet or 35 cubic feet of regulated asbestos material, or a regulated demolition, needs an application to the Department of Natural Resources at least ten working days ahead, based on a certified inspector's survey. Which residential projects the program reaches depends on the federal rule, so ask the department before renovating or demolishing. Cautious course: before work that could disturb old flooring, insulation, ceilings or siding, have a certified inspector check, use a certified abatement contractor, and keep tenants out of the work area. If you have received a report that the property is contaminated with hazardous material, the separate contamination disclosure applies.

title: Well Water in Missouri Rentals
bodyText: Missouri has no law requiring you to test a private well that serves a rental, or to give tenants well test results, before or during a tenancy. If your well serves at least 15 connections, or regularly serves an average of 25 or more people at least 60 days a year (a larger apartment complex or mobile home park, for example), it may be a public water system under Missouri's drinking water law, which brings required testing, reporting to the Department of Natural Resources and to customers, and notice to users of any violation. Ask the department before you rely on a well that size. If you stop using a well, Missouri law requires the landowner to plug it under the state's rules. Testing a rental's well periodically and sharing the results with tenants is a sensible precaution, and a county health ordinance may require it.

title: No Balcony Inspection Rule in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no law requiring you to have balconies, decks, porches or other exterior elevated elements inspected on a schedule, or to report their condition to tenants or a building department. The one statewide rule is for fire escapes: stair fire escapes on buildings that must have them need safe balconies with rails at least three feet high at each story, and the owner must repair an unsafe fire escape after written notice from the city building commissioner or fire chief (or the county sheriff outside a city). Local property maintenance codes may require balconies and railings to be kept safe, and regular inspection of wooden decks and balconies is a sensible precaution.

title: No Common Area Lighting Rule in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no statute requiring you to light common hallways, stairways, entrances or parking areas, and none on whether a lease may make a tenant pay for common-area lights wired to the tenant's own meter. Local property maintenance codes often set lighting standards for shared areas. If common-area lights run on a tenant's electric service, say so in the lease before the tenancy starts, so the tenant agrees to the cost. Keeping shared areas well lit is also a sensible safety and liability precaution.

title: Bed Bug and Pest Cooperation in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on bed bug or pest cooperation in rentals: no duty for the tenant to report, prepare the unit or allow treatment, no landlord treatment timetable and no rule on who pays. Missouri's housing-code receivership law does require occupants of buildings under that law to take reasonable care to dispose of garbage and other waste that could feed rodents, and local housing codes often assign extermination duties. So cover it in the lease: require the tenant to report suspected bed bugs or other pests promptly, allow entry for inspection and treatment under the lease's entry terms, and follow written preparation instructions, and say who pays (the tenant if the tenant's household or guests caused the infestation, otherwise you). Collect a tenant's share of treatment costs as a separate charge, not as rent.

title: No Pest Control Notice Rule in Missouri
bodyText: Missouri has no law requiring you to notify tenants before a pest control treatment or pesticide application in or around a rental, or to post warning signs. The state's Pesticide Use Act regulates applicators: restricted-use pesticides may be applied only by or under a certified applicator, and the Department of Agriculture may set rules on how pesticides are used and may require notice to neighboring landowners. Because you'll usually need to enter the unit, give the notice the lease's entry terms require, tell the tenant what will be applied and any preparation or re-entry instructions from the pest control operator, and follow the product label.

title: Required Disclosures for a Missouri Rental
bodyText: Missouri has no single list of required lease disclosures and no state form that must go at the front of a lease. State law requires these, each covered in its own library entry: (1) always, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of the person who manages the property and of an owner or an agent authorized to accept legal papers, notices and demands, in writing, kept current; (2) if you know the home is or was used to make methamphetamine, a written disclosure of that fact to the prospective tenant, whether or not anyone was convicted; (3) if you have received a report stating that the home is or was contaminated with radioactive or other hazardous material, a written disclosure of that fact to the prospective tenant (knowingly failing to disclose is a crime). Give items 2 and 3 before the lease is signed. Federal law adds the lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet for housing built before 1978, and a 30-day notice to vacate for properties the federal CARES Act covers (those in certain federal housing programs or with a federally backed mortgage). Two special cases: if you buy a person's home and rent it back to them (a sale-leaseback of a one- to four-unit home), you must give the seller a state-written warning in bold type on a single page at least 14 calendar days before the agreement is signed, both of you sign it when the agreement is signed, the seller gets a signed copy within five days, and title may not pass for 30 days; these duties cannot be waived. If a real estate licensee works on the rental, the licensee must give the landlord or tenant the real estate commission's broker disclosure form at the earliest practicable opportunity during or following the first substantial contact unless that person already has a written agreement with a broker. Missouri has no rent-control or just-cause law (local rent control is banned), so no lease must say whether a unit is covered by one, and adding an option to buy does not trigger any state property-condition disclosure: Missouri has no general seller-disclosure statute, though the methamphetamine, contamination and landfill disclosures apply to a sale. That the property was the site of a homicide, other felony or suicide, or that an occupant had HIV, AIDS or another disease highly unlikely to spread through occupancy, is not a fact the law requires to be disclosed in a sale or transfer.

title: Missouri Statutory Notice Forms
bodyText: Missouri has no statutory lease form and no wording that must appear in an ordinary residential lease. State law prescribes wording only for a few side documents, and where it does, use the statute's words: (1) the abandonment notice: to treat a unit as abandoned when you reasonably believe the tenant has moved out and does not intend to return and rent has been unpaid for 30 days, you post a notice on the premises and mail it by both first-class and certified mail, return receipt requested, and the notice must include the statute's paragraph (rent unpaid for thirty consecutive days, the landlord believes you have moved out, possessions may be removed unless you write within ten days, with your name and street address inserted); (2) after a trustee's foreclosure sale, the new owner's notice to a residential occupant must contain the statute's text in substance, go by certified or registered mail (or regular mail to "occupant" in an envelope marked "Notice to Occupant Following Foreclosure"), and be posted on the door; (3) in a sale-leaseback of a home, the buyer must give the seller the statute's warning, word for word, in bold on a single page; (4) a landlord who rents land for a manufactured home and enforces a lien for rent on an abandoned home uses the statute's notice contents and its sale notice. Missouri's arbitration act requires a capital-letter notice next to the signatures in a contract it covers, but the library does not offer an arbitration clause for Missouri leases. The federal lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978 is a separate federal requirement with its own content rules.

title: No Required Lease Contents Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute listing what a residential lease must contain, and no rule that the start and end dates, the rent or anything else appear on the first page or in a set order. The one written item state law requires at or before the start of every tenancy is the name and address of the person who manages the property and of an owner or agent authorized to accept legal papers, notices and demands; putting it in the lease is the simplest way to deliver it. Other required items attach only in particular cases (a known methamphetamine history, a contamination report, housing built before 1978) and are covered in their own entries. A lease for longer than one year can't be enforced unless it, or a memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party it is enforced against. Beyond that, state the essential terms clearly (the parties, the premises, the term and its start and end dates, the rent, when and where it is paid, and the deposit), because a missing or unclear term invites a dispute.

title: No Blank-Spaces Rule for Leases
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires every blank in a residential lease to be filled in before signing, or makes an incomplete lease a breach by the landlord. Missouri bans signing with blank spaces only for other kinds of consumer contracts (retail installment contracts and consumer legal funding contracts), and those rules do not reach a lease. Still, fill in or strike every blank before anyone signs, give the tenant a complete copy, and have any later insertion initialed by both sides: a term left blank may be unenforceable or disputed, and a blank completed after signing invites a claim that the tenant never agreed to it.

title: No Rule Requiring Initials on Lease Terms
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires a tenant to initial any residential lease term, or to sign a particular term separately, for it to bind the tenant; the signatures on the lease are what state law asks for. Missouri's initial-each-page and separately-signed rules belong to other contracts (consumer legal funding contracts, and leases of goods under the commercial code), and its arbitration act requires a capital-letter notice next to the signatures of a contract it covers, but the library does not offer an arbitration clause for Missouri leases. Having the tenant initial unusual or important terms (a fee, a rule the tenant might not expect, a term that departs from what the law would otherwise supply) is still good evidence that the tenant saw and agreed to them.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: Missouri has no plain-language law for residential leases: no readability test, no rule that a lease be divided into captioned sections, no minimum type size for lease terms and no dollar threshold below which a consumer-contract rule reaches a lease. Missouri's plain-language and easy-to-read-type rules are written for particular consumer products (extended service contracts, debt waivers, vehicle protection products, cemetery plot sales and some advertising), not leases. The Merchandising Practices Act still bars deception and unfair practices in connection with a lease, so a term that is hidden, misleading or written to confuse is a risk even without a formatting rule. Write the lease in clear, everyday words, use headings, and keep type readable.

title: No Consumer-Restrictions Statement
bodyText: Missouri has no plain-language consumer-contract statute that reaches residential leases, so there is no required front-page statement listing the terms that restrict the tenant or every right the tenant gives up, no readability test, no option to have the attorney general preapprove a lease form, and no dollar threshold to check. Missouri's own limits on lease terms work differently: certain terms are simply void (see the entry on lease terms Missouri law voids), and the Merchandising Practices Act bars deceptive and unfair practices in connection with a lease. A short summary of key restrictions (fees, rules, waivers of notice the law allows) is optional good practice, not a requirement.

title: No Single-Family Occupancy Notice
bodyText: Missouri has no rule requiring a landlord of a single-family home to put a notice about lawful or unlawful occupancy at the top of the lease, in larger type or anywhere else, and no presumption that an occupant is unlawful unless the lease is notarized or states particular facts. What Missouri has instead is a fast court route to remove people who were never tenants from a residential property: the owner files a verified petition and the court can order removal at once, with a hearing within 48 hours. The petition must say, among other things, that the property has not been leased to anyone for three consecutive months and that the occupants are not current or former tenants, so the route is not for anyone who holds a lease from you. A signed written lease kept on file is your best proof of who is lawfully in possession; current and former tenants are removed only through the ordinary eviction process.

title: No Lease Translation Duty
bodyText: Missouri does not require you to translate a lease, or give a translated copy, when you advertise or negotiate in a language other than English, and it sets no type-size floor tied to translation. That holds for the sale-leaseback warning too: the state-written warning a buyer must give a home seller who will rent the home back is required in bold on a single page, with no translation duty. Missouri's translation rules are for other businesses (receipts from money transmitters, insurance policies offered in another language). The constitution makes English the language of official public meetings, which does not reach private leases. If you negotiate in another language, giving the tenant a translation is good practice: say in the lease which version controls, and make sure the translation matches, since a misleading translation could be a deceptive practice.

title: No State Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: Missouri has no state-agency statement of tenant rights that you must give tenants, attach as the first page of a lease or renewal, or have each tenant sign, and no rule barring you from suing until such a statement has been given. The only rights notices Missouri law calls for in housing are narrow: a developer converting an apartment building to condominiums must give each residential tenant a conversion notice that sets out generally the tenants' rights under the conversion law, and licensed long-term care facilities give residents a list of resident rights (a care-facility rule, not a lease rule). The state health department posts lead-law information for owners and tenants on its website, but you are not required to hand it out. No state law bars a city or county from requiring a local tenant-rights notice, so check the local code.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Statement
bodyText: Missouri has no truth-in-renting law: no state agency publishes a statement of landlord and tenant rights that landlords must distribute to tenants, post in the building or give at signing, and no building-size threshold triggers one. The state health department posts lead-law information for owners and tenants on its website, but delivering it is not your duty. What Missouri requires you to hand tenants is specific to the facts (the manager and owner identity disclosure, the methamphetamine and contamination disclosures, and the federal lead disclosure for housing built before 1978), each covered in its own entry. No state law bars a local tenant-information ordinance, so check the city or county code.

title: Notices Missouri Requires in Writing
bodyText: Missouri requires these notices in writing, and a lease cannot turn them into spoken notices: (1) ending a year-to-year tenancy (at least 60 days before the end of the year), ending a tenancy at will or for less than a year (one month), and ending a month-to-month tenancy (one month, ending on a rent day); if the tenant lives in and has an ownership interest in a mobile home and rents the lot it sits on, your notice ending a tenancy of less than a year must end it no sooner than 60 days from the next rent due date; (2) the demand and written notice that must come before you can claim double the yearly value from a tenant who willfully holds over, and the demand for possession before an unlawful detainer suit; (3) the abandonment notice, posted on the premises and mailed by first-class and certified mail; (4) the itemized list of deposit deductions within 30 days after the tenancy ends, and the notice of the date and time of the move-out inspection; (5) the manager and owner identity disclosure, and the methamphetamine and contamination disclosures to a prospective tenant; (6) after a foreclosure sale, the new owner's notice to the occupant, and, if you buy a rented property, your written notice to the tenants of the transfer, its means and its date, attached to a copy of the recorded deed (or, in first-classification counties, to a notarized affidavit), before you can recover rent as the successor in title. Before an expedited drug-activity eviction for conduct by someone other than the tenant, the tenant gets at least five days' written notice first. A tenant's notice to quit is also written, and a tenant who gives one and stays past the date owes double rent. A tenant using the repair-and-deduct right must notify you in writing. Where a statute does not say how a notice is served, Missouri's general rule is delivery of a copy to the person, or leaving a copy at the person's home with a family member over 15. An electronic record can satisfy a writing requirement when both sides have agreed to deal electronically, but not where the law requires posting, mailing or another method.

title: Agreeing on How Notices Are Delivered
bodyText: Missouri landlord-tenant law has no "actual notice" standard and no provision that lets you and the tenant add a delivery method, such as a text message, that counts for a statutory notice. Two general laws decide the question instead. First, where a statute requires a notice but does not say how to serve it, delivering a copy to the person, or leaving a copy at the person's home with a family member over 15, is valid service. Second, under Missouri's electronic transactions act, if both of you have agreed to deal electronically, a law requiring information to be given in writing is met by an electronic record the recipient can print or store; but where a law requires posting, a particular kind of mail or another specific method (the abandonment notice, the unlawful detainer demand), that method still has to be used, and either side may refuse to continue dealing electronically, a right the lease cannot take away. So an email or text can carry routine written notices if the lease says so, but use the statutory method for notices that end the tenancy, demand possession, declare abandonment or start a court case, and send any electronic copy only in addition. An optional lease clause sets this up.

title: Optional Terms the Lease Can Set
bodyText: Several Missouri rules work only if the lease takes them up, and a silent lease loses them. (1) Carpet cleaning: you may withhold carpet-cleaning costs from the deposit only if the lease states the agreed amount or fee and also tells the tenant that the tenant may be liable for actual carpet-cleaning costs beyond ordinary wear and tear; you must then give a receipt for the actual cost within 30 days after the tenancy ends. (2) Domestic violence exit: a tenant who ends the lease early under Missouri's protections for victims of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking may be charged a reasonable termination fee, which the lease should state. (3) Holdover: the statutes give double the yearly value only for a willful holdover after a written demand, and double rent only where the tenant gave written notice to quit and stayed; a lease holdover charge fills the ordinary case. (4) Electronic notices: email can carry routine written notices only if both sides agreed to deal electronically, so that agreement belongs in the lease (with the right to withdraw it kept). (5) Marijuana: you may prohibit or limit marijuana cultivation and smoking on the property, but a lease signed after the constitutional amendment took effect may not bar a tenant from lawfully possessing and consuming marijuana by means other than smoking. Late fees, attorney fees and ending the lease after a fire or other casualty are covered in their own entries. Missouri has no statute regulating a lease with an option to buy or a rent-to-own home sale, so the option terms are the parties' own; but if you buy a person's home and rent it back to them, the sale-leaseback act's warning, waiting period and non-waivable remedies apply.

title: No State Lead Notice With the Lease
bodyText: Missouri adds no lead notice, certificate or information packet of its own that you must give a tenant with the lease; the federal lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet for housing built before 1978 is the only lead paperwork tied to signing. Missouri's lead law works after a problem is found: once the state health department (or a licensed local health department) has been notified that an occupant has an elevated blood lead level, it may inspect, and if it confirms a lead hazard it sends written notice to you and to an adult occupant, with options and a deadline to abate or put in interim controls; you must comply or take the home off the rental market. A lead abatement contractor, and a public or community program funding abatement, must tell owners and tenants that lead hazard information is on the health department website, and the risk assessor's findings are disclosed to owners and tenants in the contractor's notice. Apart from taking the home off the rental market, you may not evict a tenant because a resident has an elevated blood lead level or because of what the lead law requires you to do; eviction for any other lawful reason is not affected.

title: No Sex Offender Disclosure Duty
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires you to tell a tenant or applicant that a registered sex offender lives in the building or nearby, or to put a notice about the sex offender registry in the lease. The State Highway Patrol keeps a public online registry that anyone can search by name, zip code or a radius around an address, and a toll-free line, so you can point applicants to it if asked. Missouri's residency restriction (certain offenders may not reside within 1,000 feet of a school, a child care facility or a former victim's residence) is a crime by the offender, not a duty on the landlord. Fair housing law still applies to how you screen applicants, including on criminal records (see the screening entry).

title: No Pending-Foreclosure Disclosure
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires you to tell an applicant or tenant that the property is in default, that a foreclosure has been started or that a trustee sale is scheduled, before or after the lease is signed. Tenants learn of a foreclosure in other ways: in a court foreclosure the lender may name the actual tenants as defendants; after a county tax-foreclosure judgment the collector mails a copy to the occupant; and after a trustee foreclosure sale the new owner must give a residential tenant written notice of the sale and at least ten business days before any action for possession. Federal law on tenants after foreclosure may also apply; it is not covered here. Concealing a known pending sale while taking a new lease and deposit can still be a deceptive practice under the Merchandising Practices Act, so the cautious course is to tell applicants if you know a sale is scheduled.

title: Notices About Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText: Missouri splits this in two. You have no statutory duty to tell tenants that the property is in foreclosure, that taxes are delinquent, that a code-enforcement receivership is being sought or that the property is being condemned; the notices tenants get come from others (the lender who names the actual tenants in a court foreclosure, the collector who mails an occupant a copy of a tax-foreclosure judgment, the new owner after a trustee sale, the utility that posts a notice before shutting off heat in a master-metered building, and the court clerk in a condemnation once the damages are paid in). The tenant, on the other hand, has a statutory duty: a tenant served with a summons in an action to recover the property must promptly notify you or your agent, or forfeit to you the value of three years of rent. And a tenant cannot shift allegiance to a stranger: an agreement by the tenant to hold under someone else is void unless you consent, it follows a court judgment or a sale under execution or deed of trust, or it is made to a mortgagee after the mortgage has been forfeited. A buyer who takes title must give tenants written notice of the transfer before collecting rent. The library's clause asking the tenant to forward notices of proceedings applies in Missouri.

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure
bodyText: Missouri has no statewide rule that a rental must have a certificate of occupancy before it is leased, or that you disclose a certificate (or its absence) to a tenant, or that a lease is unenforceable without one. Occupancy permits are issued by cities and counties under their own codes, and state law assumes local permits exist: zoning statutes, for example, do not exempt group homes from local occupancy-permit rules except as to the number and relationship of occupants, and a 2024 law that bars local governments from requiring a home inspection before a sale expressly leaves occupancy-permit inspections alone. Cities and counties may require an occupancy permit or rental inspection, for example when a unit changes tenants, so check the local code before each new lease.

title: No Code-Order Disclosure to Tenants
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires you to tell an applicant or tenant about an outstanding housing-code violation, inspection order, notice of deficiency, placard or condemnation order before signing a lease or afterwards. What Missouri has instead are enforcement routes that can reach your tenancy: a county, city, local housing corporation or neighborhood association may, after 60 days of written notice to interested parties, ask a court to appoint a receiver to abate code violations that threaten public health or safety; a local dangerous-building ordinance must make the owner, occupant and lessee parties to a nuisance declaration, so your tenant may get the notice; in St. Louis the building commissioner notifies the owner or lessee in writing to repair or secure a dangerous structure; and in an eminent-domain condemnation the circuit clerk notifies the owners or those in possession once the damages are paid in. Renting out a unit under an order you know about, without telling the tenant, risks a claim under the Merchandising Practices Act for concealing a material fact, so the cautious course is to disclose any outstanding order that affects the unit. Local codes may require more.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: Missouri has no defective drywall law: no duty to disclose corrosive or imported drywall, or any other defective building material, to a tenant or applicant, and no remediation standard for it. The one general disclosure that could reach a building-material problem is narrow: if you have received a report stating affirmatively that the home is or was contaminated with radioactive material or other hazardous material, you must disclose that in writing to the prospective tenant (a separate library entry covers it). If you know of a defect that affects health or the tenant's use of the home, fix it or disclose it; concealing a known material defect when renting can be a deceptive practice.

title: No Military or Airport Zone Disclosure
bodyText: Missouri has no rule requiring you to disclose to a tenant that the property lies near a military installation, in an air installation compatible use zone, an accident potential zone or an airport noise zone, and gives tenants no right to end a lease because of such a location. Missouri deals with land near bases and airports only through zoning: one county with a military base (Johnson County, by population bracket) must provide for planning and zoning in all or part of the unincorporated area within 3,000 feet of the base and in its accident potential zones, local governments may adopt military-airport and airport-hazard zoning, and a major-airport authority may set aircraft noise zones. Those rules limit what can be built and where, not what a lease must say. If you know the home sits under a flight path or in a noise zone, telling applicants avoids a later claim that you hid a material fact.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure
bodyText: Missouri requires none of the three pre-signing disclosures some states group together. Ordnance: there is no duty to tell an applicant or tenant that the property is near a former military ordnance or munitions site. Demolition: there is no duty to tell an applicant or tenant that you plan to demolish the building or have applied for a demolition permit; demolition is governed by local building and dangerous-building codes, and a fixed-term lease still binds you until it ends or is lawfully terminated. Shared meters: no statute requires you to disclose that a tenant's gas or electric meter also serves other units or common areas; if you pass a shared bill through to tenants, state in the lease how it is split (see the utility entries). The one related state rule is for sales, not leases: a seller of property containing a solid-waste disposal site or demolition landfill must disclose it to the buyer early in negotiations.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: Missouri has no shoreline, beach or public-water-access disclosure: no rule requires a lease to say whether the property has access to a lake, river or shore, whether a shoreline is public or private, or what limits apply to its use. Lake and river frontage is governed by zoning, permits and private covenants outside the landlord-tenant statutes, and no state statute turns them into a lease disclosure. If a rental includes lake access, a dock or a shared shoreline, describe in the lease exactly what the tenant may use and on what rules, and attach any association or permit rules that bind the tenant.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no chemical-exposure warning law of the kind California has, so you do not need to post or deliver a warning that a rental contains chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. The disclosures Missouri does require about substances in a rental are specific: methamphetamine production you know of, and radioactive or hazardous contamination shown in a report you received, each disclosed in writing to the prospective tenant; and the federal lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978. Missouri's only statutory health-warning sign of this kind is for liquor licensees (drinking during pregnancy), which does not apply to rentals.

title: Rent Certification for the Property Tax Credit
bodyText: Missouri does not require you to give tenants an annual statement, or a statement on each rent change, of the share of rent that goes to property taxes. It does have a renter's property tax credit: an eligible renter (for example, a renter 65 or older, a disabled renter or a 100% service-disabled veteran, within the statute's residency and income limits) may claim a credit counting 20% of the gross rent paid during the year as rent constituting property taxes. The statute lets the Department of Revenue require, by rule, a return of information from a landlord certifying for a calendar year the gross rent received from a tenant who claims the credit, and set how the tenant certifies the rent paid; neither a landlord nor a tenant may be required to provide data on utilities, furniture, home furnishings or appliances, though data on health and personal care services and food furnished with the rental may be required. If a tenant asks you to confirm the rent paid for a credit claim, give an accurate written statement of the rent received for the year and keep a copy, and check the Department of Revenue's current claim form, which may ask the tenant for a rent statement. The Department of Revenue rules checked (its income tax, senior tax relief, general tax and homestead credit chapters) contain no rule requiring you to file one yourself.

title: No Rent-Cap or Just-Cause Notice
bodyText: Missouri requires no lease notice telling tenants about a rent cap, just-cause eviction protections or a tenant right to buy, because it has none of those laws. There is no statewide rent cap or rent stabilization, no just-cause requirement for ending a tenancy, and no tenant opportunity to purchase or right of first refusal when you sell. Missouri also bars every county and city, including charter cities and counties, from enacting, keeping or enforcing an ordinance that regulates the rent charged for privately owned residential rental property, or one that requires tenants to automatically receive a right of first refusal. Narrow exceptions let a local government regulate its own property, agree with an owner on rent for subsidized housing, or restrict rent on properties assisted with community development block grant funds. Do not put a California-style rent-cap or just-cause notice in a Missouri lease.

title: No Rent-Cap Exemption Notice
bodyText: Missouri requires no notice telling a tenant that a property is exempt from a rent cap, a just-cause rule or a tenant purchase right, because Missouri has none of those regimes and bars local rent control. There is no two-tier scheme of covered and exempt rentals, and no single-family-home or small-landlord exemption to claim, so a California-style exemption statement has nothing to refer to and should not go in a Missouri lease; it would state a legal conclusion about a law that does not exist. The only owner-based carve-out in the deposit law runs the other way and needs no notice: a housing authority or other government landlord is not bound by the rule on where deposits must be held.

title: No Landlord-Tenant Law on a Repeal Clock
bodyText: As of November 9, 2026, none of Missouri's core landlord-tenant statutes is on a repeal or expiration date: the landlord-tenant chapter (including the domestic violence, repair-and-deduct and local-preemption sections), the unlawful detainer and squatter-removal chapter, the rent-and-possession chapter with the security deposit law, and the fair housing law have no sunset clause, and none of their sections is printed with a second, later version waiting to take effect. Missouri has no tenant-protection act of the rent-cap or just-cause kind whose expiry you would need to watch. Laws still change by amendment; the 2026 session's changes, in force since August 28, 2026, are reflected here.

title: No Repair-Remedy Exemption Notice
bodyText: Missouri has no rent-escrow remedy (no procedure for a tenant to pay rent into court or to an escrow agent until repairs are made) and so no small-landlord exemption from one and no exemption notice to give. Do not put an Ohio-style notice in a Missouri lease saying the tenant's repair remedies do not apply because you own few units: Missouri's repair-and-deduct right has no unit-count or owner-occupancy exemption, and a lease may not waive it. That right is narrow: it is available only to a tenant who has lived there six consecutive months, paid all rent and charges, and received no uncured written lease-violation notice in that time; it covers a local housing or building code violation affecting habitability, sanitation or security that costs less than $300 or half a month's rent (whichever is greater, but never more than one month's rent) to fix; the tenant must give you written notice and 14 days (or less in an emergency); if you dispute the repair in writing, the tenant needs a local government's certification first; and deductions are capped at one month's rent in any 12 months and are not allowed for a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent. Separately, rent can be redirected to a court-appointed receiver in a housing-code or unpaid-heat-utility receivership, which is a court process, not a lease exemption.

title: No Automatic Renewal Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute that regulates automatic renewal clauses in residential leases. There is no required reminder notice before a renewal takes effect, no type-size or initials rule, and no limit on how early you may ask a tenant to renew. Missouri's consumer statutes ban automatic renewal only in particular contracts, such as discount buying club memberships, not leases. So an automatic renewal clause is a matter of contract, within the general rules: once a written lease has ended, a court will not accept oral evidence that it was renewed or extended, so the renewal terms must be in the signed lease or another signed writing; a lease for longer than one year can't be enforced unless it, or a memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party it is enforced against; a fixed term ends on its end date without any notice to quit; and a lease that continues month to month ends only by a written notice ending it on a rent-paying date at least one month after the other party receives it (if the tenant lives in and has an ownership interest in a mobile home and rents the lot it sits on, your notice must end it no sooner than 60 days from the next rent due date). The library offers an optional automatic renewal clause built on these rules.

title: Tenancies at Will and by Sufferance
bodyText: Missouri recognizes tenancies at will and by sufferance. A lease that isn't put in writing and signed by the parties (or by agents authorized in writing) has the effect of a tenancy at will only. But an unwritten rental of a house, apartment or other building (other than farmland) is treated as a month-to-month tenancy, which either party may end with one month's written notice. A tenancy at will or by sufferance, or one for less than a year, may be ended by the person entitled to possession giving the occupant one month's written notice to vacate (if the tenant lives in and has an ownership interest in a mobile home and rents the lot it sits on, your notice ending a tenancy of less than a year must end it no sooner than 60 days from the next rent due date). The statute speaks only of that notice; it sets no separate notice for a tenant who wants to leave a tenancy at will, so the cautious course for both sides is one month's written notice. Once a notice under these rules is given, it can be changed only by a later dated writing, not by oral testimony. You don't need to give the one-month notice before filing a rent-and-possession case for unpaid rent. A tenant at will or by sufferance may not assign or transfer the tenancy without your written consent. Where someone occupies under an agreement not made by deed, you may recover a reasonable amount for the use and occupation. To avoid an uncertain at-will arrangement, use a signed written lease with a stated term or a stated month-to-month period.

title: No Seasonal Tenancy Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no seasonal tenancy category and no statute that takes a summer, winter or vacation rental of a home out of the ordinary landlord-tenant rules. Missouri's definition of a lease covers any written or oral agreement for the use or possession of premises, whatever its length, so a seasonal rental of a dwelling is treated like any other tenancy. The general rules then decide how it ends: a lease for a term that ends on a stated date ends then with no notice to quit; an unwritten rental of a house or other building is month to month and ends only on one month's written notice; and a lease for longer than one year can't be enforced unless it, or a memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party it is enforced against. If you rent seasonally, use a signed written lease with a stated start and end date. Whether a short stay in a hotel, motel or other lodging establishment is a tenancy at all is a separate question this library hasn't reviewed; local short-term rental ordinances may also apply.

title: No Student Housing Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no special rules for renting to students: no student-housing license or certification, no separate lease terms, and no exemption that takes privately owned student rentals out of the ordinary landlord-tenant rules. Renting to students is ordinary renting. Missouri's fair housing law doesn't list student status as a protected class, but its protected classes (including sex, disability and familial status) apply to student renters like anyone else, so a student-only or no-student policy must not work as a proxy for one of them. A few related points: a 16- or 17-year-old who is homeless or a domestic violence victim (and not under children's division supervision or juvenile court jurisdiction), self-supporting and living apart from parents with their consent can sign a binding housing contract, and you are protected from liability for deciding to contract with such a minor unless you act with gross negligence or by willful or wanton acts or omissions; state colleges and universities may build and run their own student housing, under their own rules, which this library hasn't reviewed. With several student roommates, put every adult on the lease and use the joint liability clause; if a parent is to guarantee the rent, use a signed written guaranty.

title: Lease Length and Signatures
bodyText: Missouri sets no maximum length for a residential lease, but length changes the formalities. A lease for longer than one year can't be enforced unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party it is enforced against (or that party's authorized agent). A lease that isn't in a signed writing has the effect of a tenancy at will only, and an unwritten rental of a house or other building is month to month. Assigning, granting or surrendering a lease must also be done by a signed writing (or by operation of law). Missouri's recording statute says every written instrument by which real estate may be affected is to be recorded, and an unrecorded one is not valid against anyone but the parties and those with actual notice; whether and when that reaches a residential lease is a question for case law this library hasn't reviewed, so for a long lease consider recording a memorandum of it. If you manage property as a conservator for a minor or disabled person, you may lease it without court approval only for terms of up to one year (renewable for a like term). Missouri has no statute requiring a spouse's consent to lease, but if the property is owned jointly, have every owner sign.

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute requiring the same terms, or limiting a rent difference, between month-to-month and fixed-term leases. You may offer a month-to-month tenancy at a higher rent or on different terms than a fixed-term lease, so long as the difference isn't based on a class protected by fair housing law. What differs by law is how each ends: a fixed-term lease ends on its end date without notice to quit, while a month-to-month tenancy ends only by a written notice ending it on a rent-paying date at least one month after the other party receives it (if the tenant lives in and has an ownership interest in a mobile home and rents the lot it sits on, your notice must end it no sooner than 60 days from the next rent due date). During a fixed term, terms change only by written agreement; during a month-to-month tenancy, the route is to end the tenancy and offer new terms.

title: No Lease Type-Size Rule
bodyText: Missouri sets no minimum type size or print format for a residential lease. Use type large enough to read easily, since a term a tenant can't reasonably read invites a dispute over whether it was agreed. A few particular documents do carry format rules: a contract with a binding arbitration provision must carry a set statement in ten-point capital letters next to the signatures (the library doesn't offer arbitration in Missouri), and a sale-leaseback of a home requires a one-page boldface disclosure to the seller before signing.

title: Rent Increases During a Lease
bodyText: Missouri has no general statute on rent escalation clauses: no cap, no limit on how often rent may rise, and no required notice period for an increase written into the lease. Local rent control is preempted. So a lease may set rent changes in advance, either as a schedule of amounts and dates or as a formula tied to a published index; the library offers an optional clause for this. Two narrow limits apply: a manufactured or mobile home land lease community may not raise rent (except for property-tax increases) for 60 days before, or at any time after, giving its 120-day notice of a change in use; and an owner who takes additional subsidies from the Missouri Housing Development Commission agrees to raise rent on subsidy units no more than once a year and by no more than the CPI increase, unless the agency approves more. During a fixed term, rent otherwise changes only as the lease provides or by written agreement; for a month-to-month tenancy, the route is to end the tenancy on proper notice and offer new terms. A clause letting you raise rent on your own during a fixed term (with notice and a right for the tenant to leave) isn't barred by any Missouri statute, but the library doesn't offer it in Missouri: whether a court enforces a one-sided change of a fixed-term rent hasn't been reviewed, and it would conflict with the library's rule that fixed-term terms change only by written agreement. A landlord who wants one can add a custom clause, after taking advice.

title: No Rent Reporting Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on reporting rent payments to credit bureaus. You aren't required to offer positive rent reporting, and no Missouri statute sets a notice before you report late rent or an unpaid balance. If you or a service you use reports rent or debts to a credit bureau, federal credit reporting law may also apply to what is reported; this library hasn't reviewed it for this topic, so report only what you can document and correct errors promptly. Missouri does protect your side of the screening process: no city or county may restrict your use of credit scores or credit reports, applied by your own customary criteria, in deciding whether to rent.

title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on using software or an algorithm to set rents or lease terms. Missouri's general antitrust law still applies to landlords as to any business: every contract, combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade is unlawful. Using a pricing service that pools confidential rent data from competing landlords and recommends rents could raise antitrust questions under Missouri or federal law, which this library hasn't reviewed for this topic. The cautious course is to set your own rents, treat any software output as advice you are free to reject, and not share your nonpublic rent or occupancy data with competitors, directly or through a vendor. Cities and counties can't regulate the amount of rent on private rentals in Missouri.

title: Guarantors and Lease Renewals
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on lease guaranties. Nothing limits a guarantor's liability to the original term, requires a guaranty to state a maximum or an end date, or caps what you may collect from a guarantor. So the guaranty itself decides whether it covers renewals, extensions and a month-to-month continuation: say so expressly, because a guaranty silent on renewals invites the argument that it ended with the original term. A promise to answer for another person's debt must be in writing and signed by the guarantor, so have the guarantor sign the lease or a separate written guaranty. Missouri also has an old surety statute: a surety on a bond, bill or note may, once a claim has accrued, demand in writing that the creditor promptly sue the principal debtor, and is released if suit isn't started within 30 days and pursued diligently. Whether that statute reaches a lease guaranty hasn't been reviewed, so if a guarantor serves you such a written demand, the cautious course is to file against the tenant within 30 days and keep the case moving.

title: No Double-Letting Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on double letting: nothing specifically bars renting the same home or room to two tenants for the same period or sets a rent-abatement remedy for it, and no statute sets what you owe a new tenant if you can't deliver possession on the start date. Leasing the same premises to two people for the same time is still a breach of at least one lease, and the general law of contract and damages applies. One Missouri rule helps when the problem is a tenant who won't leave: if you have already rented the home to a new tenant and the old tenant holds over after the tenancy ends, the new letting is no defense to your eviction case, and the new tenant may bring their own unlawful detainer case against the holdover after a written demand for possession, if you haven't already sued. Use the library's possession-delay clause to set what happens if the home isn't ready on the start date.

title: No Rule on Terms Added to a Notice to Vacate
bodyText: Missouri has no general statute on notices to vacate that carry extra terms, and none that bars changes to a unit while a notice to vacate is pending. A notice to vacate can't add obligations that aren't in the lease; ask for anything new in a separate signed agreement. Where the tenancy is an oral letting for an agricultural year, a tenancy at will or by sufferance, or a letting for less than a year, and a notice ending it under the statutes has been given, oral testimony can't vary or withdraw that notice in a later lawsuit between you; only a later dated writing can. A tenant who gives written notice of moving out on a stated date and then stays owes double rent for the time they stay. One narrow rule: when a building is converted to a condominium, tenants can't be required to vacate on less than the statutory notice (except for nonpayment, waste or disturbing other tenants), and the terms of the tenancy may not be altered during that period. Keep the unit habitable and services running while any notice is pending; willfully interrupting essential services is unlawful except for health or safety reasons.

title: No Statutory Penalty for Entry Without Notice
bodyText: Missouri has no statute setting how much notice you must give before entering or inspecting a rental, so it also has no statutory penalty, damages formula or tenant termination right for entering without notice. Your notice duty comes from the lease: the library's lease gives 24 hours' notice except in emergencies, and an entry that breaks that promise is a breach of the lease, with the ordinary remedies for breach of contract. Entry that goes beyond the lease could also expose you to claims for trespass or invasion of privacy under case law this library hasn't reviewed. And never use entry to lock a tenant out or remove their belongings: removing or excluding a tenant without judicial process and a court order is unlawful, except under Missouri's abandonment procedure. Lead-hazard inspectors from the health department or a licensed local agency may enter a home only with the owner's or an adult occupant's consent or a court order.

title: No Key Control Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute requiring a key-control policy, limits on master keys, re-keying between tenants, or background checks for employees who have keys to tenants' homes, whatever the size of the property. Missouri also has no statute requiring particular locks or security devices. Good practice is still worth adopting: keep a log of who holds keys, re-key between tenants, store master keys securely, and screen employees and contractors who will have access, since a careless key policy can be evidence of negligence if a tenant is harmed. The lease decides tenant-side rules: the library offers clauses on keys (receipts, duplication and re-keying costs) and on tenant lock changes. Never change the locks to keep a tenant out: removing or excluding a tenant, or removing doors or locks, without judicial process and a court order is unlawful, except under Missouri's abandonment procedure.

title: No Smart Lock Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on smart locks, keypad or app-based entry systems in rentals. You may use one, and nothing requires you to offer a physical key, limit the data the system collects or let a tenant opt out. Because the general rules still apply, set it up carefully: say in the lease how access codes or credentials are issued and changed, who holds administrator access, and what happens if the system fails; change codes between tenants; and don't use the system's entry logs or remote access in a way the lease doesn't allow. Disabling a tenant's access to keep them out is a lockout, which is unlawful without judicial process and a court order (except under Missouri's abandonment procedure). If tenants must use an app, remember that a tenant who agrees to deal electronically may later refuse to conduct further transactions electronically, so keep a non-electronic way to give notices.

title: Tenant Security Cameras and Video Doorbells
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on tenants installing security cameras or video doorbells, or on landlords limiting them. The lease decides: you may allow, limit or require approval for cameras, especially anything attached to the building or aimed at common areas, as an alteration or rules matter. Two criminal laws apply to anyone, tenant or landlord. It is a crime to knowingly photograph or film a person without consent while that person is fully or partly nude in a place where one would reasonably expect privacy, so no camera may view bathrooms, bedrooms or similar spaces of another person. And Missouri's wiretap law makes it a felony to intercept a wire communication unless you are a party to it or one party consents, and also reaches some devices that pick up conversations by radio transmission; whether a doorbell's audio recording falls within it hasn't been reviewed here, so the cautious course is to have doorbells and cameras that face shared spaces record video only. Don't use cameras to monitor a tenant inside their home.

title: No Guest Rights Statute
bodyText: Missouri has no statute giving tenants or their guests a right to visit, limiting guest rules, or barring a fee for guests. The lease decides: you may set reasonable guest rules, including a limit on how long a guest may stay before becoming an occupant who needs your consent, and the library offers guest clauses for this. Apply guest rules the same way to everyone, since fair housing law bars treating tenants differently because of race, sex, disability, familial status or another protected class, and a rule that targets visitors of one group could do that. A tenant is a person who occupies with your consent, and a tenant may not assign or sublet without your written consent; in the housing-code receivership sections, occupants may not take in additional occupants without the owner's knowledge and consent. Someone who moves in without anyone's permission and isn't a guest may be removed through Missouri's unlawful-occupant procedure; a guest of your tenant who overstays is removed through the tenant, or through an eviction case if needed, never by self-help.

title: Home-Based Businesses
bodyText: Missouri law lets anyone who lives in a home run a home-based business there unless a deed restriction, covenant or other agreement restricting the use of the land, or a condominium or homeowners association document, restricts it.
