Cities and counties can't ban a no-impact home business (one with no more employees and clients at a time than the home's occupancy limit, no substantial traffic, no parking violations, all activity inside the home or yard and nothing visible from the street) and can't require a home-business license or rezoning, though they may adopt narrowly tailored health and safety rules. Whether a lease counts as an agreement that can restrict a home business hasn't been settled by a Missouri statute, so state your rule in the lease: use the residential-use-only clause to bar business use, or the home-business permission clause to allow a named business on conditions. Illegal activity is different: the lease becomes void if the tenant permits gambling or a brothel on the premises, or allows the illegal possession, sale or distribution of controlled substances there.

title: No Family Child Care Rule for Rentals
bodyText: Missouri has no statute requiring a landlord to allow a tenant to run a child care home, or setting conditions a landlord may impose. Child care for pay is a home-based business, so the lease decides whether it is allowed (see the home-business guidance), and an association's documents may also restrict it. State licensing is separate: a person caring for more than six children at one address (counting no more than three under age two, and not counting the caregiver's own school-age children) needs a child care license, and an unlicensed provider must tell parents in writing that it is unlicensed. If you allow child care, put the permission and its conditions in the lease, such as compliance with licensing, liability insurance, limits on the number of children and on use of common areas, and responsibility for damage. Whether refusing child care use could be familial-status discrimination hasn't been reviewed here, so aim any child care rule at the business use only, and don't let it limit tenants' own children.

title: No House Rules Statute
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on landlord rules and regulations: no list of conditions a rule must meet, no notice period for adopting a rule, and no limit on rules beyond fair housing law and the general law of contract. Rules bind a tenant as lease terms, so attach them to the signed lease or refer to a written set the tenant receives before signing. During a fixed term, a new or changed rule binds the tenant only if the tenant agrees in writing; a lease clause letting you change rules on your own mid-term isn't backed by any Missouri statute, and the library doesn't offer one. For a month-to-month tenancy, the route is to end the tenancy on proper written notice and offer a new tenancy on the new rules. Keep rules reasonable, written, applied the same way to every tenant and tied to safety, the property or fair use of shared facilities; a rule that is enforced against some tenants and not others invites a discrimination claim.

title: No Parking Rules Notice Requirement
bodyText: Missouri has no statute requiring you to give tenants parking rules before they sign, to put parking terms under a set heading, or limiting changes to parking rules during the lease. State your parking rules in the lease or attach them, and change them during a fixed term only by written agreement. Missouri's towing law is what binds you on enforcement: without a police officer's authorization, an owner, lessee or full-time property or security manager may have a vehicle towed from a restricted or assigned space only while present, and only if a sign of the required size is posted at every entrance (or, for an abandoned vehicle, after notifying police and waiting 10 hours at an owner-occupied property of four units or less, or 96 hours elsewhere). Missouri doesn't set a separate waiting period before towing a tenant's car for expired registration. Local ordinances may add rules.

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute requiring parking to be offered separately from the rent, or barring it. You may include parking in the rent, rent a space for a separate charge, or offer it as an option. If parking is charged separately, state the space, the charge and when it is due in the lease (the library's parking clauses do this). A separate parking charge that isn't part of the rent can be claimed in a rent-and-possession case but doesn't count as rent there, so unpaid parking charges alone won't get you possession. The security deposit cap is two months' rent; to stay clear of any argument, base the cap on the rent alone, not on rent plus parking.

title: Children in the Home
bodyText: Missouri's fair housing law protects familial status: households with children under 18 living with a parent or custodian (or the custodian's written designee), and anyone who is pregnant or securing custody of a child. You may not refuse to rent, set different terms, or advertise a preference because a household has children, and a lease can't bar children or set a children-only limit (Missouri's narrow exemptions for some small owners, which never reach advertising, are in the fair housing entry). Missouri doesn't require a lease to address children. An occupancy limit must be neutral: Missouri presumes a limit of two persons per bedroom reasonable, and that limit doesn't apply to a child born to the tenants during the lease, so the presumed limit gives you no ground to end the tenancy because a child is born to the tenants during the lease. Reasonable local or state occupancy limits still apply. Housing for older persons that qualifies under the law (62 and over, or 55 and over with the required facilities and policies) is exempt from the familial-status rules. Safety rules for common areas are fine if they are reasonable and don't single out children more than safety needs.

title: No Alternate-Housing Duty
bodyText: Missouri law does not require you to provide, arrange or pay for a hotel room or other substitute housing while a unit is being repaired or is unlivable, and it gives the tenant no statutory right to move to substitute housing at your expense. Three related rules: (1) if a home is destroyed by fire, a tornado or another natural or man-made disaster that the tenant did not cause, the tenant owes no rent for the rest of the lease term; (2) if a lead hazard you were notified to fix is still not reduced on the health department's re-inspection, local health and building officials may use community or other available resources to relocate the occupants until you comply, and you may not evict a tenant because someone with an elevated blood lead level or suspected lead poisoning lives there or because of action the lead law requires of you (you may still take the unit off the rental market, or evict for another lawful reason); (3) relocation payments when property is taken for a public project are paid by the government body or redeveloper doing the taking, not by you as landlord. A lease may promise temporary housing or a rent credit during repairs if you choose to offer one; if you do, say who pays and for how long.

title: Animals Left in a Rental
bodyText: Missouri law gives you no special right to enter a rental to check on, feed or remove a tenant's animal, and no procedure for taking custody of an animal a tenant leaves behind; your entry rights come from the lease. Knowingly abandoning an animal without arranging its adequate care, or failing to give adequate care to an animal in one's custody, is the crime of animal neglect. If you find an animal left without care, try the tenant and any emergency contact, then call local animal control or the police: public health and law enforcement officials can ask a court for a warrant, on an affidavit of probable cause, to enter private property and impound a neglected animal, placing it with a veterinarian, animal control or an animal shelter. Do not take the animal in yourself or treat it as abandoned property to sell or discard; under the animal-welfare law, anyone who feeds or shelters an animal at the same place for three or more days in a row counts as its owner and takes on the care duty. To plan ahead, use the optional clause in which the tenant names a person you may let in to care for or remove the animal.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacate Notice Rule
bodyText: Missouri law does not require a tenant to tell you before leaving the unit empty in cold weather, or to keep the heat on or protect pipes from freezing while away. If you want that notice, for example so you can check that pipes do not freeze, put it in the lease as a duty to tell you before any long absence and to leave the heat at a safe level. Missouri's cold weather rule is a different thing: from November 1 to March 31 a gas or electric utility may not shut off heating service to a home, including a tenant's apartment, for an unpaid bill on days when the forecast calls for temperatures below freezing, and the Public Service Commission's rules add other cases. If a tenant gives you written notice that they will move out on a set date and then stays on, the tenant owes double rent for the time they stay.

title: No Government Approval of a Lease
bodyText: Missouri state law has no communal, family or tribal land tenure, and no statute makes a residential lease of privately owned land wait for a government officer's approval before it is valid. If you own the property and rent it out, the lease binds when you and the tenant sign it, subject to the rule that a lease for more than one year must be in writing. The only state approval rule found for a lease of land is for oil and gas leases of publicly owned land, which the legislature, county commission or city council must approve. If the land is held in trust by the United States for a tribe or a tribal member, federal law governs leasing; this library does not cover that case, so get advice first.

title: Contractor Liens for Tenant Work
bodyText: In Missouri, a contractor or supplier who is not paid for work or materials a tenant ordered on leased property can put a mechanic's lien on the improvement and on the tenant's lease interest, whether or not the tenant may remove the improvement at the end of the lease. Your own ownership can be at risk too: a lien reaches the land of the owner who contracted for the work, directly or through an agent, and the lien law counts as an owner anyone for whose immediate use, enjoyment or benefit the improvement is made. How far that reaches a landlord who only consented to a tenant's work is decided by the courts, not the statute. Missouri has no notice of nonresponsibility you can post or record, and no lease wording that the statute says keeps your interest lien-free. Cautious course: approve tenant alterations in writing only, say in the lease that the tenant pays for and is responsible for its own work and is not your agent, have the tenant tell contractors that, and use the optional no-liens clause. A contractor's advance agreement to give up lien rights in return for getting the job is unenforceable, though lien waivers as a condition of payment are allowed.

title: Rent After a Unit Is Condemned
bodyText: No Missouri statute says that you may not collect rent once a city or county condemns a unit, posts it as unfit to live in or orders it vacated. Related rules: if a home is destroyed by fire, a tornado or another natural or man-made disaster that the tenant did not cause, the tenant owes no rent for the rest of the lease term; when a court appoints a housing-code receiver, rent paid to the receiver is a defense to your nonpayment case; and you may not evict a tenant because of lead-hazard enforcement, though you may take the unit off the rental market or evict for another lawful reason. Whether a tenant owes rent for a unit that is unfit to live in is otherwise left to court decisions, which this library has not reviewed. Cautious course: do not charge or sue for rent for any period when a government order bars anyone from living in the unit, and check your city's or county's housing or dangerous-building code, which may say more.

title: Who Does Repair-and-Deduct Work
bodyText: Missouri has no statute that lets a lease name the person or firm who must do repairs a tenant makes at your expense. The tenant's repair-and-deduct remedy, where it applies, requires only that the work be done in a workmanlike manner and that the tenant give you an itemized statement with receipts, and the tenant may deduct only the actual and reasonable cost. State law says no lease may contain a waiver of that remedy, so a clause forcing the tenant to use your contractor, or making the right depend on it, risks being treated as a void waiver; the library therefore offers no such clause for Missouri. What you can do: require repair requests to come to you, use your own contractors for repairs you make, give the tenant a list of contractors you would accept, and fix code violations within 14 days of the tenant's written notice (or as promptly as an emergency requires) so the remedy never arises. If you think a repair is not needed, say so in writing within that period; the tenant must then get the local government's written certification of a code violation before repairing.

title: No Disaster Guest Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute that lets a tenant take in people displaced by a fire, flood, tornado or other declared disaster beyond the lease's guest or occupancy limits, and none that stops you from enforcing those limits during an emergency. Your lease's guest and occupancy terms, and any local occupancy code, apply as usual. If a tenant asks to shelter displaced family or friends, the practical course is to agree in writing to a temporary exception with an end date, the names of the guests and the usual rules of conduct, rather than treating the stay as a lease violation. Fair housing rules still apply to how you handle such requests.

title: Rent and the Lease After a Disaster
bodyText: Missouri has one statute on rent after a disaster: if a home is destroyed by an act of God, such as a fire or tornado, or by another natural or man-made disaster, and the tenant did not cause it, the tenant owes you no rent for the rest of the lease term. A tenant's general promise to make repairs does not make the tenant rebuild after a fire not brought about by the procurement, connivance or neglect of the tenant or the tenant's agents or servants, unless the lease specifically says the tenant will rebuild after fire. Missouri law does not say that a declared disaster ends the lease, does not set rent for a unit that is damaged but not destroyed, and does not address rent while an evacuation order or road closure keeps the tenant out. Your lease's fire or casualty terms decide those cases, so make sure the lease says who may end it, how rent is reduced for partial damage and when rent resumes. During a declared state of emergency the governor may take over housing facilities (with compensation to the owner) and regulate the sale and price of goods and services; follow any order issued.

title: Drug-Free Lease Addenda
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires, supplies a form for, or limits a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum, and Missouri has no recovery-housing (sober living) lease rules. You do not need a separate addendum: the library's optional criminal-activity clause covers illegal drug activity. Missouri law already makes a lease void if the tenant allows the illegal possession, sale or distribution of controlled substances on the premises, and you then have the same remedies to recover the property as against a tenant holding over; drug-related criminal activity also supports Missouri's expedited eviction case. Marijuana use that Missouri law permits is handled by the lease's smoking and cultivation terms, not as illegal drug activity. Federally assisted housing programs have their own required lease terms, which this library does not cover.

title: When Rental Property Is Taken for Public Use
bodyText: Missouri has no statute saying what happens to a lease, or to the rent, when the government or another body with eminent-domain power takes all or part of a rental property, and no statute lets a court end the lease in the condemnation case. The lease decides, so use the optional condemnation clause. In the condemnation case, the people claiming a share of the award may file an agreement dividing it; if they do not, the court sets each party's share. The statute does not say whether a lease term giving you the award controls that division, a point for the courts, but the term records the parties' agreement, which can be filed with the court within 30 days after the award is paid. A tenant in actual possession may need to be made a party. Separately, a tenant displaced by a public acquisition, including a month-to-month tenant, may be entitled to relocation help and payments from the public agency or redeveloper, such as moving costs, utility and rent deposits, with advance notice before having to move; you cannot waive those for the tenant. A state of emergency lets the governor take over housing facilities, with compensation set as in an eminent-domain case.

title: No Employee Screening Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statute requiring you to run background checks on maintenance workers, leasing agents, managers or other employees who have keys to or access to tenants' homes, and none setting how such checks must be done. Screening such employees is a sensible precaution, since they enter homes and handle keys. If you use a background-check company's report to make a hiring decision, follow the federal consumer-report rules and the general employment discrimination laws, which this library does not cover; local ordinances may limit when criminal history may be asked about.

title: Ending a Lease After an Environmental Event
bodyText: Missouri gives neither you nor the tenant a statutory right to end a lease because a flood, contamination, sewer failure, public health emergency or a government order makes the home unfit or unlawful to occupy. Two related rules: if the home is destroyed by an act of God or another natural or man-made disaster the tenant did not cause, the tenant owes no rent for the rest of the term; and if you are notified of a lead hazard, you must abate the hazard or put interim controls in place as the health department directs, and you may also take the unit off the rental market; otherwise you may not evict a tenant because someone living in the home has an elevated blood lead level or suspected lead poisoning, or because of the lead action itself. Otherwise the lease decides. The library offers an optional environmental-event clause that lets either party end the lease when such an event, not caused by the tenant's side, makes the home unfit or a government order bars occupancy, with rent stopping while occupancy is barred. If the tenant does not leave after a termination, you must go to court; you may not lock the tenant out.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land
bodyText: In Missouri, hunting, fishing or trapping on private land, or retrieving game from it, without permission from the owner or the lessee of the land is a crime, so a tenant who leases the land can give that permission as well as you can. No Missouri statute decides whether a tenant of rented farmland or a rural home has hunting or fishing rights, or whether you keep them; that is left to the lease. If you want to keep hunting rights for yourself or others, or forbid the tenant from letting anyone hunt, fish or trap, say so in the lease, and name who may give permission. The state's recreational-use law, which limits an owner's liability to people allowed on the land without charge for hunting, fishing and other recreation (though not for injuries in a swimming pool or in a residential area, which that law defines to include any land used for farming or agricultural purposes, or for a malicious or grossly negligent failure to guard or warn against a danger the owner knew or should have known of, or a negligent failure to guard or warn against an ultrahazardous condition the owner knew or should have known of), counts a lessee or anyone with a right of possession as an owner. Because of that farming carve-out, don't count on the law to limit your liability, or a farm tenant's, for injuries on farmland; how courts apply it is case law this library hasn't reviewed. Licenses, seasons and landowner permits are set by the Conservation Commission's rules, which this library does not cover.

title: Tenant Paying to Stop a Rent Eviction
bodyText: In a Missouri rent-and-possession case, a tenant can stop the eviction by paying. If, on the date the court gives a money judgment, the tenant pays you, or pays into court, all rent then in arrears and all costs, the case stops. If the tenant pays the full money judgment and costs after the trial but before the judgment becomes final, the execution for possession stops, though you may still appeal the money judgment. If the judgment is for possession only, with no money judgment, payment does not stop it, unless an appeal bond, the court rules or your agreement says otherwise. Once a judgment for possession has been carried out, the tenant and anyone claiming under the lease lose the right to re-enter, and you hold the property free of the lease, subject to an appeal or new trial. A lender holding a mortgage on the lease itself, if not in possession, has three months after execution to pay all back rent, costs and your charges and, by performing the tenant's lease obligations, keep the lease. Only rent counts: other sums the lease calls fees can be sued for in the same case but do not by themselves win possession. Ending a lease for a non-rent violation is covered in its own entry.

title: Which Building Code Edition Applies
bodyText: Missouri has no statewide building, fire or housing code for ordinary private rental housing, so the code that applies to your property, and its edition, is whatever your city or county has adopted; check the local ordinance, not the newest national edition. The 2026 state fire and life safety standards, due by rule by July 1, 2027 and applying from January 1, 2028 (and then only on new construction, a major renovation affecting egress, detection, alarm or suppression systems, a transfer of ownership or a substantial improvement), cover only buildings the state fire safety division already inspects, and the law says they create no statewide code for anything else. Two state laws fix a code edition: (1) cities and counties in the New Madrid earthquake zone must require new construction, additions and alterations to meet the seismic standards of the 1990 or later edition of the Uniform Building Code or the BOCA code, though single-family homes and duplexes, and private buildings under 10,000 square feet unless the local government includes them, are outside the state mandate, and existing buildings need not be rebuilt to the current code just because of an addition or alteration; (2) a local government that adopts the 2009 or a later International Residential Code without its sprinkler mandate must keep the 2006 edition's fire-separation language for two-family dwellings and townhouses. Builders of one- and two-family homes and townhouses must offer buyers the option of fire sprinklers.

title: Furnished Rentals
bodyText: Missouri has no statute on furnished rentals: no required inventory, no special deposit and no separate rules for furniture you provide. Use the optional furnishings clause and attach a signed inventory listing each item and its condition at move-in. The deposit law lets you keep part of the deposit only for unpaid rent, for restoring the dwelling unit to its move-in condition apart from ordinary wear and tear, and for actual losses when the tenant fails to give adequate notice to end the tenancy, if you make reasonable efforts to mitigate; it does not say whether furniture you supplied counts as part of the dwelling unit. Wrongfully withholding deposit money costs you twice the amount withheld. Cautious course: deduct for damaged or missing furniture only when the inventory shows the item and its condition, explain the deduction in your itemized statement, and for anything doubtful bill the tenant separately or sue for it; the deposit law does not limit your right to recover actual damages beyond the deposit.

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate
bodyText: Missouri state law does not require a residential landlord to carry liability insurance on a rental, or to show proof of insurance to register or license a rental. Some cities and counties run rental registration or licensing programs whose ordinances may ask for it, so check the local rules where the property is. Liability and property coverage is still prudent, and lenders and associations often require it. If you want tenants to carry renter's insurance, the lease must say so; the library's tenant insurance clause does that.

title: Elevators and Other Building Equipment
bodyText: If your rental building has an elevator, dumbwaiter, escalator, inclined or stairway lift, or moving walk, Missouri's elevator safety law applies: each installation must have a state certificate of inspection and meet the state elevator safety code, the owner, agent or lessee must post the operating permit (for an elevator, framed in the machine room), and willfully violating the law or running equipment ordered out of service is a crime. Elevators in private single-family homes are not covered, nor are devices built before 1940 that are not open to the public and do not carry passengers. Missouri has no statute on garage doors or automatic garage door openers in rentals. Other building equipment has its own rules, covered in their own entries: steam and hot water boilers, whose state inspection depends on the boiler's pressure and rating and the size of the building (heating), fire escapes for tenement houses and similar buildings (fire code), and swimming pools.

title: No Pet Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: Missouri has no state fact sheet or notice about pets and eviction that you must give a tenant who has a dog, cat or other animal, and no rule about what happens to pets when an eviction is carried out. Your pet clause governs pets during the tenancy. If you recover possession and find an animal left behind, call local animal control rather than treating the animal as abandoned property; the separate entry on animals left in a rental explains why.

title: Rules That Depend on How Much You Own
bodyText: Missouri's core landlord-tenant law (deposits, notices, evictions, repair-and-deduct) applies the same way whether you rent one unit or a thousand; there is no small-landlord exemption. A few rules turn on the size of your holdings or building: (1) Fair housing: the state fair housing law, apart from its ban on discriminatory advertising, does not apply to renting a single-family house by a private individual owner who owns or has an interest in no more than three single-family houses at a time and rents without a broker or agent and without advertising, or to rooms or units in a building for no more than four families where the owner lives in one of them; both conditions of the house exemption must be met, and federal fair housing law has its own exemptions. (2) Accessible design: buildings of four or more units with an elevator, and ground-floor units in other buildings of four or more units, first occupied after March 13, 1991, must meet the accessible-design features. (3) Other size-based rules, covered in their own entries: towing waiting periods are shorter at owner-occupied property of four units or fewer; elderly and disabled tenants have extra protections in condominium conversions of buildings of six or more units; state boiler inspection exempts, in private homes and apartment houses of fewer than six families, steam heating boilers of up to 15 psig, hot water heating boilers of up to 30 psig and hot water supply boilers of up to 160 psig or 250 degrees Fahrenheit, and, in any building, steam heating boilers of up to 10 psig and hot water heating boilers of up to 20 psig within set radiation ratings; a utility's heat-service notices and receivership apply where the owner pays for heat in a building of two or more units; and the state seismic mandate for earthquake-zone localities excludes single-family homes, duplexes and smaller private buildings.

title: Questions About Protected Traits
bodyText: Missouri's fair housing law has no separate rule that forbids asking applicants about, or keeping records of, their race, color, religion, national origin, ancestry, sex, disability or familial status. It does make it unlawful to make or publish any notice or statement about renting a dwelling that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on those traits, or an intention to discriminate, and to refuse to rent, set different terms or misstate availability because of them. A question on an application or in an interview can be such a statement, and asking it can be used as evidence that a later decision was discriminatory. Cautious course: do not ask about these traits, or about the nature or severity of a disability, except as needed to handle a request for a reasonable accommodation or modification; apply the same written screening criteria to everyone; and ask only for the number of occupants, not their ages or family relationships, unless you run qualifying housing for older persons. Federal fair housing law has its own rules on inquiries, which this library does not cover here.

title: Illegal Use Voids the Lease
bodyText: Missouri has one statute that voids a residential lease because of how the premises are used. If the tenant permits illegal gaming tables or devices to be set up or used on the premises, keeps a bawdyhouse, brothel or common gaming house there, or allows the illegal possession, sale or distribution of controlled substances on the premises, the lease becomes void and you have the same remedies to recover the premises as against a tenant holding over after the term. The statute also gives you a right to re-enter after 10 days' notice to vacate, but only by the procedure the law specifies, so you still need a court order: removing a tenant or the tenant's belongings, or removing the doors or locks, without judicial process and a court order (except under the abandonment procedure) is forcible entry and detainer. If you rely on illegal possession, sale or distribution of controlled substances as the ground, you must prove it, but you are not liable for damages for relying on a written notice from law enforcement that the premises are being used for drug activity. No Missouri statute voids a lease for other misuse, such as running a business in a home leased as a residence; that is enforced as an ordinary breach of a condition of a written lease (for a tenancy of two years or less, or at will or by sufferance), again by 10 days' notice to vacate and a court case. Separately, a building regularly used for prostitution or unlawful gambling, resorted to for drug activity, or used by a criminal street gang is a public nuisance, and if the owner knew or had reason to believe of the use (for gang use, if the owner knew of it), a court may order it closed for up to a year, so act promptly once you learn of such use.

title: No Quiet Enjoyment Statute
bodyText: No Missouri statute writes a covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession into a residential lease. The statutory covenants Missouri reads into the words "grant, bargain and sell" apply only to conveyances of ownership in fee simple, not to leases. Whether a lease carries an implied promise of quiet enjoyment, and what counts as a breach of it, is decided by Missouri courts, not by statute, so assume your lease carries one and that substantial interference with the tenant's use of the home can make you liable even if the lease says nothing. The tenant's possession is also protected directly by statute: you may not remove or exclude the tenant or the tenant's belongings, or remove the doors or locks, without judicial process and a court order, except under the abandonment procedure, and you may not willfully interrupt essential services such as electricity, gas, water or sewer unless you do so for health or safety reasons. Either is forcible entry and detainer.

title: No Recycling Notice Rule
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires you to provide recycling at a rental property or to tell tenants where and how to recycle. Missouri's solid waste law puts collection and disposal on cities and counties and lets them adopt their own ordinances on storing, collecting and disposing of solid waste, so check your city or county rules and your hauler's contract for any recycling or container requirements. Statewide, major appliances, waste oil and lead-acid batteries may not be thrown away in a landfill, and yard waste generally may not either, which matters when you clear out a unit after a tenant leaves.

title: Paying to Stop a Rent-and-Possession Case
bodyText: In a Missouri rent-and-possession case, the tenant can stop the case by paying. If, on the date the court gives a money judgment, the tenant tenders to you, or pays into the court, all the rent then in arrears and all the costs, the case stops. After the trial but before the judgment becomes final, the tenant can also stop execution for possession by satisfying the money judgment and paying all costs; you can still appeal the money judgment. Only rent counts toward that payment: other charges you join in the case, such as fees, are not rent for this purpose and a judgment for them alone does not give you possession. There is no limit on how often a tenant may do this. If the judgment is for possession only, with no money judgment, payment does not stop execution unless the tenant posts an appeal bond, a court rule allows it or you agree. Once a judgment for possession has been executed, the tenant is barred from re-entering and you hold the premises free of the lease, subject to an appeal or trial de novo; a mortgagee of the lease that is not in possession can still keep the lease by paying all arrears, costs and your charges and performing the lease within three months. If your written lease declares the lease forfeited for nonpayment of rent for a stated time, you must wait until that time has passed before the court issues process. No Missouri statute addresses payment by a charity or rental assistance program for the tenant; the cautious course is to treat such a payment of the full amount as the tenant's own tender.

title: No Renters Insurance Rule
bodyText: No Missouri statute regulates a landlord's requirement that a tenant carry renters insurance. Missouri law does not require you to tell tenants in writing that your insurance does not cover their belongings, does not require you to let the tenant choose the insurer, and sets no rules for buying coverage on the tenant's behalf and charging for it. Missouri's insurance statutes regulate the insurers that write renters policies, not landlords. A renters insurance requirement is therefore a matter of contract: put it in the lease, with the minimum coverage you require and how the tenant shows proof, as the library's tenant insurance clause does.

title: No Right to End the Lease Over Repair Costs
bodyText: No Missouri statute lets you, or the tenant, end a lease because a needed repair would cost too much compared with the rent or the value of the property. Missouri's landlord-tenant statutes also impose no general repair duty, so what you owe comes from your lease, local housing and building codes and court decisions; a repair promise in your lease does not end because the repair is expensive. Your ways out are the ordinary ones: a fixed-term lease ends on its end date, a month-to-month tenancy ends by written notice on a rent-paying date at least one month after the other party receives it (if the tenant lives in and has an ownership interest in a mobile home and rents the lot it sits on, your notice ending a tenancy of less than a year must end it no sooner than 60 days from the next rent due date), and a year-to-year tenancy ends by written notice at least 60 days before the end of the year. If the home is destroyed by fire, a storm or another disaster the tenant did not cause, the tenant owes no rent for the rest of the term, and a tenant's general promise to repair does not oblige the tenant to rebuild after a fire not brought about by the procurement, connivance or neglect of the tenant or the tenant's agents or servants. The library's fire or casualty clause sets out what happens to the lease after major damage; use it rather than relying on repair cost.

title: Repair Requests and Notice
bodyText: Missouri's only statutory repair-notice rule is in its limited repair-and-deduct remedy. For a condition that violates a local housing or building code and harms habitability, sanitation or security, the tenant's remedy starts with the tenant notifying you of the intention to correct it at your expense; your 14 days to make the repair (or less in an emergency) run from the tenant's written notice. If you dispute in writing, within that period, that the repair is needed, the tenant may not deduct unless the tenant first gets written certification from the local government that the condition violates the code, and you then have 14 days from the certification or the tenant's notice, whichever is later. No lease may waive this remedy, so a lease term about how tenants report repairs cannot take it away. Missouri has no statute that ties any other landlord duty to a particular kind of notice, so your lease can ask tenants to report repairs promptly and in writing, as the library's maintenance clause does. Whether a tenant's verbal report, or your own knowledge of a condition, is enough notice for any other claim the tenant may bring is decided by Missouri courts; the cautious course is to act on any report you actually receive, however it arrives, and to keep a dated record of each request and what you did.

title: No Code Variance Notice Rule
bodyText: Missouri has no statewide housing or sanitary code for rental homes, and no Missouri statute requires you to give tenants, or attach to the lease, a variance, waiver or exception you obtain from a housing, health or building code. Housing and building codes in Missouri are local, so any variance procedure, and any duty to post or share a variance, comes from your city or county code. If you hold a local variance that affects the unit, the cautious course is to give the tenant a copy before signing.

title: No Senior Housing Staff Work Card Rule
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires a work card, permit or criminal background check for people who work at senior or 55-and-older rental housing. Missouri's employee background check law reaches licensed care providers, such as facilities licensed under the long-term care chapter, in-home service providers, mental health facilities and adult day care, and applies before a hire has contact with patients or residents; it does not reach an ordinary apartment community that is simply age-restricted. If your property also provides licensed care, that law applies to the care operation. Missouri's fair housing law recognizes housing for older persons (housing for people 62 and older, or housing intended and operated for at least one person 55 or older per unit that meets the Missouri Commission on Human Rights' tests), but it sets no staffing rule.

title: Refusing a Service Dog
bodyText: Missouri law, separate from fair housing law, gives a blind or visually impaired person with a guide dog, a deaf or hard-of-hearing person with a hearing dog, and a physically disabled person with a service dog full and equal access to housing offered for rent. You may not charge extra for the dog, though the tenant is liable for any damage the dog does to the premises. A no-pets rule or pet fee in your lease therefore must give way for these dogs. This housing section excludes a single-family home whose occupants rent out no more than one room, and it does not require you to modify the property. Missouri also makes it a class B misdemeanor to deny or interfere with admittance to the places listed in its public-access law (such as hotels, lodging places and places of public accommodation), or otherwise to interfere with a disabled person's rights under that law. The criminal section names only the public-access law, not the housing section, and whether its reference to lodging places reaches an ordinary residential rental has not been settled by statute, so the cautious course is to treat refusing a service dog as potentially criminal as well as unlawful discrimination under Missouri's fair housing law. Separately, a person who knowingly misrepresents an animal as a service dog or assistance animal commits a misdemeanor.

title: Sex Offender Residence Limits
bodyText: Missouri bars a person found guilty of the sexual offenses listed in its residence-restriction law (and comparable offenses elsewhere) from living within 1,000 feet of a public school, a private school teaching grade 12 or below, or a licensed or state-regulated child care facility that existed when the person began living there, or within 1,000 feet of the property line of a former victim's residence. The distance is measured from the edge of the offender's property to the nearest edge of the school, facility or victim's property. If a school or child care facility opens nearby later, or a former victim moves within the distance, the offender may stay but must notify the county sheriff within a week and prove the earlier residence. The duty and the criminal penalty fall on the offender, not on you: no Missouri statute makes it a crime for a landlord to rent to an offender near a school, or to rent one dwelling to two or more registered offenders. You can commit a felony, however, if you know a tenant is a sexual offender required to register, have reason to believe the tenant is not complying with the registration rules and, intending to help the offender elude law enforcement, you withhold information from or do not notify the police, harbor or conceal the offender, or give officers false information. If a tenant's residence would violate the 1,000-foot rule, the tenant's continued occupancy is a crime by the tenant; take advice before relying on that alone as a ground to end the tenancy.

title: No Shutdown Rent Protection
bodyText: No Missouri statute delays rent, bars late fees or stops an eviction for a federal, state or other government employee or contractor who goes unpaid during a government shutdown or furlough. Rent is due as your lease says, and the usual rules apply: in a rent-and-possession case the tenant can still stop the case by paying all rent in arrears and costs on the judgment date. Missouri also forbids counties, cities and other local governments to impose or enforce a moratorium on eviction cases unless state law specifically authorizes it, so a local shutdown relief rule cannot halt evictions. You may agree with an affected tenant to a payment plan or a delay; put any agreement in writing.

title: No Special District Statement
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires a lease to state that the property lies in a special taxing, improvement or development district, such as a community improvement district, transportation development district or neighborhood improvement district, or requires you to tell a tenant about district charges or plans. The district statutes deal with how districts are formed and how their taxes are collected, not with leases. If a district charge affects what the tenant pays, for example through a utility or service charge you pass on, state the charge in the lease like any other charge.

title: Program Inspections in Subsidized Rentals
bodyText: No Missouri statute addresses housing program inspections of a rental, either as a reason a landlord may refuse a voucher tenancy or as a ground against a subsidized tenant who refuses an inspection. Missouri law does not protect a renter's source of income, and no county or city may enact, maintain or enforce an ordinance that bars a landlord from refusing to rent because the renter's income includes federal or other housing assistance, so declining a voucher because of the program's inspection is generally not a violation of state law. Two limits remain. If your multifamily project received additional subsidies from the Missouri Housing Development Commission, your agreement must bar you from refusing housing vouchers or Section 8 certificates in partial payment of rent and from discriminating against households that use them. And any refusal must not be a pretext for discrimination Missouri's fair housing law forbids, such as discrimination because of race, disability or familial status. Once you accept a voucher, the program's inspection and entry terms come from your federal or program contract; Missouri has no statute on landlord entry, so the lease's entry clause governs your own inspections.

title: No Subsidy Rent Proration Rule
bodyText: No Missouri statute reduces or prorates rent when part of a unit becomes uninhabitable, whether or not a housing subsidy pays part of the rent, and none says how a reduction would be split between the tenant's share and the subsidy payment. Missouri's only rent-relief rule for damage is for a residence destroyed by fire, a tornado or another natural or man-made disaster the tenant did not cause: the tenant then owes you no rent for the rest of the lease term. That rule speaks only of the tenant's liability; what happens to the subsidy payment is governed by your housing assistance contract. For partial damage, your lease's fire or casualty clause and your subsidy contract decide whether rent is reduced. Missouri's limited repair-and-deduct remedy caps a deduction at the greater of $300 or half the periodic rent, but not more than one month's rent, and does not say whether periodic rent means the full contract rent or only the tenant's share; the cautious course is to assume the full contract rent.

title: Tenant Information and Privacy
bodyText: No Missouri statute bars a landlord from disclosing information about a tenant or applicant, or says what consent is needed before you share it. Two general Missouri laws still reach the information you collect. First, if you own or license computerized personal information of Missouri residents, such as a name together with a Social Security number, driver's license number, financial account number with its access code, or medical or health insurance information, and there is a breach of security, you must notify the affected people without unreasonable delay, with the content the law requires; if you notify more than 1,000 people at once you must also notify the Attorney General and the nationwide consumer reporting agencies. Notice is not required if, after an appropriate investigation, you determine in writing that identity theft or fraud is not reasonably likely, and you keep that determination for five years. Second, you may not publicly post or display anyone's Social Security number, or require a tenant to send it over the internet unless the connection is secure or the number is encrypted. If a real estate licensee represents you, the licensee has its own statutory duties not to disclose a client's confidential information. Beyond these rules, the cautious course is to share tenant information only to run the tenancy, as the law requires, or with the tenant's written consent. Domestic violence information has its own row.

title: Housing Your Employees
bodyText: Missouri has one statute aimed at housing you provide to an employee. When premises are occupied incident to the terms of employment and the employee holds over after the employment ends, the employee commits unlawful detainer if, after a written demand for possession from you or your agent or attorney, the employee refuses or neglects to vacate. You then recover possession through an unlawful detainer case in court. Missouri does not require you to give an employee a signed statement of the conditions for occupying and vacating the housing, does not require you to offer a rental agreement when the job ends, and has no special exclusion that takes employee housing outside its landlord-tenant statutes. Whether an employee who pays rent under a separate lease is a tenant entitled to the ordinary notice to quit is decided by the arrangement and by the courts, so make the link to the job explicit in writing: the library offers an optional employee housing clause that states the occupancy is incident to the employment and ends with it. Never lock out a former employee or remove belongings without a court order; removing a tenant without judicial process and a court order (except under the abandonment procedure) is forcible entry and detainer, and the cautious course is to treat an employee occupant the same way.

title: No Rule on Claims Against Tenant Insurance
bodyText: No Missouri statute says whether you may require a tenant to make a claim on the tenant's own renters insurance, whether you may file a claim on the tenant's policy, or whether your insurer may pursue a tenant by subrogation. Requiring renters insurance in the lease is lawful, but the policy belongs to the tenant: any claim on it is the tenant's to make, so get the tenant's written agreement at the time before you rely on it. One old Missouri statute matters here. No action may be brought against a tenant or other person in whose house or apartment a fire accidentally begins, and that person owes no compensation for the damage, whatever the lease or custom says; and a tenant's general promise to repair does not oblige the tenant to rebuild after a fire not brought about by the procurement, connivance or neglect of the tenant or the tenant's agents or servants, unless the tenant specially agreed to rebuild after fire. So you, and your insurer standing in your place, generally cannot recover from a tenant for an accidental fire. For damage the tenant causes deliberately or negligently, see the tenant-caused damage rows.

title: Tenant Records and Data Security
bodyText: No Missouri statute requires you to keep a rent ledger, give a tenant a statement of payments and charges on request, put an account statement in a nonpayment notice, or keep tenant records for a set period. Keeping a dated ledger is still wise, because a rent-and-possession case requires a sworn statement of the amount of rent actually due. Missouri's data-breach law does reach landlords: if you own or license computerized personal information of Missouri residents, such as an applicant's name with a Social Security number, driver's license number, or bank or card account number with its access code, and that data is breached, you must notify the affected people without unreasonable delay, and the Attorney General and the nationwide consumer reporting agencies as well if you notify more than 1,000 people at once. Missouri does not require an ordinary landlord to adopt a written information security program; that mandate applies to insurance licensees. You may not publicly post or display a Social Security number or require a tenant to send it over an insecure internet connection. The cautious course is to collect only the data you need, keep it secured or encrypted, and destroy it securely when you no longer need it.

title: Barring People From the Property
bodyText: Missouri's trespass law can help you keep a non-resident who causes trouble off your property, but notice matters. A person commits first-degree trespass, a misdemeanor, by knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully in a building or on real property; for land (as opposed to a building) it applies only if the property is fenced or enclosed to keep intruders out, or notice against trespass was given by actually telling the person or by posting reasonably likely to come to intruders' attention. Purple paint marks on trees or posts that meet the statute's height and spacing rules count as such posting. Entering or remaining is unlawful only when the person is not licensed or privileged to be there, and a person who enters premises then open to the public is licensed unless the person defies a lawful order not to enter or remain personally communicated by the owner or another authorized person. So, to bar someone, tell the person in writing, in person if you can, that they may not enter the property, and keep a copy. Whether your notice overrides a tenant's invitation to that person as a guest of the tenant's own unit is not settled by statute, so do not rely on trespass alone against a tenant's guest inside the unit; the library offers an optional barred-person clause that makes admitting a barred person a lease violation instead. Never use a barring notice against a tenant's household member because that person is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, and apply any ban consistently to avoid fair housing problems. Second-degree trespass, entering unlawfully on another's land, is an infraction.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest that Missouri statutes do not use, so the rule about leases granted by a usufructuary does not arise in Missouri. The closest Missouri interest is a life estate, for example a surviving spouse who holds a home for life while the children own the remainder. Missouri's statutes on leases by a tenant for life deal only with rent: if a life tenant who has leased the property dies on a rent day, the life tenant's executor or administrator may recover the whole rent, and if the life tenant dies before the rent day, the proportion of rent that accrued before death. No Missouri statute says whether a lease signed by a life tenant ends when the life estate ends or binds the remainder owners; that is decided by Missouri courts. If you lease property you hold for life, the cautious course is to tell the tenant in the lease that you hold only a life estate, and to have the remainder owners sign the lease, or a written consent to it, if the lease is to run beyond your life. If you die or transfer the property during the term, your heirs, devisees, grantees or executors have the same unlawful detainer remedies against a tenant who holds over that you would have had.

title: No Veterans Rental Incentive
bodyText: No Missouri statute gives landlords a tax credit, grant, deposit guarantee or other incentive for renting to veterans, or pays veteran rental assistance to landlords. One Missouri rule does matter: although cities and counties may not bar landlords from refusing tenants because their rent is paid partly by housing assistance, they may enact and enforce ordinances that bar a landlord from discriminating against a tenant or applicant solely because the person receives veterans' benefits. Check your city or county ordinances before treating veterans' benefits differently from other income. Federal programs for veterans, such as housing vouchers for veterans, have their own rules, which are not covered here.

title: No Waterbed Rule
bodyText: No Missouri statute addresses waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture in rentals. Missouri law gives a tenant no right to keep one, does not bar you from refusing one, and sets no insurance, liner, floor-load or notice rule. Whether to allow a waterbed, and on what conditions, is a matter for your lease; the library offers an optional clause requiring your written consent, a proper frame and liner, an approved location and water-damage insurance. If you want money to secure against waterbed damage, it counts as part of the security deposit, so the total deposit, however labelled, may not exceed two months' rent, and any amount withheld at move-out is limited to restoring the unit, ordinary wear and tear excepted.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Missouri follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 400.3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 400.1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Missouri's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Mo. Rev. Stat. chs. 441 and 535 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Missouri's courts do is case law this library has not reviewed, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
